Season with the rest of the soy sauce and a pinch of white pepper. Ladle into bowls and top with scallion, the rest of the ginger, sesame seeds and a few drops of sesame oil.
Put the second portion in a shallow container within 2 hours, refrigerate and eat within 3 days. Reheat with a splash of water until it bubbles (74 °C).
tip: Leftover cooked rice is exactly what congee wants. Short on time? Simmer 20 minutes, then give it a few pulses with a stick blender for a smooth jook.

name: Sardines in tomato with garlicky bok choy and brown rice
inspiredBy: Vietnamese ca moi sot ca (sardines in tomato sauce)
about: Canned sardines warmed in a ginger and garlic tomato sauce, spooned over brown rice with garlicky bok choy, shredded carrot and cool cucumber. A quick Vietnamese-style lunch. **Sardines canned with their soft bones** are a top calcium food, and they bring vitamin D and omega-3 too.
steps: Reheat the rice with a splash of water, covered, until steaming hot (74 °C). Wash the bok choy, cucumber, carrot and scallion before cutting.
Toss the carrot with the vinegar and leave it to pickle while you cook.

Warm half the oil in a pan over medium heat. Soften the scallion whites, half the garlic and the ginger for 1 minute, then add the sardines with their tomato sauce and 3 tablespoons of water. Break the fish into big pieces and simmer gently 4 minutes, with a pinch of chili flakes.
In a second pan, heat the rest of the oil and the remaining garlic, add the bok choy cut-side down and cook 2 minutes. Add a splash of water, cover and steam 2 minutes, until tender.
Pile the rice in a bowl and top with the sardines, bok choy, cucumber and pickled carrot. Finish with the scallion greens.
tip: Open the can over the pan so none of the tomato sauce is lost. The little bones mash into the sauce, so you will not notice them.

name: Cold sesame udon with sardines, edamame, egg and cucumber
inspiredBy: Sichuan cold sesame noodles (liang mian), with udon and canned sardines
about: Chewy cold udon in a nutty tahini and vinegar sauce, piled with cucumber, edamame, ribbons of egg and flaked canned sardines, with a little chili for heat. Cool, filling and ready in 20 minutes. **Sardines canned with their soft bones** bring calcium and omega-3, and tahini and edamame add more calcium.
steps: Boil the edamame in water for 4 minutes until tender, drain and cool under cold water. Rinse the udon under cold water until chilled and loosened.
Beat the egg with a pinch of salt, pour into a non-stick pan over medium-low heat as a thin sheet, and cook until completely set, about 2 minutes. Roll it up and slice into ribbons.
Whisk the tahini with the soy sauce, vinegar, garlic, sugar and 2 to 3 tablespoons of warm water until smooth and pourable like cream.
Wash the cucumber and scallion, then cut the cucumber into matchsticks and slice the scallion. Drain the sardines and break them into chunks.
Toss the udon and edamame with most of the sauce. Pile into a bowl and top with the cucumber, egg, sardines, scallion and sesame seeds. Drizzle with the rest of the sauce and a pinch of chili flakes.
tip: Whisk a spoonful of warm water into the sauce if it seizes up. Tahini thickens at first, then loosens. Packing it? Keep the sauce separate and toss just before eating.
ingredients: canned in oil, with bones; drained

name: Braised pork and tofu with gai lan, over brown rice
inspiredBy: Sichuan home-style tofu (jiachang doufu), with the pork leading and gai lan
about: Ground pork and a few golden-seared slabs of tofu braised in a savoury, gently spicy sauce with ginger, garlic and crisp-tender gai lan (Chinese broccoli). Makes two portions, so tomorrow's lunch is done. **Gai lan** brings most of the calcium, with iron from the pork.
steps: Wash the gai lan and scallion, then cut the gai lan in 5 cm pieces, mincing the ginger, garlic and scallion whites. Pat the tofu dry.
Heat half the canola oil in a wide pan over medium-high heat and sear the tofu slabs until golden on both sides, about 6 minutes. Remove to a plate.

Add the rest of the oil, then the ginger, garlic, scallion whites and chili bean paste. Stir 30 seconds until fragrant, add the pork and stir-fry, breaking it up, until cooked through (71 °C) and no pink remains, about 4 minutes. Wash your hands after handling the raw pork.

Add 150 ml of water, the soy sauce and a pinch of salt. Return the tofu, add the gai lan stems and braise 3 minutes, then the leaves for 2 minutes more, until the gai lan is bright and crisp-tender and the sauce is reduced by half.
Finish with sesame oil and scallion greens. Reheat the rice until steaming (74 °C) and serve alongside.
Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch within 2 hours, refrigerate and reheat once until steaming hot (74 °C).
tip: Chili bean paste (doubanjiang) is salty, so no more soy sauce is needed. Find it at any Asian grocery; it keeps for months in the fridge.
ingredients: extra-lean, or finely chopped pork tenderloin
stems and leaves, cut in pieces

name: Ginger soy-glazed salmon with sesame bok choy and brown rice
inspiredBy: Japanese teriyaki, without the mirin
about: A seared salmon fillet glazed in a quick ginger soy sauce, beside bok choy cooked in the same pan and brown rice. Ready in 30 minutes. The **salmon brings omega-3 and vitamin D**, and the bok choy and sesame add calcium.
steps: Wash the bok choy, carrot and scallion. Reheat the rice with a splash of water, covered, until steaming hot (74 °C).
Stir the soy sauce, sugar, rice vinegar and ginger together in a small bowl with 2 tablespoons of water.

Pat the salmon dry. Heat half the oil in a non-stick pan over medium-high heat and sear the salmon skin-side down for 4 minutes, until the skin is crisp. Flip and cook 2 to 3 minutes more, until the thickest part reaches 70 °C. Wash your hands and board after handling the raw fish.
Pour the sauce around the fish and let it bubble and reduce to a glaze, about 1 minute, spooning it over. Lift the fish out onto a plate.

Wipe the pan, add the rest of the oil and the garlic, then the bok choy cut-side down and the carrot. Cook 2 minutes, add a splash of water and a pinch of salt, cover and steam 2 minutes until tender.
Serve the salmon and bok choy over the rice, scattered with sesame seeds and scallion.
tip: Fish cooks fast, so have everything else ready first. Frozen salmon is fine: thaw it in the fridge overnight and use within 2 days.

name: Lemongrass chicken and crispy tofu rice plate with fried egg and pickles
inspiredBy: Vietnamese com tam with lemongrass chicken, with brown rice and tofu
about: Charred lemongrass chicken and golden tofu over rice with a fried egg, tangy pickled carrot and daikon, and a sweet-sour dipping sauce, the way a Vietnamese rice plate is served. Makes two portions for tomorrow's lunch. **Tofu** adds calcium, and the egg adds choline.
steps: In a bowl, mix the chicken with the lemongrass, half the garlic, the soy sauce and a third of the sugar. Marinate in the fridge for at least 20 minutes. Discard any leftover marinade; do not reuse it. Wash your hands and board after the raw chicken.

Meanwhile, pickle the carrot and daikon: toss with half the vinegar, half of the remaining sugar and a splash of water, and leave 15 minutes. Make the dipping sauce by stirring the fish sauce, the rest of the vinegar and sugar, the rest of the garlic and 4 tablespoons of water, with chili flakes to taste.
Heat a third of the oil in a non-stick pan over medium-high heat and fry the tofu until golden on all sides, about 8 minutes. Remove it to a plate.
Add a third of the oil and cook the chicken until browned and cooked through (74 °C), 5 to 6 minutes.
Fry the egg in the rest of the oil until the white is set and the yolk is firm. Cook it fresh for each portion.
Reheat the rice until steaming (74 °C). Pile it on plates and top with the chicken, tofu, egg and pickles, with the dipping sauce on the side.

For the second portion, refrigerate the chicken and tofu within 2 hours (pickles and sauce separate), eat within 3 days, reheat to 74 °C, and fry a fresh egg tomorrow with the yolk cooked firm. Do not store a runny yolk.
tip: Short on time? Skip frying the tofu and eat it as soft cubes. It is still good with the sauce.

name: Korean braised mackerel with daikon and soybean sprout namul
inspiredBy: Korean godeungeo jorim (braised mackerel and radish)
about: Atlantic mackerel simmered with daikon in a soy and chili braise, with a bowl of sesame soybean sprouts and brown rice. It tastes even better the next day, so there is a portion for tomorrow's lunch. **Mackerel gives omega-3 and B12**, while the soybean sprouts and sesame add a little calcium.
steps: Wash the daikon, sprouts and scallion. Cut the daikon in thick half-moons and slice the scallion.
Make the sauce: stir the chili flakes, soy sauce, sugar, half the garlic and the ginger with 180 ml of water.
Lay the daikon in a wide pan, pour in the sauce and bring to a boil. Simmer covered 10 minutes, until the daikon is just tender.

Nestle in the mackerel. Spoon the sauce over, cover and simmer 8 minutes, until the fish is opaque and reaches 70 °C. Uncover, add the scallion and boil hard for about 5 minutes, spooning the sauce over the fish, until it coats the fish like a glaze. Wash your hands and board after the raw fish.

For the namul, cook the soybean sprouts in a covered pot with a splash of water for 6 minutes, keeping the lid on the whole time. Drain, then toss with the sesame oil, the rest of the garlic and the sesame seeds.
Reheat the rice until steaming (74 °C) and serve with the fish and namul. Put the second portion in a shallow container within 2 hours, eat within 3 days and reheat once until steaming hot (74 °C).
tip: Keep the lid on while the soybean sprouts cook: it keeps the nutty flavour and loses the raw bean taste.
ingredients: Atlantic mackerel fillet, cut in pieces

name: Soft tofu and shrimp stew (sundubu jjigae) with kimchi and egg
inspiredBy: Korean sundubu jjigae, with shrimp instead of clams
about: A bubbling red stew of silky soft tofu, shrimp, kimchi, shiitake, carrot and bok choy, with an egg cracked in at the end, served with brown rice. Makes two portions, so Saturday's lunch is ready. **Soft tofu, shrimp and bok choy** make it a protein-rich bowl with a little calcium.
steps: If the shrimp are frozen, thaw them overnight in the fridge and cook them within 2 days. Wash the bok choy, carrot, mushrooms and scallion before cutting, then chop the bok choy and slice the carrot, mushrooms and scallion.
In a heavy pot, warm the sesame oil over medium heat. Stir in the garlic, chili flakes and kimchi and cook 2 minutes, until fragrant and the kimchi has softened.
Pour in about 500 ml of water, add the soy sauce, carrot and shiitake, and bring to a boil. Simmer 5 minutes.
Add the soft tofu in big spoonfuls, the bok choy and the shrimp. Simmer gently for 4 to 5 minutes, until the shrimp are pink and opaque all the way through (70 °C).

Put half the stew in a shallow container for tomorrow, then crack the egg into the stew that is left in the pot, cover and simmer gently for 2 to 3 minutes, until the white is firm and the yolk has thickened. Top with scallion and serve with the reheated rice (74 °C). Wash your hands and board after the raw shrimp and egg.

Refrigerate the second portion within 2 hours and eat it within 2 days. Tomorrow, reheat it once until bubbling (74 °C), crack in a fresh egg and cook 2 minutes until the white is firm and the yolk has thickened.
tip: Look for soft or silken tofu in a tub or tube, ideally about 10% DV calcium on the label. Use a bit less chili flake for a milder bowl.

name: Whole-wheat pork, napa and tofu jiaozi with garlicky gai lan
inspiredBy: northern Chinese jiaozi, with whole-wheat wrappers
about: Hand-folded dumplings with whole-wheat wrappers, filled with juicy pork, napa cabbage, tofu and ginger, steamed and pan-seared, with a vinegar dip and garlicky gai lan on the side. The weekend project: dinner tonight and Sunday's lunch. **Napa, tofu and gai lan** add calcium, and a batch freezes well.
steps: Make the dough: stir the flour with about 55 to 60 ml of hot water per 100 g of flour, adding a spoonful more if it stays crumbly, until shaggy, then knead 8 minutes until smooth. Cover and rest 30 minutes.
Wash the napa, scallion, gai lan and mushrooms. Chop the napa very fine, toss with a pinch of salt and let it sit 10 minutes, then squeeze out the water in a clean towel.
Mix the pork, napa, tofu, ginger, scallion, shiitake, soy sauce and sesame oil by hand until sticky. Keep the filling covered in the fridge while you roll the wrappers.

Roll the dough into a log, cut it into small pieces and roll each into a thin 8 cm round. Put a spoonful of filling in each, then fold and pleat to seal. Set the finished dumplings on a floured tray, cover with a damp towel and keep them in the fridge until you cook them. Wash your hands and board after the raw pork.

Heat half the canola oil in a lidded non-stick pan over medium heat. Set in the dumplings flat side down, fry 2 minutes until golden, add 80 ml of water, cover and steam 8 minutes until the filling reaches 71 °C. Uncover and let the bottoms crisp.
While they steam, stir-fry the gai lan with the garlic in the rest of the oil for 4 minutes with a splash of water, until crisp-tender. Serve the dumplings with the vinegar dip.

Freeze any extra uncooked dumplings on a tray, then bag them, and cook from frozen with 3 minutes longer, until the centre reaches 71 °C. Refrigerate the cooked second portion within 2 hours and reheat once in a covered pan to 74 °C.
tip: No time to roll wrappers? Packaged round dumpling wrappers work: just check the label for dairy. Folding is better with a friend.

name: Chicken, tofu and napa nabe with sesame dipping sauce and udon
inspiredBy: Japanese nabemono, with a sesame dipping sauce (goma dare)
about: A one-pot Japanese hot pot of chicken, tofu, napa, shiitake and carrot in a light bonito broth, with a nutty sesame and soy dipping sauce and a nest of udon with a swirl of egg at the end. Cosy, light and quick to clean up. **Napa and tahini** bring some calcium, and the chicken and egg bring protein.
steps: Wash the napa, mushrooms, carrot and scallion. Cut the napa into big pieces and slice the scallion at an angle.
Whisk the tahini with the soy sauce, rice vinegar, sugar and 2 tablespoons of warm water for the dipping sauce.
In a wide pot, bring about 600 ml of water and the ginger to a simmer. Add the bonito flakes, steep 2 minutes, then strain them out. Add the carrot and napa stems and simmer 5 minutes.

Add the chicken, shiitake and tofu, and simmer gently for 8 minutes, until the chicken is cooked through (74 °C) and no pink remains. Add the napa leaves for the last 2 minutes. Wash your hands and board after the raw chicken.

Add the udon and scallion and warm for 2 minutes. Drizzle the beaten egg over the top, cover and simmer 1 minute until it is completely set. Ladle everything into a bowl with some broth and serve with the dipping sauce.
tip: Leftover broth makes a great starter for tomorrow: add a handful of cooked rice and a beaten egg for zosui.

name: Warm salted edamame
about: Warm green soybeans with a little sea salt, a very Japanese snack. **Edamame brings protein and fibre** and a little calcium.
steps: Boil the edamame in water for 4 minutes, until tender and bright green. Drain well.
Toss with a small pinch of salt and eat warm.

name: Iriko and walnut bokkeum
inspiredBy: Korean myeolchi hodu bokkeum
about: Tiny dried anchovies stir-fried crisp with walnuts in a sweet soy glaze, a classic Korean banchan. **The little fish are packed with calcium**, and the walnuts add omega-3.
steps: Toast the dried anchovies in a dry non-stick pan over medium heat for 2 minutes, until crisp and fragrant. Add the walnuts and toast 1 minute more.
Stir the soy sauce, sugar and 1 tablespoon of water into the pan and bubble 1 minute until it is a sticky glaze.
Stir in the sesame seeds and spread on a plate to cool. Make a double batch if you like: it keeps in a jar in the fridge for up to 1 week.
ingredients: small dried anchovies (myeolchi, iriko or niboshi); the tiny ones need no gutting

name: Mandarin and walnuts
about: A juicy mandarin with a small handful of walnuts. **Walnuts bring omega-3** and the mandarin brings vitamin C.
steps: Peel the mandarin and eat with the walnuts.

name: Mandarin and almonds
about: A juicy mandarin with a small handful of almonds. **Almonds bring vitamin E and a little calcium**, and the mandarin brings vitamin C.
steps: Peel the mandarin and eat with the almonds.

name: Steamed sweet potato with sesame
inspiredBy: Korean goguma and Japanese yaki-imo
about: Soft steamed sweet potato with toasted sesame, a favourite Korean and Japanese street snack. **Sweet potato brings vitamin A**, and the sesame adds a little calcium.
steps: Scrub the sweet potato and cut it into thick chunks. Steam for 15 minutes, until a knife slides in easily.
Sprinkle the toasted sesame over the warm sweet potato.

name: Warm walnut soy milk
inspiredBy: Chinese hetao doujiang (walnut soy milk)
about: Fortified soy milk whisked with ground walnuts and a touch of sugar, a Chinese comfort drink. **Walnuts add omega-3**, and the soy milk adds calcium.
steps: Grind the walnuts to a rough powder in a mortar or small grinder.
Warm the soy milk with the sugar until steaming, then whisk in the ground walnuts.
ingredients: plain, unsweetened, fortified; shake the carton well

name: Carrot and daikon sticks with sesame miso dip
inspiredBy: Japanese yasai sticks with miso
about: Crunchy carrot and daikon sticks with a little miso, sesame and rice vinegar to dip in, a Japanese yasai stick snack. **Carrot brings vitamin A**, and the sesame adds a little calcium.
steps: Wash and peel the carrot and daikon and cut them into sticks.
Stir the miso, sesame seeds, rice vinegar and a teaspoon of water into a thick dip, and serve with the sticks.

name: Sesame cucumber salad
inspiredBy: Korean oi muchim
about: Crisp cucumber in a sesame oil, vinegar and chili dressing, a cool Korean side (oi muchim). **Sesame adds a little calcium**, and the crunch is a good break from soft foods.
steps: Wash the cucumber and slice it thinly.
Toss with the sesame oil, vinegar, sesame seeds and chili flakes. Eat right away or chill 10 minutes.

name: Mayai na sukuma wiki, soft eggs with kale and sweet potato
inspiredBy: Kenyan sukuma wiki cooked with eggs, with sweet potato (viazi vitamu) instead of chapati
about: Soft eggs folded through onion, tomato and silky ribbons of kale, with sweet potato for something warm and a little sweet. It is a Kenyan home favourite and it is on the table in 15 minutes. The eggs bring **protein and choline**, and the kale adds vitamin K and calcium.
steps: Put the sweet potato chunks in a covered microwave dish with a splash of water and cook until a knife slides in easily, about 6 minutes. Or reheat sweet potato you roasted earlier in the week.
Meanwhile, roll the kale leaves up and slice them into thin ribbons. This is what makes sukuma wiki silky instead of chewy.
Warm the oil in a pan over medium heat. Cook the onion, garlic and jalapeno until the onion is soft and just golden at the edges, about 4 minutes.

Add the tomato and cook until it collapses into a thick sauce, about 3 minutes. Stir in the kale with a splash of water and half the salt, and cook until it is bright green and tender, about 3 minutes.
Beat the eggs with the rest of the salt and pour them over the greens. Stir gently until they are softly set and still glossy, about 1 minute.
Serve with the sweet potato.
tip: Sukuma wiki means "push the week" in Swahili, because greens stretch a budget. Collards work just as well as kale.

name: Millet uji with milk, ginger, banana and peanuts
inspiredBy: Kenyan and Tanzanian uji, the everyday millet porridge, cooked from whole millet and finished with milk
about: A creamy, spoonable millet porridge warmed with ginger and cardamom, topped with banana and a crunch of roasted peanuts. It is gentle, filling and sweet from the banana alone. Millet is a whole grain with plenty of **magnesium**, and the milk adds calcium and protein.
steps: The evening before you want it, rinse the millet and soak it in plenty of cold water for 30 minutes or longer. It is optional, but it shortens the cooking time.

Drain the millet and tip it into a pot with three times as much fresh water, the ginger and the salt. Bring to a boil, then simmer gently, stirring often, until the grains have burst, about 20 minutes.

Stir in the milk and cardamom and simmer for 8 more minutes, stirring, until the porridge is creamy and spoonable. For a smoother uji, give it a few pulses with a stick blender, or leave it a little rustic. This makes two portions.
Chill both portions. In the morning, warm one with a splash of milk or water, then top with the banana and peanuts. Reheat the second the next morning the same way.
tip: Cook it in the evening while dinner simmers, so breakfast is only a reheat. On Sunday, make the batch on Saturday while the doro wat simmers, and the spare keeps three days, so have it Monday instead of eggs. Sorghum works the same way and is just as traditional.

name: Ethiopian-style ful with egg, ayib and injera
inspiredBy: Ethiopian and Eritrean ful, spiced mashed fava beans, with fresh ayib-style cheese and injera for scooping
about: Mashed fava beans warmed with cumin, tomato, onion and a little jalapeno, finished with lemon, crumbly fresh cheese, a boiled egg and a spoon of spiced butter. You scoop it up with torn injera. It is a very filling start with **iron, folate and fibre** from the beans.
steps: Hard-boil the egg for 8 minutes, then cool, peel and halve it. Boil it the night before if you like.
Warm half the niter kibbeh in a pan over medium heat. Cook the onion, garlic and jalapeno with the cumin until the onion is soft, about 3 minutes.
Add the tomato and cook until it breaks down, about 3 minutes.
Tip in the beans with a splash of their liquid and the salt. Mash them roughly with the back of a spoon and simmer for 5 minutes, until thick but still spoonable.
Stir in the lemon juice. Spoon into a bowl and top with the egg, crumbled cottage cheese and cilantro.
Spoon the rest of the niter kibbeh, melted, over the top with a pinch of berbere. Eat with the torn injera, scooping up the beans with it.
tip: Drain the cottage cheese on a paper towel for a drier, more ayib-like crumble. Use plain oil in place of the niter kibbeh for a fasting-day version, without the egg and cheese.
ingredients: with a splash of the liquid saved
for the ayib, drained and crumbled

name: Azifa, cold green lentil salad with mustard, lemon and a little injera
inspiredBy: Ethiopian azifa, the tangy lentil salad of the fasting days, with tomato, cucumber, spinach and avocado added for crunch and freshness
about: A cold, punchy salad of tender green lentils, onion, jalapeno, tomato and cucumber on baby spinach, in a mustard and lemon dressing, with avocado and a little injera to scoop. It is the kind of lunch that tastes better after ten minutes in the fridge. The lentils bring **iron, folate and protein**, and the lemon helps you absorb the iron.
steps: Stir the mustard powder into a spoonful of cold water and leave it for 10 minutes. This is what gives azifa its sharp, clean heat.
Toss the onion and jalapeno with the lemon juice and half the salt, and leave them for 5 minutes. The acid softens their bite.
Stir the mustard paste and the oil into the onions to make a thick, tangy dressing.
Fold in the lentils and leave them to soak up the dressing while you chop the tomato and cucumber.
Pile the spinach on a plate and spoon the lentils over it. Add the tomato, cucumber and avocado, and scatter on the cilantro and the rest of the salt.
Serve with the torn injera for scooping.
tip: Cook dried green or brown lentils for 20 to 25 minutes if you prefer. Azifa keeps in the fridge for two days.
ingredients: canned or pre-cooked, drained and rinsed

name: Chicken mishkaki with roast potatoes and kachumbari
inspiredBy: Tanzanian and Kenyan mishkaki, the marinated grilled skewers of the street stall, here as an oven tray with chips-style potatoes
about: Juicy, charred chicken in a lemon, garlic and ginger marinade with a little heat, roasted alongside crisp-edged potatoes and served with a bright kachumbari of tomato, onion, cilantro and creamy avocado. The marinade does the work while you do something else. The chicken brings **protein, niacin and B6**, and the kachumbari brings vitamin C.
steps: Mix the garlic, ginger, paprika, cumin, cayenne, black pepper, half the oil and two thirds of the lemon juice into a paste. Toss the chicken in it and marinate for at least 30 minutes, or overnight in the fridge.
Heat the oven to 220 C (425 F). Toss the potato chunks with the rest of the oil and a pinch of the salt, spread them on a tray and roast for 15 minutes.

Push the potatoes to one side, add the chicken to the tray and roast everything for 12 to 13 minutes more, turning the chicken once. It is done when it is browned at the edges and no longer pink in the middle.
Make the kachumbari: toss the tomato, onion and cilantro with the rest of the lemon juice and salt, and let it sit while the tray finishes. Fold in the avocado just before serving.
Serve the chicken and potatoes with the kachumbari spooned alongside.
tip: Marinate it on Wednesday morning and roast the tray that evening with the sweet potato, then make the kachumbari fresh at lunch. Thread the chicken on skewers and grill it for the street-stall version. Beef liver on its own skewer is the classic mishkaki ya maini, if you like liver.

name: Shiro wot with tikil gomen and injera
inspiredBy: Ethiopian shiro and tikil gomen, the chickpea stew and the cabbage, carrot and potato dish served together
about: A velvety, berbere-spiced chickpea stew beside a mild, golden pan of cabbage, carrot and potato, scooped up with soft injera and a little ayib. It is the comfort food of Ethiopian home kitchens and it tastes even better the next day. Chickpeas and cabbage bring **protein, folate and fibre**, and teff injera adds iron.
steps: For the shiro, put most of the onion in a wide pot over medium heat with no oil and a splash of water. Cook, stirring, until it is soft and starting to stick, about 8 minutes. Add a splash more water if it catches.
Stir in three quarters of the niter kibbeh, the garlic, ginger, berbere and tomato paste. Cook for 3 minutes, until the paste is deep red and smells toasty.

Whisk the chickpea flour with cold water in a bowl until it is completely smooth, enough to make about four cups for two portions. Pour it into the pot slowly, stirring all the time so it does not lump.
Simmer gently for 15 minutes, stirring and scraping the bottom often, until it is thick and glossy like a loose porridge. Add a splash of water if it gets tight, and stir in half the salt.

While the shiro simmers, make the tikil gomen. Melt the rest of the niter kibbeh in a wide pan, cook the rest of the onion with the turmeric for 2 minutes, then add the potato, carrot and cabbage with a splash of water and the rest of the salt.
Cover and steam for 12 to 15 minutes, until the potato is tender and the cabbage is silky.

Serve the shiro and tikil gomen on the injera, with a spoonful of crumbled ayib (cottage cheese) on the side. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch, and warm the injera wrapped in foil or a damp cloth.
tip: For a fasting-day version, use oil for the niter kibbeh and skip the cheese. Shiro thickens as it sits, so loosen it with a splash of water when you reheat. An Ethiopian grocery sells ready-made shiro powder, which skips the chickpea flour and berbere steps.
ingredients: for the ayib, crumbled on the side

name: Samaki wa nazi, mackerel in tomato and coconut curry with plantain
inspiredBy: Swahili coast samaki wa nazi, usually kingfish in coconut sauce, with garam masala standing in for the local spice mix
about: Meaty mackerel simmered in a golden, tangy sauce of tomato, ginger, lemon and a little coconut milk, with kale and soft green plantain to soak it up. It is the flavour of Mombasa and Zanzibar in a single pan. The mackerel brings **omega-3, vitamin D and B12**, and the sauce keeps the coconut light.
steps: Score the plantain skin lengthwise, pry it off and slice the plantain into thick coins. Simmer in salted water until tender, about 20 minutes, then drain.
While it cooks, warm the oil in a wide pan and soften the onion for 4 minutes. Add the garlic, ginger, garam masala, turmeric and jalapeno and stir for 30 seconds, until fragrant.
Add the tomato and cook until it breaks down into a thick sauce, about 6 minutes.
Pour in the coconut milk with a splash of water and the salt, and bring to a gentle simmer for 5 minutes so the sauce stays thick and the coconut shows.
Nestle in the mackerel, skin side up. Cover and cook gently for 7 minutes, until the fish flakes easily. Spoon the sauce over it as it cooks.
Stir the kale into the sauce around the fish for the last 3 minutes so it wilts, then squeeze in the lemon juice, scatter on the cilantro and serve with the plantain.
tip: Kingfish or any firm fish works too, but mackerel is the one that brings the omega-3. Frozen mackerel from an Asian or African grocer is fine.
ingredients: fillets or steaks, cut in 4 pieces
sliced, or a pinch of cayenne
peeled and cut in thick coins

name: Githeri with beef, carrot, tomato and spinach
inspiredBy: Kenyan githeri, the dried maize and bean stew, with beef as many families add
about: A comforting pot of dried maize and kidney beans stewed with beef, onion, tomato and carrot, with spinach wilted in at the end. It is simple and honest and tastes even better the next day. The beans, beef and spinach bring **iron, zinc and folate**, and the tomato adds vitamin C to help you absorb it.
steps: The night before, cover the maize and beans with plenty of cold water and leave them to soak. This makes two portions.

Drain them, put them in a pressure cooker with fresh water to cover by 3 cm and cook for 45 minutes, then let the pressure drop naturally. Without a pressure cooker, simmer for 2½ to 3 hours, topping up the water.
While they cook, warm the oil in a wide pot over medium heat and brown the beef for 4 minutes. Add the onion, garlic and jalapeno and cook until the onion is soft and golden, about 5 minutes.
Add the carrot and tomato with a cup of water and the salt. Cover and simmer for 35 minutes, until the beef is tender.
Tip in the cooked maize and beans with a little of their cooking water. Simmer for 15 minutes, stirring now and then, mashing a few beans against the side of the pot, until the stew is thick.
Stir in the spinach and cook for 2 minutes, until it just wilts. Finish with the cilantro. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: Githeri keeps four days in the fridge and freezes well, so a double batch is no extra work. Leave the beef out for a vegetarian pot. Buy dried maize at an African grocer, or maiz mote in the Latin aisle.

name: Misir wot with gomen and injera
inspiredBy: Ethiopian misir wot, red lentils in berbere, and gomen, collard greens with garlic and ginger
about: Red lentils simmered into a thick, brick-red stew with slow-cooked onion and berbere, beside a pan of garlicky collards, all scooped up with injera. It is deeply savoury, a little fiery and very filling. The lentils and collards bring **iron, folate and calcium**, and a squeeze of lemon at the end helps you absorb them.
steps: Put most of the onion in a wide pot over medium heat with no oil and a splash of water. Cook, stirring, until soft and sticking, about 8 minutes. Add a splash more water if it catches.
Stir in the niter kibbeh, two thirds of the garlic and ginger, the berbere and tomato paste. Cook for 3 minutes, until deep red and toasty.

Add the lentils and plenty of water, enough to cover by about 3 cm for two portions. Simmer, stirring now and then and adding water if it dries out, until the lentils have collapsed into a thick stew, about 20 minutes. Stir in half the salt and the lemon juice.

For the gomen, warm the canola oil in a pan. Cook the rest of the onion with the jalapeno and the remaining garlic and ginger for 3 minutes, then add the collards, a splash of water and the rest of the salt.
Cover and cook for 12 minutes, stirring now and then, until the collards are tender and the water has cooked off.
Serve the misir wot and gomen on the injera. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: Berbere varies a lot in heat. Start with less and add more at the end. No injera nearby? Serve it with warm cooked teff or brown rice.

name: Beef and liver suqaar with collards, sorghum and basbaas
inspiredBy: Somali suqaar, small pieces of beef sauteed with onion and spices, with xawaash, a little liver as Somali cooks add and a fresh basbaas sauce
about: Tender small pieces of beef and a little beer (liver), quickly sauteed with onion, tomato, collard greens and warm xawaash spices, served over nutty sorghum with a zesty cilantro and lemon basbaas. It is a Somali home-kitchen staple and tastes even better the next day. The beef and liver bring **iron, zinc and B12**, and the sorghum adds fibre and magnesium.
steps: The evening before, while dinner is on, rinse the sorghum and soak it for 30 minutes. Drain it and cook it in fresh salted water until tender but still chewy, 25 minutes under pressure or about an hour simmering. Drain and chill. This makes two portions.
Toss the beef and liver with half the xawaash and a pinch of salt.
Heat half the oil in a wide pan over high heat. Sear the beef and liver in a single layer for 2 to 3 minutes, until browned, then scoop them out.
Add the rest of the oil and the onion, most of the garlic and half the jalapeno. Cook for 5 minutes, until soft and golden. Add the rest of the xawaash and cook for 30 seconds.
Add the tomato and the collards and cook for 6 minutes, until the collards are tender. Return the meat and cook for 3 more minutes, until the sauce clings.
For the basbaas, chop the rest of the jalapeno and garlic very finely and mix with the cilantro, lemon juice and a pinch of salt.
Warm the sorghum with a splash of water. Serve the suqaar over it with the basbaas. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch. Cooked sorghum keeps well for 4 days in the fridge.
tip: Serve it with rice or canjeero, the Somali pancake bread, if you cannot find sorghum. Goat or lamb are very traditional. Leave out the liver and use 40 g more beef if you prefer.
ingredients: sliced thin then cut in small pieces

name: Doro wat, slow-cooked chicken and egg stew with injera
inspiredBy: Ethiopian doro wat, the celebration stew of chicken and boiled eggs
about: A rich, deep red stew built on mountains of slowly cooked onion and berbere, with tender chicken and a soft boiled egg in each bowl, and a pan of garlicky collards on the side. It is the Ethiopian holiday dish and the best thing to cook on a slow Saturday. The chicken and egg bring **protein, B12 and choline**.
steps: Toss the chicken with the lemon juice and half the salt and leave it for 20 minutes or longer while you chop the onions.

Put the onions in a wide heavy pot over medium heat with no oil. Cook, stirring, for 30 to 40 minutes, until they have released their water and cooked down to a thick paste. Add a splash of water whenever they stick. This slow step is the whole dish.

Stir in the niter kibbeh, garlic, ginger, berbere and tomato paste. Cook for 10 minutes, stirring, until the colour deepens to burgundy and the stew looks glossy, adding a splash of water if it sticks.
Add the chicken, cardamom, pepper and about two cups of water for two portions. Cover and simmer for 35 minutes, stirring now and then, until the chicken is very tender and the sauce is thick.
While it simmers, hard-boil the eggs for 8 minutes, cool and peel them, and prick them all over with a fork so the sauce soaks in.
Slip the eggs into the stew for the last 10 minutes and add the rest of the salt. Taste and adjust.

In the last 15 minutes, wilt the collards in a covered pan with a splash of water, a pinch of salt and a spoonful of the stew sauce, stirring now and then, until tender. This is a quick gomen to serve beside the stew.
Serve the stew on the injera with the collards alongside. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch. It keeps for 3 days in the fridge and freezes well.
tip: Do not rush the onions. If you cannot find injera, serve it with brown rice or boiled potatoes.

name: Somali-spiced sardines with potatoes in tomato sauce
inspiredBy: Somali kalluun in tomato and onion sauce, with canned sardines for fresh fish and xawaash for the spice
about: Whole sardines warmed in a thick tomato, onion and jalapeno sauce with soft potatoes and a squeeze of lemon, with a crisp cucumber salad on the side. It is quick, bright and very savoury. The sardines bring **calcium, omega-3 and vitamin D**, and their soft bones are the calcium.
steps: Simmer the potato chunks in salted water until just tender, about 10 minutes. Drain.
Meanwhile, warm the oil in a wide pan and soften the onion with the garlic and jalapeno for 5 minutes. Stir in the xawaash for 30 seconds.
Add the tomato and cook until it breaks down into a thick, jammy sauce, about 7 minutes.
Stir in the potatoes with a splash of water and simmer for 4 minutes.
Lay the sardines on top and warm them through for 3 minutes without stirring, so they stay whole. Squeeze over half the lemon and scatter on the cilantro.
Toss the cucumber with the rest of the lemon juice and a pinch of salt, and serve it on the side.
tip: Fresh sardines or mackerel work beautifully if you can get them. Drop them into the sauce raw and cook for 8 minutes.
ingredients: canned in oil, drained, bones in

name: Mango with lemon and a pinch of chili
about: Ripe mango with a squeeze of lemon and a pinch of chili, the way street sellers serve it from Mombasa to Dar es Salaam. It is sweet, sour and a little hot. Mango brings **vitamin C and vitamin A**.
steps: Cube the mango and toss it with the lemon juice, chili and salt.

name: Kolo-style roasted chickpea and peanut mix
inspiredBy: Ethiopian kolo, the roasted snack mix of grains and pulses, with chickpeas and pumpkin seeds
about: Crunchy roasted chickpeas tossed with peanuts, pumpkin seeds and a pinch of chili. It is salty, nutty and keeps you going. The seeds and chickpeas bring **magnesium, zinc and vitamin E**.
steps: Heat the oven to 200 C (400 F). Pat the chickpeas very dry and toss them with the oil, chili and salt.
Roast on a tray for 20 to 25 minutes, shaking once, until crisp. Add the peanuts and pumpkin seeds for the last 5 minutes.
Let it cool on the tray, where it keeps getting crisper. Then keep it in an airtight jar for up to 5 days.
tip: Make a double batch; it stays crisp in a jar for three days.

name: Nifro, warm chickpeas with mitmita and lemon
inspiredBy: Ethiopian nifro, boiled pulses shared at home with coffee
about: Warm chickpeas tossed with fiery mitmita, salt and lemon, the way Ethiopian families share them with coffee. They are tangy, hot and very filling. Chickpeas bring **protein, folate and magnesium**.
steps: Warm the chickpeas in a small pot with a splash of water for 3 minutes.
Drain, then toss with the mitmita, salt and lemon juice. Eat warm.
tip: Mitmita is hot. Use half for a milder bowl, or berbere if you cannot find it.

name: Ayib with tomato and a little injera
inspiredBy: Ethiopian ayib, the mild fresh cheese, with cottage cheese standing in, served with tomato and a squeeze of lemon
about: Fresh, mild cottage cheese with juicy tomato, lemon and a pinch of mitmita, scooped up with a little torn injera. It is cool, creamy and tangy. The cheese brings **protein**, with a little calcium.
steps: Spoon the cottage cheese into a bowl and top with the tomato, lemon juice and a pinch of mitmita.
Eat with the torn injera.

name: Banana with roasted peanuts
about: A ripe banana with a handful of roasted peanuts. It is simple and filling. The banana brings **potassium and vitamin B6**.
steps: Slice the banana and eat it with the peanuts.

name: Parachichi kachumbari, avocado with tomato, onion and lemon
inspiredBy: Kenyan kachumbari, the fresh tomato and onion salad, with avocado
about: Creamy avocado tossed with tomato, onion, cilantro and lemon, the cooling side dish of every Kenyan barbecue turned into a snack. It is fresh, rich and light. The avocado brings **vitamin E and potassium**.
steps: Toss the onion with the lemon juice and salt and leave for 5 minutes to soften.
Add the tomato, avocado and cilantro, and fold gently.

name: Sardines with cucumber, lemon and chili on injera
inspiredBy: A quick tinned-fish plate, the way sardines are eaten with injera or bread across the Horn
about: A tin of sardines on torn injera with crisp cucumber, lemon and a little jalapeno. It is quick, salty and bright. The soft sardine bones bring **calcium**, and the fish brings omega-3 and vitamin D.
steps: Lay the injera on a plate and top with the sardines.
Scatter on the cucumber and jalapeno, and squeeze over the lemon.
ingredients: canned in oil, drained, bones in

name: Viazi vitamu choma, roasted sweet potato with lemon and chili
inspiredBy: Kenyan roadside roasted sweet potato
about: Sweet potato roasted until the edges caramelize, with lemon and a pinch of chili. It is the street-corner snack of Nairobi and it is sweet, smoky and filling. Sweet potato brings **vitamin A and potassium**.
steps: Heat the oven to 220 C (425 F). Cut the sweet potato into thick wedges and roast for 25 minutes, turning once, until soft inside and browned at the edges.
Squeeze over the lemon and sprinkle with chili and salt.

name: Karanga, roasted peanuts with lemon and chili
inspiredBy: East African karanga, the spiced roasted peanuts sold in paper cones
about: Roasted peanuts tossed with a squeeze of lemon, a pinch of chili and salt. They are salty, crunchy and satisfying. Peanuts bring **vitamin E, magnesium and protein**.
steps: Toss the warm peanuts with the lemon juice, chili and salt.
Eat right away while they are still crunchy.

name: Ndizi choma, roasted plantain with lemon and chili
inspiredBy: Swahili coast ndizi choma, roasted plantain
about: Plantain roasted until the edges caramelize, with lemon and a pinch of chili. It is sweet, smoky and filling, and the kind of thing sold on the roadside in Tanzania. Plantain brings **potassium and fibre**.
steps: Heat the oven to 220 C (425 F). Peel the plantain and cut it into thick coins or long wedges.
Roast on a tray for 25 minutes, turning once, until soft inside and browned at the edges. Squeeze over the lemon and sprinkle with the chili and salt.

name: Maziwa moto, warm spiced milk with cardamom and ginger
inspiredBy: Swahili and Somali spiced milk, drunk hot in the evening
about: Milk warmed with cardamom and a little fresh ginger until it smells like a Mombasa kitchen. It is soothing and a little sweet on its own. The milk brings **calcium and protein**.
steps: Warm the milk in a small pot with the cardamom and the sliced ginger until it steams, about 5 minutes.
Strain into a mug and sip it hot.

name: Kasha with mushrooms and a fried egg
inspiredBy: Ukrainian and Polish buckwheat with mushrooms (hrechka z hrybamy, kasza gryczana z grzybami)
about: Toasty buckwheat kasha folded through browned mushrooms and onion, with a fried egg on top and a crunchy dill pickle on the side. It is the breakfast of a thousand Ukrainian and Polish kitchens. The egg and mushrooms bring **protein, choline and B vitamins**, and the buckwheat adds magnesium.
steps: Tip the kasha into a small pot with twice its volume of boiling water and a pinch of salt. Cover and simmer very gently until the water is absorbed, about 12 minutes, then take it off the heat and keep the lid on.

While it cooks, cover the dried porcini with a few spoonfuls of hot water and leave them for 10 minutes. Warm half the rapeseed oil in a wide pan over medium-high heat. Cook the onion for 3 minutes, then add the fresh mushrooms in a single layer. Leave them alone for a few minutes so they brown, then add the chopped porcini and their soaking liquid and keep going until it has cooked off, about 8 minutes. Season with salt and pepper.
Fluff the kasha with a fork and fold it into the mushrooms with half the dill.
Push the kasha to one side, add the rest of the rapeseed oil and fry the egg until the white is set and the yolk is still runny, about 3 minutes.

Toast the sunflower seeds in a dry pan for 2 minutes, until golden. Drizzle the kasha with the sunflower oil, which gives it that nutty, toasted-seed flavour. Serve with the egg on top, scattered with the seeds and the rest of the dill, with the pickle on the side for a sharp, crunchy bite.
tip: Cook a double batch of kasha the night before. It warms through in the pan in two minutes, which makes this about a 15-minute breakfast.
ingredients: dried porcini (soaked in hot water for 10 minutes, then chopped, with the soaking liquid kept)

name: Kefir with soaked buckwheat, apple and raspberries
inspiredBy: Ukrainian and Polish kefir with soaked buckwheat (hrechka z kefirom, kasza gryczana z kefirem)
about: Toasted buckwheat groats soaked overnight in cold kefir until they turn tender and nutty, then topped with grated apple, raspberries, toasted sunflower seeds and a sprinkle of poppy seeds. It is a classic cool, sour-sweet breakfast across Ukraine and Poland. The kefir and poppy seeds bring **calcium**, and the sunflower seeds add **vitamin E**.
steps: The night before, rinse the buckwheat in a sieve and stir it into the kefir in a jar or bowl with a pinch of cinnamon. Cover and refrigerate for at least 10 hours, until the groats are tender with a little nutty chew.
In the morning, toast the sunflower seeds in a dry pan for 2 minutes, until golden and fragrant.
Grate the apple straight into the bowl and stir it through.
Top with the raspberries, the warm sunflower seeds and a sprinkle of poppy seeds.
tip: Use pear or whatever berries are in season.

name: Baked tvorog and oat syrniki with raspberries
inspiredBy: Ukrainian syrnyky and Polish placuszki z twarogu, baked and made with oats
about: Little golden tvorog cakes, bound with oats instead of flour and baked instead of fried, served with a spoonful of sour cream and crushed raspberries. It is a slow Saturday morning breakfast that makes the next morning's too. The tvorog and oats give you **protein, calcium and slow carbohydrate**.
steps: Heat the oven to 200 C and line a tray with parchment. Whizz the oats in a blender for a few seconds, until they look like a coarse flour.

Mash the tvorog with the egg, grated apple, cinnamon, lemon juice and salt until mostly smooth, then stir in the ground oats. Let the dough rest for 10 minutes so the oats swell and it firms up. If it is too soft to shape, spoon it onto the tray in rounds.
With wet hands, shape it into 8 small, thick rounds and set them on the tray. Brush the tops with half of the oil.
Bake for 12 minutes, flip them, brush with the rest of the oil and bake another 8 minutes, until golden and set.
While they bake, toast the sunflower seeds in a dry pan for 2 minutes. Crush half the raspberries with a fork to make a quick sauce and keep the rest whole.

Serve 4 syrniki per person with the raspberries, a spoonful of sour cream and a scatter of sunflower and poppy seeds. Keep the second portion in the fridge and warm it in the oven or a dry pan on Sunday morning.
tip: If the dough feels soft, chill it for 20 minutes before shaping. Frozen raspberries are fine.
ingredients: farmer's cheese. If you use cottage cheese, drain it in a sieve for 10 minutes first
rapeseed oil, for the tray and the tops

name: Open rye sandwiches with pickled herring, egg, onion and dill
inspiredBy: Polish and Baltic herring on rye (śledź na chlebie)
about: Dark rye topped with pickled herring, sliced egg, thin onion and dill, with a few slices of dill pickle on the side. It is the plate you would be served at a Polish or Baltic lunch table. The herring and egg bring **omega-3, vitamin D, B12 and choline**, and the rye keeps you full.
steps: Boil the egg for 9 minutes, cool it under cold water, then peel and slice it. Slice the onion very thin and rinse it under cold water for a minute to take off the sharpest bite. Drain the herring, pat it dry and cut it into bite-size pieces.
Lay the egg slices and the herring on the rye and scatter the onion rings on top.
Finish with dill and a grind of black pepper. Serve the pickle alongside for crunch and extra tang.
tip: If pickled herring is too salty for you, rinse the pieces for a minute and pat them dry. Rollmops work too, and a spoonful of sour cream is a lovely addition.

name: Ukrainian borscht with white beans and beef, with rye bread
inspiredBy: Ukrainian borscht with beans, as cooked in Kyiv and Chernihiv homes
about: A ruby-red Ukrainian borscht with beets, cabbage, carrot and white beans, built on a little beef and finished with garlic, dill and a spoonful of sour cream, with dark rye alongside. Frying the beets with tomato paste and vinegar first keeps their colour. It makes two portions and it is even better tomorrow, with **iron, folate and potassium** in every bowl, and half a boiled egg adds choline.
steps: Put the beef in a large pot with the bay leaf, allspice and a pinch of salt. Cover with cold water by about 3 cm, bring to a boil, skim off any foam and simmer gently, partly covered, for 40 minutes.

While the beef simmers, boil the egg for 9 minutes, cool it under cold water, then peel and halve it. Warm the oil in a wide pan over medium heat. Cook the onion until soft and golden, about 6 minutes. Add the carrot and beets, the tomato paste and half the vinegar and cook, stirring, until they have softened and the pan smells sweet and sharp, about 10 minutes.
Add the cabbage to the beef pot and simmer for 10 minutes.

Stir in the beet mixture and the beans and simmer 10 minutes more, until the cabbage is soft and the beef is falling apart. Stir in the rest of the salt and vinegar and taste: it should be pleasantly sweet and sour.
Stir in the garlic and half the dill. Ladle into bowls with half an egg each, a spoonful of sour cream and the rest of the dill, and serve with the rye.
Cool the second portion and pack it for tomorrow's lunch. Reheat it gently, since boiling hard dulls the colour.
tip: In a pressure cooker, simmer the beef for 15 minutes, then add everything else and cook 5 more.
ingredients: from a tin, drained and rinsed
half a hard-boiled egg per bowl, so one egg for two portions

name: Georgian lobio, red bean stew with walnuts and herbs, with warm cheese and lavash
inspiredBy: Georgian lobio, with canned beans and lavash for shoti and mchadi
about: Soft red kidney beans in a golden onion and garlic base, scented with khmeli-suneli and thickened with a paste of ground walnuts, cilantro and vinegar. Georgians eat it with a slice of soft sulguni cheese and flatbread. The beans, walnuts and cheese bring **iron, folate, calcium and plant omega-3**.
steps: Warm the oil in a pot over medium heat. Cook the onion until deeply golden, about 10 minutes, stirring now and then.
Add the garlic and khmeli-suneli and stir for a minute, until it smells fragrant.
Tip in the beans with a good splash of water and simmer for 10 minutes. Mash about a quarter of the beans against the side of the pot so the stew turns creamy.
Mix the walnuts with half the cilantro, the vinegar and a ladle of the bean liquid to make a rough paste. Stir it in and simmer 3 more minutes. Season with salt and pepper.
Lay tonight's cheese slices over the hot lobio for the last 2 minutes, lid on, until soft. Keep the rest of the cheese to warm over tomorrow's portion.
Finish the lobio with the rest of the cilantro and the pomegranate seeds. Serve with warm lavash.
Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch. It firms up in the fridge, so loosen it with a splash of water when you warm it.
tip: Georgians eat lobio with pickled vegetables too, and with a spoonful of adjika for heat. Sulguni is salty, so taste before you add more salt to the pot.

name: Gołąbki, Polish cabbage rolls with barley and pork in tomato sauce
inspiredBy: Polish gołąbki, with barley as in the old village version
about: Tender cabbage leaves rolled around lean pork, barley and onion, then braised in a tomato and dill sauce until sweet and soft. Barley, kasza jęczmienna, is the old village filling, with rice a later arrival. The cabbage and tomato bring **vitamin C and K**, and the barley adds slow fibre.
steps: Simmer the barley in salted water until just tender, about 30 minutes, then drain, keeping a few spoonfuls of the cooking water. While it cooks, cut out the core of the cabbage and put the whole head in a big pot of boiling water for a few minutes, peeling off the outer leaves as they soften.
Warm half the oil in a pan and cook the onion and carrot until soft, about 6 minutes. Cool for a few minutes.
Mix the pork, egg, barley, onion mixture, garlic, half the dill, the paprika, marjoram, salt, pepper and 3 tablespoons of the barley's cooking water with your hands, so the filling stays moist.
Shave down the thick rib on each cabbage leaf. Put a spoonful of filling at the base, fold in the sides and roll up tightly.

Shred the remaining cabbage into a wide oven dish or pot. Whisk the tomato paste with about 2 cups of hot water (for two portions) and the rest of the oil, season it with a pinch of salt, and pour about half over the cabbage. Set the rolls on top, seam side down, and pour over the rest.
Cover and bake at 180 C for 45 minutes, then uncover for the last 15 so the sauce thickens, until the cabbage is soft. Stir in the lemon juice and the rest of the dill.
Serve the rolls with plenty of sauce. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: Roll the cabbage on Tuesday night while the lobio simmers, then keep the rolls covered in the fridge and bake them on Wednesday. Freezing the whole cabbage head overnight and thawing it also makes the leaves peel off soft with no blanching.
ingredients: one small green cabbage, about 4 big outer leaves per portion, the rest shredded for the pot
one egg for two portions, to bind the filling

name: Chicken with kasha and mushrooms, with mizeria
inspiredBy: Polish and Ukrainian chicken with kasha and mushrooms, with Polish mizeria made lighter with kefir
about: Browned chicken thighs cooked on a bed of toasted kasha and mushrooms with plenty of dill, and a cool, tangy cucumber mizeria on the side. The kasha soaks up all the juices, so it is one pan with no rice or potatoes. The chicken and mushrooms bring **protein, niacin and B vitamins**, and the buckwheat adds magnesium.
steps: Season the chicken with half the salt, the pepper and the paprika. Warm the oil in a wide pan with a lid over medium-high heat and brown the thighs for about 4 minutes a side. Set them on a plate.

Meanwhile, cover the dried porcini with a few spoonfuls of hot water. In the same pan, cook the onion and fresh mushrooms until the mushrooms are browned, about 6 minutes, then add the chopped porcini and keep the soaking liquid. Add the garlic for the last minute.

Beat the egg in a bowl, stir in the kasha until every grain is coated, then push the mushrooms aside and toast it in the clear space for 2 minutes, stirring, until the grains separate and smell nutty. This is the old trick for fluffy, crumbly kasha. Pour in the porcini soaking liquid and enough hot water to make about 1¼ cups (300 ml) in all for both portions, roughly twice the volume of the kasha. Nestle the chicken on top, cover and simmer gently for 15 minutes without stirring, until the water is absorbed and the chicken is cooked through with no pink.
Scatter over half the dill and leave the pan covered, off the heat, for 5 minutes.
For the mizeria, toss the cucumber with a pinch of salt and let it sit for 10 minutes, then squeeze out the water. Stir in the kefir, lemon juice and the rest of the dill.
Serve the chicken and kasha with the mizeria on the side. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch, and dress its cucumber just before eating so it stays crisp.
tip: Do not stir once it is covered, or the grains go sticky. Slice and salt the cucumber for the second portion only on the day.
ingredients: one egg for two portions, to keep the kasha fluffy
dried porcini (soaked in hot water for 10 minutes, then chopped, with the soaking liquid kept)

name: Balkan white bean and sweet pepper stew with beef
inspiredBy: Serbian pasulj and Bosnian grah, with smoked paprika in place of smoked meat, and sweet pepper and spinach added
about: A thick Balkan-style white bean stew with sweet red pepper, carrot and tender beef, scented with smoked paprika and bay, and finished with a splash of vinegar and dill. It is honest, filling cold-weather food that you eat with rye bread and a pickle. The beans, spinach and peppers bring **iron, folate and vitamin C**.
steps: Warm the oil in a heavy pot over medium-high heat and brown the beef for 5 minutes. Take it out.
Lower the heat, add the onion, carrot and red pepper and cook until soft and sweet, about 8 minutes. Stir in the garlic and tomato paste for a minute.
Take the pot off the heat for a moment, stir in both paprikas and then return it to the heat. This keeps the paprika sweet instead of bitter.

Return the beef with the bay leaf, salt, pepper and enough water to just cover. Simmer, partly covered, for 40 minutes, then add the beans and simmer 20 minutes more, until the beef is tender and the stew is thick. Mash a few beans against the pot to thicken it.
Stir in the spinach, vinegar and dill and cook for 2 minutes, until the spinach wilts. Serve with rye bread and sliced pickle.
Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch. It tastes even better after a night in the fridge.
tip: A pressure cooker does the beef in 25 minutes. With dried beans (soaked overnight) the broth gets thicker, so use about a third of a cup of dry beans per portion.
ingredients: from a tin, drained and rinsed

name: Satsivi, Georgian chicken in walnut sauce, with cucumber and herb salad
inspiredBy: Georgian satsivi, with chicken thighs and a lighter sauce
about: Poached chicken under a rich, silky sauce of ground walnuts, garlic, onion and warm spices, traditionally served at room temperature at feasts. The sauce is thickened only by walnuts, with a splash of vinegar for sparkle. The chicken and walnuts bring **protein, plant omega-3 and magnesium**, and it gets better as it sits.
steps: Put the chicken in a pot with the halved onion, the bay leaf, a pinch of salt and enough water to cover. Bring to a gentle simmer and cook for 25 minutes, until cooked through. Leave it in the broth for 10 minutes, then lift it out.
Warm the oil in a small pan and cook the chopped onion until golden, about 8 minutes. Stir in the khmeli-suneli, coriander, cinnamon, turmeric and clove for a minute, until fragrant.

Grind the walnuts and garlic in a food processor to a fine paste. Add the onion and spices, then slowly blend in about a cup of the warm broth (for two portions) until the sauce is the thickness of heavy cream. Stir in most of the vinegar and season.
Warm the sauce in a small pot for 5 minutes. Do not let it boil, or it can split and turn bitter.
Slice or shred the chicken, spoon over the sauce and leave it for 20 minutes so the flavours settle. Garnish with the pomegranate seeds and half the cilantro.
Toss the cucumber with the rest of the cilantro, a pinch of salt and a splash of vinegar. Serve alongside the chicken, with lavash for scooping.
Pack the second portion for tomorrow. It is best at room temperature, and the sauce thickens in the fridge, so loosen it with a spoonful of water.
tip: Georgian cooks often add a pinch of dried marigold petals (Imeretian saffron) and a little blue fenugreek (utskho suneli). If you can find them at a Georgian or Eastern European shop, they are worth a try.
ingredients: half in two pieces for the pot, the rest finely chopped

name: Baked trout with dill potatoes and sauerkraut salad
inspiredBy: Baltic and Carpathian baked trout with dill potatoes
about: A plump trout fillet baked with garlic and lemon, served with hot potatoes tossed in butter and dill, with a glass of cold kefir alongside, and a crunchy sauerkraut and carrot salad. It is the simple supper of the Carpathians and the Baltics. The trout brings **omega-3, vitamin D and B12**, and the sauerkraut adds a tangy crunch.
steps: Heat the oven to 200 C. Put the potatoes in a pot of cold salted water with a few dill stems, bring to a boil and cook until tender, about 15 minutes.
While they cook, make the salad. Squeeze the sauerkraut dry (rinse it first if it is very sour) and mix with the carrot and onion. Drizzle with the sunflower oil and a grind of pepper.

Set the trout skin-side down on a piece of parchment on a tray. Scatter over the garlic, lemon juice, a pinch of salt and half the butter in small pieces. Bake for 12 to 15 minutes, until the flesh turns opaque and flakes with a fork.
Drain the potatoes and toss them with the rest of the butter and most of the dill. Serve the cold kefir in a glass alongside, or pour some over, the way Polish cooks eat new potatoes with dill.
Serve the trout on the potatoes with the sauerkraut salad and the rest of the dill.
tip: Salmon or mackerel fillets work the same way. A whole gutted trout takes about 25 minutes.
ingredients: scrubbed, halved or quartered so the pieces match
cold, to serve with the potatoes
chopped, plus a few stems for the pot
unrefined sunflower oil, to drizzle on the salad

name: Spinach pkhali with pomegranate and lavash
inspiredBy: Georgian spinach pkhali
about: Georgian spinach and walnut pâté, bright with garlic, cilantro and a little vinegar, shaped into small balls and topped with ruby pomegranate seeds. Scoop it up with warm flatbread. The spinach and walnuts bring **folate, iron and vitamin K**.
steps: Drop the spinach into boiling water for 1 minute, then cool it under cold water and squeeze out as much water as you can with your hands. Chop it finely.
Pound or blitz the walnuts with the garlic and salt to a thick paste.
Mix the spinach with the walnut paste, cilantro, vinegar and khmeli-suneli. Taste for salt and a little more vinegar.
Shape into 4 small balls, top with the pomegranate seeds and serve with warm lavash.
tip: Make it a day ahead if you like: the flavours settle, and it keeps 3 days in the fridge. Beets, cabbage and green beans make good pkhali too.

name: Apple with toasted sunflower seeds
about: Crisp apple wedges with a handful of warm, toasted sunflower seeds, the semechki that Ukrainians crack and munch all year round. The seeds bring **vitamin E and magnesium**.
steps: Toast the sunflower seeds in a dry pan for 2 to 3 minutes, until golden and fragrant. Eat them with the apple wedges.

name: Smoked sprats on rye with dill pickle and lemon
inspiredBy: Baltic and Ukrainian smoked sprats on rye (shproty na chornomu khlibi)
about: Smoked sprats from the tin laid on a slice of dark rye with sliced dill pickle, fresh dill and a squeeze of lemon, the classic Baltic and Ukrainian zakuska. Sprats are eaten whole, bones and all, so they bring **omega-3 and calcium**.
steps: Lay the sprats on the rye. Top with the pickle slices and dill, squeeze over the lemon and finish with black pepper.

name: Tvorog with dill and cucumber on rye
inspiredBy: Polish twarożek with dill and cucumber on rye (twarożek z koperkiem i ogórkiem)
about: Fresh tvorog mixed with chopped dill and cucumber and spread on dark rye, a Polish twaróg sandwich that makes a good afternoon snack. The tvorog brings **protein, calcium and B12**.
steps: Mix the tvorog with the cucumber, dill, lemon juice and pepper. Spread it on the rye.

name: Kefir with raspberries
about: A glass of cold kefir with crushed raspberries and a pinch of cinnamon, a classic Slavic afternoon drink. The kefir brings **calcium and B12**.
steps: Pour the kefir into a glass or bowl, crush half the raspberries into it and top with the rest, with a pinch of cinnamon.

name: Baked apple with walnuts and honey
inspiredBy: Polish and Ukrainian baked apples (pieczone jabłka)
about: A soft baked apple filled with chopped walnuts and cinnamon, a cosy Polish and Ukrainian winter treat. The apple adds fibre and the walnuts bring **plant omega-3**.
steps: Heat the oven to 190 C. Core the apple, leaving the bottom intact, and stand it in a small dish.
Mix the walnuts with the cinnamon and spoon them into the apple. Add a splash of water to the dish.
Bake for 25 minutes, until the apple is soft and the skin starts to wrinkle.

name: Chicken liver pâté on rye with pickle
inspiredBy: Polish and Ukrainian chicken liver pâté (pasta z wątróbki, pechinkovyi pashtet)
about: Chicken livers cooked with plenty of onion until just done, mashed into a rough pâté and piled on dark rye with a slice of dill pickle. It is a Polish and Ukrainian classic that tastes like home. A little liver goes a long way: it brings **iron, B12, folate and choline** in one small snack.
steps: Melt the butter with the rapeseed oil in a small pan over medium heat and cook the onion until soft and golden, about 5 minutes.
Add the liver and marjoram and cook, stirring, until the liver is browned outside and just cooked through with no pink inside, about 5 minutes. Season with salt and pepper.
Mash with a fork, or pulse a few times, to a rough pâté. Spread it on the rye and top with the pickle.
tip: Once a week is plenty of liver.

name: Tvorog with apple and poppy seeds
inspiredBy: Polish and Ukrainian twaróg and poppy seed sweets (twaróg z makiem)
about: Fresh tvorog with grated apple, a pinch of cinnamon and a spoonful of poppy seeds, a Polish and Ukrainian sweet snack that tastes like a cheesecake. The tvorog brings **protein and calcium** and the poppy seeds add a little extra **calcium**.
steps: Spoon the tvorog into a bowl and grate the apple over it. Stir in the cinnamon and let it sit for 5 minutes so the apple softens.
Sprinkle over the poppy seeds and eat right away.

name: Baked apple with poppy seeds and cinnamon
inspiredBy: Polish and Ukrainian baked apples with poppy seeds (pieczone jabłka z makiem)
about: A soft baked apple filled with poppy seeds and cinnamon, a Polish and Ukrainian winter treat that tastes a bit like makowiec. The apple adds fibre and the poppy seeds add a little **calcium**.
steps: Heat the oven to 180 C. Core the apple, leaving the bottom intact, and stand it in a small dish.
Mix the poppy seeds with the cinnamon and spoon them into the apple. Add a splash of water to the dish.
Bake for 25 minutes, until the apple is soft and the skin starts to wrinkle.

name: Sauerkraut and carrot slaw
inspiredBy: Polish sauerkraut surówka (surówka z kapusty kiszonej)
about: A crisp, sharp Polish surówka of sauerkraut and grated carrot with a little sunflower oil. It cuts through a rich meal as well as it makes a snack. The sauerkraut brings **fibre and vitamin C**, and the carrot adds vitamin A.
steps: Squeeze the sauerkraut dry (rinse it first if it is very sour) and put it in a bowl.
Add the carrot and onion, then dress with the sunflower oil and a grind of pepper. Toss and eat right away, or chill it for 20 minutes.

name: Arepas with huevos pericos and black beans
inspiredBy: Colombian and Venezuelan arepas with huevos pericos, the everyday scramble of eggs, tomato and scallion
about: Golden corn arepas with a soft scramble of eggs, tomato, scallion and wilted spinach, warm black beans and a squeeze of lime. Arepas are made from precooked corn flour, so they are naturally gluten-free and cook in a dry pan. The eggs, beans and spinach bring **protein, choline, iron and folate**, and the lime keeps it bright.
steps: Use black beans from your Sunday pot (see the plan notes), or canned beans at about three times the dry weight, drained and rinsed. Warm them with a splash of water.

Stir the masarepa with a pinch of the salt and enough warm water to make a soft dough, a bit firmer than play dough. Let it rest for 5 minutes, then shape it into two discs (one at the Light size) about 1.5 cm thick, pinching any cracks closed.

Cook the arepas in a dry nonstick or cast-iron pan over medium heat until they have a golden crust and sound hollow when tapped, about 7 minutes a side. Or brown them for 4 minutes a side and finish them in a 200°C (400°F) oven for 8 minutes.
While they cook, warm the oil in a second pan and soften the scallion for 2 minutes. Add the tomato and cook for about 4 minutes, until it turns jammy, then stir in the spinach until it wilts.
Beat the eggs with the rest of the salt, pour them in and stir gently until just set and still glossy, about 2 minutes. Stir in half the cilantro.
Split the arepas and fill them with the eggs, or serve them alongside. Add the beans, a squeeze of lime and the rest of the cilantro.
tip: Cook the arepas the night before and re-crisp them in a dry pan or toaster for 3 minutes, and breakfast takes 10. At the Light size, make one arepa. Check the label on the masarepa: it should say precooked corn, nothing else (buy a gluten-free line if you are celiac).
ingredients: precooked cornmeal for arepas, not masa harina

name: Tapioca crepes with queijo coalho, a fried egg and linhaça mango yogurt
inspiredBy: Brazilian tapioca, the cassava-starch crepe sold at breakfast stands in the northeast, with a fried egg and iogurte com linhaça (yogurt with ground flaxseed) on the side
about: A lacy, chewy crepe made from cassava starch, folded around golden queijo coalho that goes soft and spotty in the pan, with a fried egg alongside. Cool yogurt with mango and a spoon of ground flaxseed makes it a proper breakfast. It is **gluten-free by nature**, and the egg, cheese and yogurt bring protein, choline and calcium.
steps: Stir the tapioca starch and salt with just enough water to make it feel like damp sand that holds together when squeezed. Leave it for 10 minutes, then rub it through a sieve so it turns into fine, fluffy crumbs.
Heat a nonstick pan over medium heat. Scatter the crumbs in an even round about 18 cm wide, with no oil. After about a minute they fuse into a pale, lacy crepe.
Lay the coalho on one half, press lightly and let it soften for 1 to 2 minutes, until the cheese is spotty and the crepe is just set. Fold the crepe over and slide it onto a plate.
Fry the egg in the same pan, without oil, until the white is set and the yolk is still soft, about 2 minutes. Tuck it next to the crepe, or inside it, as many Brazilians do.
Stir the ground flaxseed into the yogurt, toss the mango with the lime juice and spoon it over the yogurt.
tip: Brazilian shops sell tapioca already hydrated (goma), which skips the first step. Or hydrate and sieve the starch the night before; it keeps in a sealed tub in the fridge, and breakfast takes 8 minutes. If you are celiac, buy the starch from a gluten-free line. Queijo coalho is sold at Brazilian shops, and halloumi grills the same way.
ingredients: ground flaxseed, stirred into the yogurt

name: Quinoa con leche with banana and cinnamon
inspiredBy: Peruvian quinua con leche, the warm breakfast quinoa simmered in milk with cinnamon and clove
about: Quinoa simmered slowly in milk with cinnamon and clove until creamy, sweetened with mashed banana and topped with a few slices. It is the kind of breakfast Lima sells in a cup on cold mornings. Quinoa and milk together bring **complete protein, magnesium and calcium**.
steps: Rinse the quinoa in a fine sieve under cold running water for a minute, until the water runs clear. This washes off the bitter coating.
Put the quinoa, milk, cinnamon, clove and salt in a pot (enough for both bowls) and bring it to a gentle simmer. A cinnamon stick, if you have one, is even better.
Cook uncovered on low heat for about 20 minutes, stirring now and then, until the grains have popped open and the porridge is creamy. Add a splash of milk or water if it gets too thick.
Mash half the banana into the pot for sweetness.
Spoon one portion into a bowl and slice half of the remaining banana on top.
Pack the second portion for tomorrow. It sets firm in the fridge, so loosen it with a splash of milk when you reheat it, and slice the last of the banana on top.
tip: Cook it on Wednesday evening while dinner is on, then reheat one bowl on Thursday and the other on Friday, about 3 minutes each. Stir in a spoon of raisins or a little honey if you like it sweeter.
ingredients: half mashed in, the rest sliced on top

name: Rice and black beans with garlicky couve, orange and grilled queijo coalho
inspiredBy: the Brazilian everyday plate of arroz e feijão with couve refogada, laranja and queijo coalho grelhado
about: Rice and black beans with thin ribbons of garlicky couve (kale or collards), sweet orange slices and squares of golden grilled queijo coalho. It is the Brazilian lunch plate found in every kitchen, and the orange is there to cut through the beans. The beans, greens and cheese bring **iron, folate and calcium**, and the orange helps you absorb the iron.
steps: Use a few spoons of leftover rice, or cook it fresh: rinse it and simmer it covered in twice its volume of water for about 15 minutes, then let it rest off the heat for 5. Use the beans from your Sunday pot (see the plan notes), or canned beans at about three times the dry weight, drained and rinsed, and warm them with a splash of water.
Soften the onion in half the oil for about 6 minutes, until soft and golden, then stir it through the beans.

In the same pan, warm the rest of the oil with the garlic for 30 seconds. Add the couve and toss over high heat for 2 to 3 minutes, until bright green and still a little crisp. Season with salt and the lime juice.
Slice the coalho into thick squares and cook in a dry nonstick pan over medium heat for 1 to 2 minutes a side, until golden and spotty.
Pile the rice and beans on a plate. Add the couve, cheese and orange.
tip: Queijo coalho is sold at Brazilian shops; halloumi grills the same way.
ingredients: cook it fresh, see the steps
couve: collard greens or kale, about half a bunch, stems out, rolled and sliced into thin ribbons

name: Caldo tlalpeño with chicken, chickpeas and chipotle
inspiredBy: Mexico City caldo tlalpeño, the smoky chicken and chickpea soup
about: A brothy, smoky Mexico City soup of shredded chicken, chickpeas and carrot in a tomato and chipotle broth, finished with avocado, cilantro and lime. The sauce is fried first, which is what gives it that sweet, deep red base. Chicken and chickpeas bring **protein, iron and folate**.
steps: Blend the tomato, chipotle, garlic, half the onion, the cumin and oregano with a splash of water until smooth.
Warm the oil in a pot, add the sauce and fry it for 5 minutes, stirring, until it darkens and thickens.

Add the chicken thigh, the carrot, the cilantro stems (chop the leaves for the end), the salt and enough water to cover by 3 cm. Simmer for 15 minutes, until the chicken is cooked through. Lift it out and shred it.
Add the chickpeas to the pot and simmer for 5 minutes. Return the chicken.
Ladle into a bowl and top with the rest of the onion, finely chopped, plus the avocado, cilantro and a squeeze of lime.
tip: Check the label on the canned chipotles and on any boxed broth you use. Half a chipotle gives a gentle heat; add a whole one if you like it hot.

name: Causa with sardines, egg and avocado
inspiredBy: causa limeña, the cold layered potato terrine from Lima, here with canned sardines and avocado in the middle
about: A cool, lime-bright layer of golden mashed potato spiked with ají amarillo, filled with mashed sardines and creamy avocado, and finished with sliced egg, tomato and cilantro. It is a Lima lunch staple and a lunchbox hero because it is served cold. The sardines bring **omega-3, calcium and vitamin B12**, and the potato brings potassium.
steps: Lower the egg into a pot of boiling water with the potato chunks. Boil for 10 minutes, then lift the egg into cold water. Keep the potatoes going until very tender, about 15 minutes in all. Drain them, and let them steam dry in the pot for a minute.
Mash the warm potatoes until smooth with the ají amarillo paste, most of the lime juice, the oil and a pinch of salt. You want a smooth, bright yellow dough. Chill it for 10 minutes.
Mash the sardines (bones and all, they melt in) with the avocado, the rest of the lime juice, the sliced scallion and a pinch of salt.
Press half the potato into a flat layer on a plate, spread the sardine and avocado filling over it and top with the rest of the potato, smoothing the surface.
Garnish with the sliced egg, tomato wedges and cilantro. Eat it cold or at room temperature.
tip: Boil the potatoes the night before and lunch is a 10 minute assembly. Canned tuna or chicken are the classic fillings, and both work here. Buy sardines in oil or water, not in a sauce, and check the label on the ají paste.
ingredients: canned in oil, drained, with the bones

name: Beef in hogao with black beans and baked maduros
inspiredBy: Colombian hogao, the tomato and scallion sofrito, over lean beef, with black beans in place of red, ripe plantain and avocado from the bandeja paisa plate
about: Lean ground beef simmered in hogao, the Colombian tomato and scallion base, with spinach wilted in, next to warm black beans, sweet caramelized baked plantain and a few slices of avocado. The sweet plantain with the savoury, tangy beef is the classic Colombian pairing. The beef, beans and spinach bring **iron, zinc and vitamin B12**.
steps: Heat the oven to 220°C (425°F). Peel the plantain and slice it on a long diagonal into thick pieces. Toss with a third of the oil and a pinch of salt and roast for 20 to 25 minutes, turning once, until soft and caramelized at the edges.
For the hogao, warm half the remaining oil in a pan and soften the scallion and garlic for 2 minutes. Add the tomato and cumin and cook for 8 minutes, until it turns jammy. Scoop out a third.

Use black beans from your Sunday pot (frozen, if you stashed a tub), or canned beans at about three times the dry weight, drained and rinsed. Warm them in a small pot with the scooped-out hogao and a splash of water.
Brown the beef in a pan with the rest of the oil for about 5 minutes, breaking it up. Stir in the rest of the hogao and the salt, and simmer for 5 minutes, then fold in the spinach until it wilts.
Serve the beef with the beans, maduros and avocado, with the cilantro and lime juice over everything.
tip: The plantain should be properly ripe, with a mostly black skin, for real sweetness.

name: Peruvian quinoa soup with beef and vegetables
inspiredBy: Peruvian sopa de quinua, the everyday Andean quinoa soup, with lean ground beef and greens for a fuller meal
about: A bright, herby soup of lean beef, potato, carrot and quinoa, finished with kale, peas, a fistful of cilantro and lime. It is an Andean home classic on cold evenings and it reheats beautifully. The quinoa and beef bring **protein, iron and zinc**, and the lime helps you absorb the iron.
steps: Warm the oil in a wide pot over medium heat. Cook the onion, garlic, ají amarillo paste and cumin until the onion is soft and sweet, about 5 minutes.
Add the beef and stir for 4 minutes, breaking it up, until it loses its raw colour. Add the carrot, potato, oregano and salt, then pour in enough water to cover everything by 3 cm.
