For the sambal, toast the shrimp paste in a dry pan for 1 minute, until crumbly and fragrant (open a window). Pound or blitz it with the chili, the tomato, the rest of the lime juice and the rest of the salt into a coarse sambal. Taste: it should be hot, salty and sour.

Heat a grill, grill pan or the broiler until very hot and brush with the oil. Cook the fish skin-side down for 4 to 5 minutes, until the skin blisters and crisps, then flip it for 3 to 4 minutes, until it just flakes with a fork.

Serve the fish with the rice, a spoonful of sambal, and the cucumber, raw long beans and Thai basil on the side. The raw vegetables and herbs (ulam) are meant to be eaten with the fish and sambal, a bite at a time.
tip: Spanish mackerel or sardines work too. On a barbecue, wrap the fish in a banana leaf for the real thing.
ingredients: fillets with the skin on, or a butterflied whole fish
about 1 lime, split between marinade and sambal
raw long beans, cut into 6 cm lengths

name: Ripe papaya
about: Sweet, soft ripe papaya eaten plain, the way it's enjoyed across the islands. It brings **vitamin C, vitamin A and folate**.
steps: Cut the papaya into chunks and eat it just as it is.
tip: A squeeze of lime helps if the papaya isn't very sweet.

name: Bubur kacang hijau, sweet mung beans in ginger coconut milk
inspiredBy: Indonesian bubur kacang hijau, lighter on coconut milk and sugar
about: Whole mung beans simmered until they burst, in a sweet, gingery coconut milk scented with pandan. It's a classic Indonesian snack that brings **fibre, folate and plant iron**, with only a spoon of coconut milk per bowl. The recipe makes 2 bowls.
steps: Soak about ½ cup (110 g) of mung beans overnight if you can. Put them in a pot with about 1¾ cups (440 ml) of water, the ginger and the pandan. Bring to a boil, then simmer gently for 35 minutes if soaked, or 50 minutes if not, until most of the beans have split and the mixture is thick. Top up with a splash of hot water if it thickens before the beans split.

Fish out the ginger and pandan. Stir in the palm sugar, the coconut milk and the salt, and simmer for 5 more minutes. Serve warm, and keep the second bowl in the fridge to reheat tomorrow with a splash of water.
tip: Not eating it tomorrow? Freeze the second bowl. It reheats well.

name: Rujak-style papaya with tamarind-chili dip
inspiredBy: Indonesian rujak buah
about: Sweet, soft papaya with a sweet, sour and hot tamarind dip, the Indonesian fruit salad called rujak. The papaya brings **vitamin C and folate**, and the tamarind and chili wake it right up.
steps: Stir the tamarind, palm sugar, sambal oelek and 1 tablespoon of warm water into a smooth dip.
Arrange the papaya on a plate and dip each piece.
ingredients: peeled, seeded and cut into chunks

name: Roasted peanuts with chili salt
about: A handful of unsalted roasted peanuts tossed with a pinch of salt and a little fresh chili, the kind of snack you'd find at any warung or sari-sari store. It brings **protein, vitamin E and magnesium**.
steps: Toss the peanuts with the chopped chili and salt, and eat them right away while they're still crunchy.

name: Tempe goreng, crisp tempeh with sambal kecap
inspiredBy: Indonesian tempe goreng
about: Thin slices of tempeh rubbed with garlic and coriander, pan-fried until crisp and golden, with a quick dip of sweet soy and fresh chili, a favourite Indonesian snack. Tempeh brings **plant protein, fibre and iron**.
steps: Crush the garlic with the salt and coriander, rub it over the slices and leave them 5 minutes.
Heat the oil in a non-stick pan over medium heat and fry the tempeh slices for 3 minutes per side, until golden and crisp.
Stir the kecap manis and chili together in a small dish and dip the tempeh in it.

name: Cucumber and tomato with sambal
about: Cool cucumber and ripe tomato with a spoon of sambal and a squeeze of lime, a fresh, lively snack you'd eat alongside almost any Malaysian or Indonesian meal. It adds **vitamin C and potassium** for very few calories.
steps: Stir the sambal and lime juice together. Dip the cucumber and tomato in it.

name: Steamed kalabasa with palm sugar and pandan
inspiredBy: Filipino and Indonesian steamed squash
about: Soft steamed squash mashed with a little palm sugar and a pinch of salt, scented with pandan, a comforting sweet snack in the Philippines and Indonesia. The squash brings **vitamin A and potassium**.
steps: Steam the squash with the pandan leaf for 12 to 15 minutes, until very soft.
Discard the pandan, then mash the squash lightly with the palm sugar and the salt, and eat it warm.
ingredients: kalabasa, peeled, seeded and cut into chunks

name: Boiled egg with chili vinegar
inspiredBy: Filipino sawsawan
about: A boiled egg dipped in cane vinegar with fresh chili and a pinch of salt, the sawsawan on every Filipino table. It gives you **protein and choline**.
steps: Lower the egg into simmering water for 8 minutes, then cool it under cold water and peel it.
Stir the vinegar, chili and salt together, halve the egg and dip it.

name: Blanched okra and tomato with sambal belacan
inspiredBy: Malay ulam with sambal belacan
about: Tender blanched okra and ripe tomato with a hot, tangy sambal belacan to dip in, the way a Malaysian table serves raw and blanched vegetables (ulam). It brings **fibre, vitamin C and vitamin K** for very few calories.
steps: Blanch the okra in boiling water for 3 minutes, until bright green and just tender, then drain.
Toast the shrimp paste in a dry pan for 1 minute, until crumbly and fragrant. Mash it with the chili and lime juice into a coarse sambal, then eat the okra and tomato dipped in it.

name: Blanched kangkong with sambal and lime
about: A big handful of blanched water spinach with a spoon of sambal and a squeeze of lime, a simple Malaysian and Filipino side that makes a fine snack. It's **rich in vitamin K and folate**, and very light.
steps: Blanch the kangkong stems in boiling water for 1 minute, then the leaves for 20 seconds, and drain well.
Stir the sambal and lime juice together and toss with the kangkong.
ingredients: water spinach, cut into 6 cm lengths

name: Ginataang kalabasa, squash simmered in coconut milk
inspiredBy: Filipino ginataang kalabasa
about: Soft squash simmered in a little coconut milk with garlic and ginger, a gentle Filipino merienda. The squash brings **vitamin A and potassium**, and the coconut milk is only a spoonful.
steps: Put the squash, coconut milk, garlic, ginger, salt and a splash of water in a small pot. Cover and simmer gently for 12 to 15 minutes, until the squash is very soft.
Mash a few pieces against the side of the pot to thicken the sauce, and eat it warm.
ingredients: kalabasa, peeled, seeded and cut into chunks

name: Japanese breakfast set: tofu and wakame miso soup, tamagoyaki and brown rice
inspiredBy: a classic Japanese asa-gohan breakfast, with brown rice and a walnut furikake on top
about: A proper Japanese morning: miso soup with tofu and wakame, a rolled omelette (tamagoyaki), warm brown rice under a sprinkle of toasted sesame, nori, bonito and walnuts, and a quick cucumber pickle. With rice from your batch it is about 15 minutes. The **eggs bring protein and choline**, and the soup is warm and easy on the stomach.
steps: Reheat a portion of your batch rice with a splash of water, covered, until steaming. A couple of minutes in the microwave is fine.
Slice the cucumber thinly and toss it with a few drops of the tamari and half the sesame seeds. Leave it to soften while you cook.

Bring about 220 ml (a scant cup) of water to a gentle simmer, add the bonito flakes and steep for 2 minutes, then strain them out and squeeze them dry. Add the wakame (a pinch swells into a lot) and the tofu to the broth, and simmer for 2 minutes.
Turn off the heat. Whisk the miso with a ladle of the broth until smooth, then stir it back in. Don't boil it once the miso is in, which keeps the flavour mellow. Sprinkle with half the scallion.

Start the eggs while the dashi steeps. Beat the eggs with the mirin, the rest of the tamari and the rest of the scallion, finely sliced. Warm the oil in a small non-stick pan over medium-low heat, pour in a thin layer of egg, and roll it up when it has just set. Push the roll to one side, pour in more egg under it, and roll again until the egg is used up.

Toast the squeezed bonito flakes in a dry pan with the chopped walnuts and the rest of the sesame seeds until the flakes are dry and crisp, about 2 minutes. Take the pan off the heat and crumble in the nori. Sprinkle over the rice, and serve with the sliced tamagoyaki, the soup and the pickle.
tip: Short on time? Scramble the eggs softly with the mirin and tamari instead of rolling them. Same flavour, half the fuss.

name: Korean banchan breakfast: soy-braised tofu, soybean sprouts, kimchi, fried egg and rice
inspiredBy: Korean dubu-jorim and kongnamul-muchim, set out the way a home breakfast table has a few small side dishes
about: Golden pan-seared tofu in a garlicky soy, gochujang and gochugaru glaze, with sesame soybean sprouts, a little kimchi, a crisp-edged fried egg and brown rice. The tofu and sprouts are made once and last two mornings, so each breakfast takes about 10 minutes. The **tofu and sprouts bring plant protein and folate**.
steps: The evening before, make the banchan for two mornings (cook double the amounts for 2 portions). Cut the tofu into slabs about 1 cm (½ inch) thick and pat them dry. Warm half the canola oil in a non-stick pan over medium heat and sear the tofu until golden, about 3 minutes a side.

Mince the garlic and scallion. Stir most of them into the tamari, gochujang, gochugaru and a splash of water, pour it over the tofu, and simmer, spooning the sauce over, until it is thick and glossy, about 3 minutes.
Boil the soybean sprouts, covered, in a little water for 5 minutes, until they no longer taste raw. Drain, and toss with the rest of the garlic and scallion, the sesame oil and the sesame seeds.
Cool the tofu and the sprouts and keep them in separate containers in the fridge. They keep for 3 days.
In the morning, reheat the rice and barley with a splash of water, and warm the tofu in the microwave or a small pan for a minute.
Fry the egg in the rest of the canola oil until the white is set and crisp at the edges and the yolk is still soft.
Serve the rice with the tofu and its sauce, the sprouts, the egg and the kimchi.
tip: The evening batch takes about 20 minutes once, and you get two quick mornings out of it.
ingredients: calcium-set, check the label for calcium sulfate

name: Dak-juk, Korean chicken and vegetable rice porridge with walnuts
inspiredBy: Korean dak-juk, made from cooked rice and barley, with walnuts on top like hodu-juk
about: A silky, gently savoury porridge of rice and barley with tender chicken, carrot and zucchini, finished with toasted sesame oil, nori, scallion and crunchy walnuts. It is slow weekend comfort food that makes two bowls, so Sunday's breakfast is already done. The **chicken and barley keep you full** for hours, and the walnuts add plant omega-3.
steps: Mince the ginger and garlic, dice the carrot and zucchini, slice the scallion, and cut the chicken into small pieces.
Warm half the sesame oil in a heavy pot over medium heat. Cook the chicken with the ginger and garlic until it turns white, about 3 minutes.
Add the carrot and the cooked rice and barley, and pour in water to cover the grains by about 3 cm (1 inch). That is roughly 3 parts water to 1 part cooked grain.

Bring to a boil, then simmer over low heat, stirring often and pressing some of the grains against the side of the pot, for about 20 minutes. Add water as it thickens, until the porridge is thick and creamy. Stir in the zucchini and tamari for the last 5 minutes.
Toast the walnuts in a dry pan for 2 minutes, then chop them roughly.

Ladle one portion into a bowl and finish with the sesame oil, scallion, walnuts and crumbled nori. Chill the second portion of porridge on its own, and keep its walnuts and nori separate so they stay crisp. Loosen it with a splash of water when you reheat it.
tip: A spoonful of kimchi on the side is very Korean, and wakes the porridge up.

name: Cold soba with chilled tofu and edamame, with a ginger dipping sauce
inspiredBy: Japanese zaru soba, turned into a fuller lunch bowl
about: Chilled buckwheat noodles with cool tofu, edamame and crisp cucumber, dunked in a light, gingery bonito and soy sauce and finished with shredded nori. It is fresh, filling and ready in about 20 minutes. The **tofu and edamame carry the protein**, and the buckwheat gives it a nutty flavour and a little extra fibre.
steps: Make the dipping sauce first so it can chill. Simmer about 60 ml (¼ cup) of water with the bonito flakes, tamari and mirin for 2 minutes, then strain. Stir in the vinegar and half the grated ginger, and cool it quickly in a bowl set over ice, or the night before in the fridge.
Boil the edamame for 3 to 4 minutes, drain and cool them under cold water.

Cook the soba in plenty of boiling water for the time on the package, usually 4 to 5 minutes. Drain, then rinse really well under cold running water, rubbing gently, until the noodles are chilled and no longer slippery.
Pile the noodles on a plate with the tofu, the cucumber cut into matchsticks and the edamame. Scatter over the sesame seeds, the sliced scallion and the nori cut into thin strips with scissors.
Serve with the sauce and the rest of the ginger for dunking.
tip: Stir a little hot noodle water into the leftover sauce and drink it at the end, the Japanese way.
ingredients: calcium-set, check the label for calcium sulfate, chilled, cubed

name: Tofu steak and onigiri bento with broccoli goma-ae and carrot-daikon pickle
inspiredBy: a Japanese bento of onigiri and kohaku namasu, with a soy-glazed tofu steak for the protein
about: Two small rice balls seasoned with bonito flakes and sesame, wrapped in crisp nori, with a sweet-soy tofu steak, broccoli in a sesame dressing and a bright carrot and daikon pickle. It is the lunchbox you can eat cold at your desk. The **tofu brings plant protein**, the broccoli adds vitamin C and folate, and the pickle adds crunch.
steps: The night before, make the tofu, the broccoli and the pickle. Peel the carrot and daikon and cut them into thin matchsticks. Toss with the vinegar and half the mirin, squeeze lightly, and leave to pickle.
In the morning, reheat the rice and barley until steaming hot. The barley makes it sticky enough to shape.

Pat the tofu dry and cut it into two slabs. Sear it in the oil over medium heat until golden, about 3 minutes a side. Add most of the tamari and most of the remaining mirin to the pan and turn the tofu in the sizzling glaze for a minute, until it is sticky and dark.

Cut the broccoli into small florets and boil for 2 minutes, then drain and cool under cold water. Toss with a few drops of the tamari, a drop of the mirin and half the sesame seeds, to make the goma-ae.

Stir the bonito flakes with the last of the tamari until damp, and mix them into the warm rice with the rest of the sesame seeds. Wet your hands and press the rice firmly into 2 triangles or balls, or press it in plastic wrap and twist.
Pack the onigiri with the tofu, broccoli and pickle, and keep the nori separate. Wrap each onigiri in a strip of nori just before eating so it stays crisp.
tip: Everything except the onigiri can be made the night before. Shape the rice in the morning and wrap the balls in plastic wrap.

name: Natto soba with grated daikon, scallion, nori and kimchi, with bok choy ohitashi
inspiredBy: Japanese natto soba, with kimchi for crunch and a simple ohitashi side
about: Cold buckwheat noodles topped with sticky, savoury natto, sharp grated daikon, scallion and nori, with a spoonful of kimchi for crunch and bok choy dressed in soy and sesame on the side. It is a fast, very Japanese lunch if you like natto. **Natto is rich in iron and fibre**, and the bok choy adds calcium.
steps: Simmer about 50 ml (3 tbsp) of water with the bonito flakes, half the tamari and the mirin for 2 minutes, then strain and cool it in the fridge or over ice. This is the noodle sauce.

Boil the bok choy for 1 to 2 minutes, until just tender and still bright green. Drain, cool under cold water, squeeze lightly and cut into chunks. Toss with a few drops of the tamari and the sesame seeds.
Cook the soba in plenty of boiling water for the time on the package, then drain and rinse well under cold running water until chilled.
Grate the daikon and let it drain a little. Stir the natto briskly with chopsticks about 30 times, until it turns pale and stringy, then stir in the rest of the tamari and most of the scallion.

Put the noodles in a bowl and top with the natto, the grated daikon and the kimchi. Crumble the nori over, add the last of the scallion, pour the cold sauce around the noodles, and serve with the bok choy.
tip: Natto keeps well in the freezer, so buy a few packs on your next trip to an Asian grocery. Not a natto fan yet? Stir in extra grated daikon and a splash of vinegar. Both calm the smell and the stickiness.

name: Hot soba in ginger broth with salmon, bok choy and a soft egg
inspiredBy: Japanese hot kake soba and tsukimi soba, with canned salmon as a quick topping
about: Hot buckwheat noodles in a savoury bonito and soy broth with flaked salmon, bok choy, ginger and a soft egg that poaches in the broth. It is a warming Saturday lunch that takes about 20 minutes. The **canned salmon brings omega-3 and vitamin D**, plus calcium from its soft bones.
steps: Simmer about 300 ml (1¼ cups) of water with the bonito flakes for 3 minutes, then strain it back into the pot. Add the tamari, mirin and half the ginger, cut into thin matchsticks, and keep it at a gentle simmer.
Add the bok choy to the broth and simmer for 2 minutes, until the stems are just tender. Add the salmon in chunks. Crack the egg into the broth, cover, and let it poach for 2 minutes.
While the egg poaches, cook the soba in plenty of boiling water for the time on the package. Drain it and rinse briefly so it does not clump.
Put the noodles in a deep bowl and ladle over the broth, salmon, bok choy and egg. Top with the scallion, the rest of the ginger and the crumbled nori.
tip: A shake of shichimi togarashi on top is a good finish, if you have it.

name: Chicken teriyaki with bok choy, carrots and brown rice
inspiredBy: Japanese teriyaki, with mirin and no added sugar in the sauce
about: Juicy pan-seared chicken thigh glazed in a glossy ginger and soy sauce, with tender bok choy, carrots and chewy brown rice and barley. The sauce is just tamari, mirin, ginger and garlic, so it is far less sweet and less salty than the bottled kind. It makes two portions, so tomorrow's **lunch is already packed**.
steps: Stir the tamari, mirin, grated ginger, grated garlic and a splash of water together in a small bowl.

Pat the chicken dry and cut it into broad strips. Warm the oil in a wide non-stick pan over medium-high heat (use two batches if the pan is crowded) and sear the chicken for 2 to 3 minutes a side, until golden. Move it to a plate.
Add the carrot, sliced into thin coins, and a splash of water to the pan, cover and steam for 2 minutes. Add the bok choy and steam 2 minutes more, until the stems are just tender.
Return the chicken to the pan and pour in the sauce. Simmer, stirring, until it turns glossy and clings to the chicken, about 2 minutes. The chicken should be cooked all the way through with no pink.
Reheat the rice and barley. Serve the chicken and vegetables over the rice with a few drops of the vinegar over the bok choy, then the sesame seeds and sliced scallion.
Pack the second portion, rice and all, for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: Cold teriyaki chicken is just as good in a bento. Pack some cucumber slices on the side.

name: Miso-glazed salmon with sesame spinach, grilled mushrooms and brown rice
inspiredBy: Japanese miso salmon and spinach gomae
about: A salmon fillet broiled until nearly done, then brushed with a thin miso, mirin and ginger glaze so it caramelizes without scorching, with grilled king oyster mushrooms, spinach in a nutty sesame dressing and brown rice and barley. Salmon brings **omega-3 fats and vitamin D**, and the sesame spinach adds folate and vitamin K.
steps: Heat the broiler to high and line a tray with foil. Stir the miso, mirin and grated ginger together into a thick paste.
Pat the salmon dry and put it on the tray. Toss the mushrooms with the oil and a few drops of the tamari and set them alongside. Broil about 15 cm (6 inches) from the heat for 5 minutes.
Spread the paste thinly over the salmon and broil 3 to 4 minutes more, until the glaze browns in spots and the salmon flakes easily. The mushrooms should be golden and tender.
Meanwhile, boil the spinach for 30 seconds, then drain, rinse under cold water and squeeze it very dry. Cut it into chunks.

Crush the sesame seeds in a mortar, or in a bowl with the back of a spoon, until about half are ground. Stir in the rest of the tamari, the vinegar and a teaspoon of water, then toss the spinach through it.
Reheat the rice and barley. Serve the salmon and mushrooms with the sesame spinach and the rice, with sliced scallion on top.
tip: No broiler? Bake at 220°C (425°F) for 8 minutes, glaze, then 3 to 4 minutes more.

name: Doenjang jjigae with beef, tofu, zucchini and mushrooms, over barley rice
inspiredBy: Korean doenjang jjigae, with a bonito broth in place of dried anchovy
about: A bubbling, savoury Korean stew of thin beef, tofu, zucchini and king oyster mushrooms in a garlicky doenjang broth with a little gochujang and gochugaru, served over barley rice (boribap). It is rustic family food, and it tastes even better the next day. The **tofu and vegetables do most of the work**, with just a little beef for iron and zinc.
steps: Simmer about 350 ml (1½ cups) of water per portion with the bonito flakes for 3 minutes, then strain the broth.
Warm the sesame oil in a medium pot over medium heat. Cook the beef with the minced garlic for 2 minutes, until it has lost its pink colour.
Pour in the broth and bring it to a simmer. Whisk the doenjang with a ladle of the hot broth until smooth, then stir it into the pot with the gochujang and gochugaru.
Add the zucchini and mushrooms, cut into chunky pieces, and simmer for 6 minutes. Add the tofu in big cubes and the scallion cut into lengths, and simmer gently for 3 minutes more.
Taste the broth: it should be savoury and a little earthy, not too salty. Add a splash of water if it is.
Reheat the rice and barley, and serve the stew over or beside it in deep bowls. Pack the second portion, with its rice, for tomorrow's lunch and reheat it gently so the tofu stays tender.
tip: Add an extra spoon of gochujang for a spicier bowl. Barley is about half the grain here, the way Korean boribap is.

name: Salt-grilled mackerel with grated daikon, spinach ohitashi and wakame cucumber
inspiredBy: Japanese saba shioyaki, set out as a teishoku with ohitashi and a vinegared side
about: A mackerel fillet salted and grilled until the skin is crisp and blistered, with a mound of grated daikon and a splash of soy, spinach in a light soy dressing and a sharp wakame and cucumber salad. It is a simple, honest Japanese dinner. Mackerel is one of the best sources of **omega-3 fats**, and the daikon cuts right through its richness.
steps: Sprinkle the mackerel with most of the salt on both sides and leave it for 20 minutes, then pat it dry with paper towel.
Boil the spinach for 30 seconds, then drain, rinse under cold water and squeeze it very dry. Cut it into chunks and toss with a few drops of the tamari and half the sesame seeds.

Slice the cucumber thinly and toss it with a pinch of the salt. After 10 minutes, squeeze out the water. Soak the wakame in cold water for 5 minutes, then drain and squeeze it, and toss both with the vinegar and a few drops of the tamari.
Heat the broiler to high. Broil the mackerel skin side up on a foil-lined tray for 8 to 10 minutes, until the skin is blistered and the flesh is opaque all the way through. No flipping needed.
Grate the daikon and drain it lightly. Reheat the rice and barley. Serve the mackerel with the daikon and the rest of the tamari dribbled over, with the spinach, the salad and the rice.
tip: Open a window and turn on the fan. Grilled mackerel smells like a Japanese izakaya, which is not bad at all.

name: Dubu-kimchi, stir-fried pork and kimchi with seared tofu and rice
inspiredBy: Korean dubu-kimchi, with a little mirin to balance sour kimchi
about: Tender pork, carrot and mushrooms stir-fried with tangy, spicy kimchi, piled beside slabs of golden seared tofu with brown rice and barley. It is fast, punchy and deeply savoury, and a favourite at Korean tables. **Kimchi is already salty and sour**, so the sauce needs very little extra, and the tofu adds plant protein.
steps: Pat the tofu dry and cut it into slabs about 1 cm (½ inch) thick. Warm half the canola oil in a large non-stick pan over medium heat and sear the tofu until golden, about 3 minutes a side. Move it to a plate.
Add the rest of the canola oil to the same pan. Stir-fry the carrot, mushrooms and pork over high heat for 3 minutes, until the pork has lost its pink colour.
Add the garlic and kimchi and stir-fry for 4 to 5 minutes, until the carrot is tender and the kimchi smells toasty and its edges caramelize.
Stir in the tamari, the mirin and a splash of water, and cook 1 minute more. Take it off the heat and stir through the sesame oil.
Reheat the rice and barley. Serve the kimchi and pork beside the warm tofu and the rice, with the scallion and sesame seeds on top.
tip: Older, sour kimchi is best for cooking. Fresh kimchi works too, but add a splash of vinegar.

name: Bibimbap with beef, four namul and a fried egg
inspiredBy: Korean bibimbap, with brown rice and less oil
about: A big bowl of brown rice topped in sections with sesame spinach, soybean sprouts, carrot and shiitake namul, marinated beef and a crisp-edged fried egg, all mixed together with a tangy gochujang sauce. It is the weekend project: lots of small steps, none of them hard, and it makes two portions. The colourful vegetables carry **folate, vitamin A and vitamin K**.
steps: Make the sauce. Stir the gochujang with the vinegar, about a third of the sesame oil, a little of the garlic and a splash of water into a thick, spoonable paste.
Toss the thinly sliced beef with a little tamari, garlic and a few drops of sesame oil, and leave it to marinate while you do the vegetables.

Blanch the spinach for 30 seconds, drain, rinse cold and squeeze dry. Toss it with garlic, a few drops of sesame oil and a few drops of tamari. Boil the soybean sprouts, covered, in a little water for 5 minutes until they no longer taste raw, then drain and season the same way.

Cut the carrot into matchsticks and slice the shiitake. Stir-fry the carrot in a little sesame oil for 2 minutes, then the shiitake for 3 minutes until golden, seasoning each with a few drops of tamari. Keep the vegetables in separate piles.
Cook the beef in a hot pan for 2 minutes, until it is browned and there is no pink left.
In the same pan, with a little more sesame oil, fry an egg, sunny side up, until the white is crisp at the edges and the yolk is still runny.

Reheat the rice and barley with a splash of water. Divide the rice, namul and beef in half. Put one half in a wide bowl, arranged in sections around the edge, with the egg in the middle, a spoonful of the sauce on top and a pinch of sesame seeds. Mix everything together before you eat.
Pack the other half of the rice, namul and beef in a container for tomorrow's lunch, with the sauce on the side. Reheat the beef and rice, and fry a fresh egg then.
tip: Spinach, sprouts, carrot and shiitake can be swapped for any four vegetables you like.

name: Chicken and tofu nabe with napa cabbage and mushrooms, finished with udon
inspiredBy: Japanese mizutaki, finished with udon instead of the usual rice
about: A pot of bonito broth simmered with chicken thigh, tofu, napa cabbage, daikon, king oyster mushrooms and spinach, dipped in a bright soy and mandarin ponzu, then finished with udon noodles and a swirl of egg in the leftover broth. It is a relaxed Sunday supper you can cook right at the table, with **plenty of vegetables in a light broth** and chicken and tofu for protein.
steps: Make the ponzu. Squeeze the mandarin juice into a small bowl and stir in two-thirds of the tamari and the vinegar. Grate a little of the daikon and slice some of the scallion into it, and set it out for dipping.
Simmer about 600 ml (2½ cups) of water with the bonito flakes and the mirin for 3 minutes in a wide, shallow pot, then strain and return the broth to the pot.
Add the chicken, thin rounds of daikon and the white stems of the napa cabbage. Simmer gently for 8 minutes, skimming any foam.
Add the mushrooms (halved lengthwise) and the tofu cubes and simmer for 4 minutes. Add the napa leaves, spinach and scallion for the last minute. The chicken should be cooked through with no pink.
Eat from the pot, dipping everything in the sharp ponzu.

For the finish, add the udon (rinsed under hot water to loosen it) to the remaining broth with the rest of the tamari. Simmer for 2 minutes, then pour in the beaten egg in a slow spiral, cover, and turn off the heat for a minute. Spoon into a bowl with a little scallion.
tip: Any firm white fish works in place of the chicken, and it cooks in about 4 minutes. Fresh or frozen udon is fine too.
ingredients: boneless, skinless, cut into bite-size pieces
calcium-set, check the label for calcium sulfate

name: Warm edamame with sea salt
inspiredBy: Japanese izakaya edamame
about: A bowl of warm shelled edamame with a pinch of salt, the izakaya classic. It is a snack with real staying power. The **edamame bring protein, folate and fibre**.
steps: Boil the edamame for 3 to 4 minutes, or as the package says, then drain well.
Sprinkle with a pinch of salt and eat warm.

name: Mandarin and walnuts
about: A juicy mandarin with a handful of walnuts, the way Jeju mandarins are enjoyed in Korea. It is sweet, crunchy and easy to carry. **Walnuts add plant omega-3 fats**, and the mandarin adds vitamin C.
steps: Peel the mandarin and eat it with the walnuts.

name: Mandarin and toasted almonds
about: A juicy mandarin with a small handful of warm toasted almonds. It is sweet, crunchy and keeps you going. The **almonds bring vitamin E** and calcium, and the mandarin adds vitamin C.
steps: Toast the almonds in a dry pan over medium heat for 3 minutes, until golden and fragrant. Peel the mandarin and eat it with the warm almonds.

name: Mandarin with almonds and walnuts
about: A juicy mandarin with a small handful of almonds and walnuts. It is sweet, crunchy and easy to carry. The **almonds bring vitamin E**, the walnuts bring plant omega-3 fats, and the mandarin adds vitamin C.
steps: Peel the mandarin and eat it with the almonds and walnuts. Toast the nuts in a dry pan for 2 minutes first if you like.

name: Asian pear and walnuts
inspiredBy: Korean fruit and nuts after a meal
about: Cold, crisp, juicy Asian pear slices with a handful of walnuts, a very Korean way to end a meal. It is sweet and crunchy. **Walnuts add plant omega-3 fats** and the pear adds fibre.
steps: Slice the pear and eat it with the walnuts.

name: Asian pear and toasted almonds
inspiredBy: Korean fruit and nuts after a meal
about: Cold, crisp, juicy Asian pear slices with a small handful of warm toasted almonds. It is sweet and crunchy, and a very Korean way to end a meal. The **almonds bring vitamin E**, and the pear adds fibre.
steps: Toast the almonds in a dry pan over medium heat for 3 minutes, until golden and fragrant. Slice the pear and eat it with the warm almonds.

name: Hiyayakko, chilled tofu with ginger and bonito
inspiredBy: Japanese hiyayakko
about: A block of chilled tofu topped with grated ginger, scallion, bonito flakes and a dash of tamari. It is cool, silky and savoury, and takes two minutes. It adds **plant protein and a little calcium**.
steps: Pat the tofu dry and set it on a plate.
Grate the ginger over the top, then add the sliced scallion, bonito flakes and sesame seeds. Dribble with the tamari.

name: Roasted sweet potato (yaki-imo)
inspiredBy: Japanese and Korean street-cart roasted sweet potato
about: A whole sweet potato roasted until the skin crackles and the inside turns jammy and caramelized, the way it is sold from street carts in Japan and Korea in winter. It is naturally sweet with nothing added. It is rich in **vitamin A and fibre**.
steps: Heat the oven to 200°C (400°F). Pierce the sweet potato a few times with a fork, set it on a tray and roast for 45 to 50 minutes, until it feels very soft and some syrup oozes from the skin.
Let it cool for a few minutes and eat it with the skin on.
tip: Roast a whole tray on Sunday and rewarm one in a toaster oven. They keep for 4 days in the fridge.

name: Cucumber and carrot sticks with miso and sesame dip
inspiredBy: Japanese moro-kyu, cucumber with miso
about: Crunchy cucumber and carrot sticks with a savoury miso and sesame dip, a very Japanese snack that is often served with beer or tea. It is light, crisp and low in calories. The carrot adds **vitamin A**, and the dip brings a little sesame for minerals.
steps: Cut the cucumber and carrot into sticks. Stir the miso, mirin, sesame seeds and a few drops of water into a thick dip, and use it for dunking.

name: Soft-boiled egg with toasted nori
inspiredBy: Korean gim and eggs
about: A soft-boiled egg with crisp toasted nori to tear and wrap around bites of the egg. It is a small, savoury snack with a lot of protein. The egg brings **protein and choline**, and the nori adds iodine.
steps: Boil the egg for 6½ minutes, cool it under cold water and peel it. Dribble with a few drops of tamari and eat it with torn pieces of nori.

name: Soy-glazed almonds and walnuts (nut jorim)
inspiredBy: Korean nut jorim (gyeongwa-jorim)
about: Almonds and walnuts toasted in a pan and glazed with a little tamari and mirin until sticky, like the Korean nut jorim side dish. They are savoury, a little sweet and very crunchy. The **almonds bring vitamin E**, and the walnuts bring plant omega-3 fats.
steps: Toast the almonds and walnuts in a dry pan over medium heat for 3 minutes, until they smell nutty.
Add the tamari and mirin and stir for about a minute, until the glaze is sticky and coats the nuts. Cool on a plate so they crisp up.
tip: Make a jar on Sunday. They keep for a week.

name: Korean spicy cucumber salad (oi-muchim)
inspiredBy: Korean oi-muchim
about: Crunchy cucumber in a quick sesame, garlic, vinegar and gochugaru dressing, a Korean side dish you can snack on. It is cool, tangy and a little spicy, and mostly water and crunch, with **almost no calories**.
steps: Slice the cucumber and squeeze it lightly to push out some of the water.
Toss with the sliced scallion, minced garlic, vinegar, gochugaru and sesame seeds, and eat right away.

name: Savoury tofu scramble with mushrooms, greens and kimchi
inspiredBy: Japanese iri-dofu and Chinese home-style scrambles, with no egg
about: Crumbled calcium-set tofu browned until golden with king oyster mushrooms, ginger and scallion, then folded with bok choy and spinach, with a spoon of kimchi on the side. A finish of perilla oil and crumbled nori gives it a Korean note, and the tofu and greens bring **calcium and plant protein** before you leave the house.
steps: Heat the canola oil in a wide non-stick pan over medium-high heat. Add the mushrooms and leave them alone for 3 minutes, until they are browned on one side.
Add the scallion whites, ginger and garlic and stir for 30 seconds, until it smells good.
Crumble in the tofu with your hands, add the turmeric and cook for 5 minutes, stirring now and then, until the tofu is golden at the edges. Do not add the greens until it is.
Add the bok choy and the tamari and toss for 2 minutes. Fold in the spinach and take the pan off the heat as soon as it wilts.
Drizzle with the perilla oil and finish with the white pepper, scallion greens, sesame seeds and crumbled nori. Serve with the kimchi.
tip: Crumble the tofu the night before and keep it in the fridge. In the morning it is a 10 minute breakfast.
ingredients: off the heat, or sesame oil

name: Japanese-style grilled salmon with miso soup and sesame spinach
inspiredBy: the Japanese asa-gohan breakfast of grilled fish, miso soup and ohitashi, with no rice
about: A Japanese breakfast tray: salmon grilled until the skin crackles, a bowl of miso soup with tofu and wakame, and spinach dressed with sesame and tamari. Grated daikon with a squeeze of lime cuts through the richness, and the salmon is your **omega-3 and vitamin D** for the day.
steps: Heat the grill (broiler) to high. Pat the salmon dry, rub the skin with the canola oil and a pinch of salt and grill skin side up for 6 to 8 minutes, until the skin is crisp and the flesh flakes.
While it cooks, bring a small pot of water to a boil. Drop in the spinach for 40 seconds, then lift it into cold water, squeeze it dry and cut it into short lengths.
Toss the spinach with the tamari, perilla oil, sesame seeds and crumbled nori.

Simmer a small bowl of fresh water (about 150 ml) with the wakame and tofu for 2 minutes. Take it off the heat, whisk the miso in through a sieve or with a spoon and add the scallion. Do not boil it after the miso goes in.
Serve the salmon with the grated daikon and lime, the spinach and the soup.
tip: Short on time? Grill the salmon the night before and eat it cold or warmed for 30 seconds. Miso soup takes 5 minutes.

name: Korean steamed egg (gyeran-jjim) with spinach namul and kimchi
inspiredBy: Korean gyeran-jjim, made with water rather than anchovy stock, and served with spinach namul, kimchi and avocado
about: A silky, custardy steamed egg with shiitake and scallion, served the Korean way with garlicky sesame spinach and plenty of kimchi, plus creamy avocado alongside. It is gentle and savoury, and the eggs and spinach together carry **choline and folate**.
steps: Blanch the spinach in a pot of boiling water for 40 seconds, cool it under cold water and squeeze it dry. Chop it roughly and toss with the garlic, half the tamari, half the perilla oil and half the sesame seeds.
Beat the eggs with a little more water than the volume of the eggs, about 60 ml for each egg, until completely smooth. Stir in the shiitake and most of the scallion.

Pour the egg into a small heatproof bowl, then set it in a pot with 3 cm of simmering water. Cover with a lid slightly ajar and steam on low for 12 to 14 minutes (a few minutes more for a big bowl), until it is set and wobbles like custard.
Drizzle the egg with the rest of the tamari and the perilla oil, and scatter with the rest of the scallion, the sesame seeds and the crumbled nori.
Serve with the spinach, kimchi and sliced avocado.
tip: Weekday shortcut: dress the spinach the night before, and cook the egg in the microwave instead, covered, on medium power for 3 to 4 minutes, checking every minute. Low heat either way, because a hard boil makes it rubbery.

name: Korean tofu and clam stew (sundubu-jjigae style)
inspiredBy: Korean sundubu-jjigae, usually made with uncurdled soft tofu
about: A bubbling red stew of tofu, sweet clams, bok choy and a soft egg cracked in at the end, built on gochugaru bloomed in oil, garlic and a little doenjang. It is warming and spicy, and the clams are a huge source of **vitamin B12 and iron**.
steps: Heat the canola oil in a small pot (or a Korean earthenware ttukbaegi, if you have one) over medium heat. Add the gochugaru, garlic and scallion whites and stir for 30 seconds, until the oil turns red and smells toasty. Do not let the chili scorch.
Add the clams and the doenjang and fry for 30 seconds, until the clams smell sweet.
Pour in 300 ml of water and the fish sauce and bring to a boil. Add the bok choy and simmer for 3 minutes, until it softens.
Slide in the tofu in big chunks and simmer gently for 3 to 4 minutes, until the tofu is hot through.
Crack the egg (or eggs) into the middle, put a lid on and cook for 1 to 2 minutes, until the whites are set and the yolks still soft.
Take it off the heat, drizzle with the sesame oil and finish with the white pepper and scallion greens. Eat it while it is still bubbling.
tip: At a Korean grocery, buy the tube of sundubu (uncurdled tofu) and spoon it in. Stir gently either way.

name: Thai tom yum with sea bass, mushrooms and a little coconut
inspiredBy: Thai tom yum pla nam khon, with extra vegetables and tofu
about: Hot, sour and fragrant with lemongrass, ginger, makrut lime and plenty of chili, made creamy with just a splash of light coconut milk. The sea bass is quick and tender, the mushrooms soak up the broth, and the lime and bok choy keep this one high in **vitamin C**.
steps: Warm the canola oil in a pot and cook the lemongrass, ginger, makrut lime leaf and half the chili for 2 minutes, until it smells like a Thai kitchen.
Add 400 ml of water and simmer the aromatics for 4 minutes, so the broth tastes of them. Add the mushrooms and simmer for 5 minutes more.
Add the tofu and bok choy and simmer for 2 minutes. Stir in the coconut milk.
Lay in the sea bass and poach it gently for 3 to 4 minutes, until it turns opaque and flakes.
Turn off the heat. Stir in the fish sauce and lime juice, taste and add more lime if it needs more sourness.
Ladle into a bowl and top with the basil and the rest of the chili. Fish out the lemongrass, ginger and lime leaves as you eat. They are for flavour only.
tip: Galangal (Thai or Chinese grocers, often frozen) is the real thing here if you have it. Use it in place of the ginger. For a Friday lunch at home, make the broth (steps 1 and 2) the night before, and at noon it is 8 minutes to the table.
ingredients: skinless fillet, cut in 3 cm chunks

name: Thai green curry with chicken, green beans and bok choy
inspiredBy: Thai gaeng keow wan gai, with less coconut and more vegetables
about: A light, fragrant green curry with tender chicken breast, crunchy green beans, bok choy and cauliflower. A little of the cauliflower is mashed back in to thicken the sauce, so it clings without much coconut. The greens carry **vitamin C and vitamin K**.
steps: Heat the canola oil in a wide pot or deep pan over medium heat. Add the curry paste, garlic and a spoonful of the coconut milk and fry for 1 to 2 minutes, until the oil turns green and it smells amazing.
Pour in the rest of the coconut milk, about 120 ml of water (a little more if the pot is very full) and the makrut lime leaf and bring to a simmer.
Add the cauliflower and simmer for 5 minutes, until soft. Scoop out a third of it, mash it with a fork and stir it back in to thicken the sauce.
Add the chicken and green beans and simmer for 6 to 8 minutes, until the chicken is just cooked and the beans are tender but still crisp.
Stir in the bok choy for 2 minutes, then take it off the heat. Season with the fish sauce and lime juice, and tear in most of the Thai basil.
Serve in bowls topped with the rest of the basil. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: Reheat gently with a splash of water, because chicken breast tightens overnight. Want it hotter? Add a sliced red chili with the curry paste.

name: Mapo-style tofu with minced pork, mushrooms and garlicky spinach
inspiredBy: Sichuan mapo doufu, with a little pork and shiitake and less oil
about: Silky tofu in a numbing, chili-spiked sauce built on doubanjiang, garlic and Sichuan pepper, with a little minced pork and shiitake for the savoury depth. It is the kind of weeknight dish that is even better the next day, and the tofu and spinach bring **calcium, iron and folate**.
steps: Bring a pot of water to a simmer with a pinch of salt and slip in the tofu cubes for 3 minutes, to firm them up. Lift out and drain.
Toast the Sichuan peppercorns in a dry pan until fragrant, about 1 minute, then crush them.

Heat two thirds of the canola oil in a wide pan over medium-high heat. Brown the pork and mushrooms for 5 minutes, until deeply golden, then add the garlic, ginger, doubanjiang and gochugaru and stir for 1 minute.
Add 120 ml of water and the tamari. Slide in the tofu and simmer gently, uncovered, for 6 minutes, pushing it around rather than stirring so it stays whole and the sauce clings.
Cook the spinach in a separate pan with the rest of the canola oil, the garlic you kept back and the rice vinegar for 2 minutes, until just wilted.

Finish the tofu with the scallions, the sesame oil and the crushed Sichuan pepper, which should go in last because the numbing tingle is the point. Serve with the spinach. Keep the second portion for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: Doubanjiang (fermented chili bean paste) is at any Asian grocery and keeps for months in the fridge. It usually contains wheat, so anyone avoiding gluten should look for a gluten-free version.
ingredients: minced, a little kept back for the spinach

name: Ginger and scallion chicken with gai lan and walnuts
inspiredBy: Cantonese ginger and scallion stir-fries, and the walnuts of Cantonese walnut chicken, with gai lan and no oyster sauce
about: A Cantonese-style stir-fry: bright, snappy gai lan (Chinese broccoli), sliced chicken breast, shiitake and toasted walnuts in a punchy ginger and scallion sauce. It is quick, it keeps well for lunch, and the gai lan and walnuts bring **calcium, vitamin K and plant omega-3**.
steps: Toss the chicken with half the tamari, a few drops of the canola oil and the white pepper and leave it for 10 minutes while you prep the rest. Toast the walnuts in a dry wok or pan for 3 minutes, until they smell nutty, then tip them out.
Heat half the canola oil in a wide pan or wok over high heat. Cook the chicken for 3 minutes, until golden and about 90% cooked, then slide it onto a plate.
Add the rest of the canola oil, then the ginger, garlic and mushrooms and stir-fry for 2 to 3 minutes.
Add the gai lan stems with a splash of water and cook for 2 minutes, then the leaves for 1 minute more, until bright green and still crisp.

Return the chicken with the walnuts, the scallion, the rest of the tamari, the rice vinegar and a splash (about 60 ml) of water. Toss for 1 minute, until the chicken is cooked through and the sauce coats everything.
Take it off the heat and drizzle with the sesame oil. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: Reheat leftovers in a pan with a splash of water.

name: Salt-grilled mackerel (saba shioyaki) with grated daikon and walnut spinach
inspiredBy: Japanese saba shioyaki and spinach kurumi-ae (walnut dressing), as served in home kitchens
about: Mackerel grilled until the skin blisters, with a pile of grated daikon and a squeeze of lime, spinach in a ground walnut dressing (kurumi-ae) and golden king oyster mushrooms. It is the simplest Japanese dinner there is, and the mackerel is a big hit of **omega-3, vitamin D and B12**.
steps: Heat the grill (broiler) to high. Pat the mackerel dry, rub the skin and flesh with the salt and let it sit for 10 minutes.
Grill the mackerel skin side up for 7 to 9 minutes, until the skin is blistered and the flesh flakes. No need to turn it.
Meanwhile, blanch the spinach in boiling water for 40 seconds, cool it under cold water and squeeze it dry.
Toast the walnuts in a dry pan for 3 minutes, then grind them in a mortar until sandy. Mix with the tamari, rice vinegar and perilla oil and toss with the spinach.
Sear the mushrooms in the canola oil in a hot pan for 4 minutes, until browned and glossy.
Serve the mackerel with the grated daikon and lime, the spinach and the mushrooms.

name: Thai holy basil-style pork (pad krapow) with green beans and cauliflower rice
inspiredBy: Thai pad krapow moo, with cauliflower rice in place of jasmine rice and no sugar
about: Hot, garlicky minced pork tenderloin stir-fried hard with plenty of chilies, green beans and a big handful of Thai basil, spooned over dry, lightly seasoned cauliflower rice. It is the Thai street-food favourite, made at home in 30 minutes, and the pork brings **thiamin**, which keto menus often run short of.
steps: Pound the garlic and chilies together in a mortar or chop them to a rough paste.
Heat a third of the canola oil in a pan, add the cauliflower and cook for 6 minutes with the lime juice, until tender and dry, not wet. Keep it warm on a plate.
Wipe the pan, add the rest of the canola oil and get it very hot. Fry the garlic and chili paste for 20 seconds.
Add the pork and stir-fry for 4 to 5 minutes, breaking it up, until browned and crisp at the edges.
Add the green beans, tamari and fish sauce with 2 tablespoons of water. Cook for 3 minutes until the beans are crisp-tender.
Take the pan off the heat and fold in the Thai basil so it wilts. Finish with the scallion and serve over the cauliflower rice. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: A fried egg on top is the classic. Add one if you have room in the day.

name: Korean beef bulgogi lettuce wraps with ssamjang, grilled mushrooms and kimchi
inspiredBy: Korean bulgogi and ssam, with no sugar or pear in the marinade
about: Garlicky, sesame-scented beef seared hot and tucked into crisp lettuce leaves with a dab of doenjang ssamjang, grilled king oyster mushrooms and tangy kimchi. With no sugar it is savoury, not sweet, and the kimchi's acid is the contrast. A pile of greens carries **vitamin K and folate**.
steps: Mix the beef with the tamari, the minced garlic for the marinade, ginger, rice vinegar and all the sesame oil. Leave it for 30 minutes, or up to a day in the fridge.
Make the ssamjang by stirring together the doenjang, the raw garlic, gochugaru, half the sesame seeds and half the scallion with a splash of water.
Heat half the canola oil in a heavy pan over high heat. Sear the king oyster slices for 3 to 4 minutes, until deeply browned, and set aside.
Add the rest of the oil and cook the beef in two batches for 1 to 2 minutes each, until browned at the edges. Do not crowd the pan.
Pile the beef, mushrooms and kimchi on a platter with the lettuce and ssamjang. To eat, tuck a bit of beef, mushroom and kimchi in a leaf with a dab of ssamjang and fold it up.
Scatter the rest of the scallion and sesame seeds over the top. Keep the second portion, already cooked, for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: Lunch tomorrow: reheat the beef in a hot pan for 2 minutes and eat it in fresh lettuce.
ingredients: sliced very thin against the grain
3 g minced for the marinade, the rest raw and minced for the ssamjang

name: Sea bass, tofu and bok choy hot pot with sesame-lime dipping sauce
inspiredBy: Japanese nabemono and Korean jeongol, with a lighter sesame dipping sauce
about: A pot of ginger, shiitake and miso broth at the table, with sea bass, tofu, bok choy and spinach cooked in it a few bites at a time. A dip of ground sesame and walnut with lime, tamari and grated daikon sits alongside. It is light, warming and slow to eat, with **calcium and folate**.
steps: Grind the sesame seeds and walnuts in a mortar until sandy. Stir in the tamari, lime juice, perilla oil and a spoon of water, then fold in the grated daikon. Spoon into a small dipping bowl.
Put about 400 ml of water in a wide pot with the ginger and shiitake and simmer for 12 minutes, until the broth smells deeply savoury.
Whisk the miso into a ladle of the broth, then stir it back into the pot. Do not let it boil hard after this.
Add the bok choy stems and tofu and simmer for 4 minutes, then the sea bass for 3 to 4 minutes, until opaque and flaking.
Add the spinach, bok choy leaves and scallion and cook for 1 minute more.
Eat straight from the pot, dipping each piece in the sesame-lime sauce, and sip the broth at the end.
tip: In North America "sea bass" means different fish in different shops. Branzino, black sea bass or cod all work; Chilean sea bass is pricey and fatty.
ingredients: skinless fillet, cut in large chunks

name: Pan-roasted pumpkin seeds with gochugaru and tamari
inspiredBy: Korean and Japanese seasoned roasted seeds
about: A palmful of pumpkin seeds toasted until they pop, then tossed with a little tamari and chili. They are crunchy and savoury, and one handful brings **magnesium, zinc and iron**.
steps: Toast the pumpkin seeds in a dry pan over medium heat for 3 to 4 minutes, shaking the pan, until they puff and pop.
Take the pan off the heat, add the tamari and gochugaru and stir until it dries onto the seeds.

name: Chilled tofu (hiyayakko) with ginger, scallion and perilla oil
inspiredBy: Japanese hiyayakko, the summer cold tofu, with the Korean touch of perilla oil
about: A block of cold, firm tofu with grated ginger, scallion, tamari and a drizzle of perilla oil. It is clean, cool and filling, and the tofu gives you **calcium**.
steps: Drain the tofu and pat it dry. Cut it in 4 slabs and put it on a plate.
Top with the ginger and scallion, then spoon over the tamari and perilla oil and scatter with the sesame seeds.
tip: Keep perilla oil in the fridge, because it goes rancid fast. Sesame oil works for flavour if you cannot find it, but perilla is what brings the omega-3.

name: Avocado with tamari, sesame and lime
inspiredBy: the Japanese way with avocado, dressed with soy sauce
about: A ripe avocado with a splash of tamari, lime and toasted sesame seeds, eaten with a spoon. It is creamy, salty and zingy, and gives you **potassium and vitamin E**.
steps: Cut the avocado in half and twist out the stone.
Splash the tamari and lime into the hollow and sprinkle with the sesame seeds and gochugaru. Eat it with a spoon.

name: Pan-toasted five-spice walnuts with tamari
inspiredBy: Chinese spiced and glazed walnuts, with no sugar
about: Walnuts toasted in a dry pan and glazed with a splash of tamari and a pinch of Chinese five-spice. They are crunchy, savoury and a bit smoky, and walnuts are one of the few nuts with real **plant omega-3**.
steps: Toast the walnuts in a dry pan over medium heat for 3 to 4 minutes, shaking the pan, until they smell nutty and darken a shade.
Take the pan off the heat, add the tamari, five-spice and gochugaru and stir until the glaze dries onto the nuts. Let them cool and crisp up for a few minutes.
tip: Toast a jar of them on Sunday. They keep for a week.

name: Avocado, wakame and cucumber sunomono
inspiredBy: Japanese sunomono, vinegared salads, with avocado added and no sugar
about: Cool cucumber ribbons, soft wakame and creamy avocado in a light rice vinegar dressing, a Japanese vinegared salad without the sugar. The avocado and wakame give you **fibre and potassium**.
steps: Soak the wakame in cold water for 5 minutes, until soft. Drain, squeeze out the water and chop.
Whisk the rice vinegar and tamari together and toss with the cucumber and wakame.
Fold in the avocado and scatter with the sesame seeds.

name: Soy-garlic king oyster mushrooms
inspiredBy: Korean saesongi beoseot bokkeum, the stir-fried king oyster mushroom banchan
about: King oyster mushrooms seared until golden and tossed with garlic, tamari and a splash of vinegar. Meaty and savoury, they are a bit like mushroom jerky and add **B vitamins and potassium**.
steps: Heat the canola oil in a pan over medium-high heat. Add the mushrooms in one layer and cook without stirring for 3 minutes, until browned.
Add the garlic, tamari and vinegar and cook for 1 more minute, until it clings.
Finish with the perilla oil and scallion. Good warm or cold.

name: Soy-garlic marinated egg
inspiredBy: Korean mayak-style marinated eggs and Japanese ajitama, made without sugar
about: A soft-boiled egg steeped in tamari, rice vinegar, garlic and a little chili until the white turns glossy and savoury, then sprinkled with sesame. It is the Korean lunchbox egg without the sugar, and a good source of **choline**.
steps: Lower the egg into boiling water and cook for 7 minutes for a soft yolk, then cool it in ice water for 5 minutes and peel.

Stir the tamari, vinegar, garlic, scallion and gochugaru with 2 tablespoons of water in a snug bag or small jar and add the egg. Marinate in the fridge for at least 4 hours or overnight, turning once.
Halve the egg and sprinkle with the sesame seeds.
tip: Make two on Wednesday night, one for Thursday and one for Sunday. After a day, lift them out of the marinade so they do not get too salty. They keep 4 days in the fridge.

name: Avocado with kimchi and sesame
inspiredBy: the Korean habit of pairing creamy things with kimchi
about: Creamy avocado topped with a spoon of chopped kimchi, a few drops of perilla oil and toasted sesame seeds. The cool, fatty avocado and the sour, spicy kimchi are made for each other, and you get **fibre and potassium** in one bowl.
steps: Slice the avocado and fan it out on a small plate.
Spoon the chopped kimchi over the top, drizzle with the perilla oil and sprinkle with the sesame seeds.

name: Toasted walnut and pumpkin seed mix with chili and tamari
inspiredBy: Chinese and Korean seasoned nuts and seeds, with no sugar
about: Walnuts and pumpkin seeds toasted together in a dry pan, then tossed with tamari, gochugaru and a pinch of five-spice. A handful is crunchy, savoury and filling, and it brings **magnesium, zinc and plant omega-3**.
steps: Toast the walnuts and pumpkin seeds in a dry pan over medium heat for 4 minutes, shaking the pan, until the seeds pop and the walnuts smell nutty.
Take the pan off the heat, add the tamari, gochugaru and five-spice and stir until it dries onto the nuts.

name: Pumpkin seeds with lime and chili salt
inspiredBy: Thai and Korean seasoned seed snacks, with no sugar
about: Pumpkin seeds toasted until they pop, then tossed with lime juice, a pinch of salt and gochugaru so the flavour sticks. It is a crunchy, tangy handful with **magnesium, zinc and iron**.
steps: Toast the pumpkin seeds in a dry pan over medium heat for 3 to 4 minutes, shaking the pan, until they start to pop.
Take the pan off the heat and toss with the lime juice, gochugaru and salt until it dries onto the seeds.

name: Huevos a la mexicana with nopales and avocado
about: Eggs scrambled soft with tomato, onion, jalapeño and tender diced nopales, the red, white and green of the Mexican flag, with sliced avocado and a squeeze of lime. It is the classic home breakfast, and the nopales, tomato and avocado bring **calcium, folate and potassium** along with the eggs.
steps: Heat the olive oil in a nonstick pan over medium heat. Cook the onion and jalapeño until soft and glossy, about 3 minutes.
Add the tomato and a pinch of the salt. Cook until it breaks down and most of the liquid is gone, 3 to 4 minutes.
Stir in the nopales and cook until they turn olive green and the sticky liquid cooks off, about 4 minutes.
Beat the eggs with the rest of the salt and pour them in. Stir slowly with a spatula until just set and still a little creamy, about 2 minutes.
Slide onto a plate, fan the avocado beside it, and finish with the cilantro and a squeeze of lime.
tip: Rinsed jarred nopalitos work, or cook a few extra when you make Wednesday's nopales salad. No ripe avocado? Spoon on a little guacamole instead.

name: Eggs in salsa verde with spinach, avocado and toasted pepitas
inspiredBy: Mexican huevos en salsa verde, with pepitas for the crunch
about: Eggs poached right in a tangy, roasted tomatillo salsa with a handful of wilted spinach, then topped with sliced avocado and a crunch of toasted pepitas. It is huevos en salsa verde, the cousin of chilaquiles verdes without the tortilla chips, and the tomatillo salsa and spinach bring **vitamin C, vitamin A and fibre** early in the day.
steps: Set the tomatillos, jalapeño, onion and garlic in a dry skillet over medium-high heat. Turn them until the tomatillos are blistered and soft, about 8 minutes.
Toast the pepitas in a dry pan until they pop and smell nutty, about 2 minutes. Tip them out.
Blend the roasted vegetables with the cilantro, the salt and a splash of water until it is a pourable salsa.
Heat the olive oil in a small pan and pour in the salsa. Simmer for 3 minutes, until it darkens and thickens a little, then stir in the spinach until it wilts.
Make a well for each egg and crack them in. Cover and cook 4 to 5 minutes, until the whites are set and the yolks still jiggle.
Top with the avocado and pepitas and eat straight from the pan.
tip: Roast a double batch of the tomatillo salsa on Monday night and keep half in the fridge for Friday.

name: Cinnamon and lime chia pudding with chile pecans
inspiredBy: Mexican chía fresca, the lime and chia drink, set into a pudding
about: Chia soaked overnight with lime and cinnamon, topped with pecans toasted with a pinch of chili. It borrows the lime and chia of a Mexican chía fresca and sets it into a spoonable breakfast with **omega-3, calcium and plenty of fibre**.
steps: The night before, stir the chia, almond milk, lime juice, a little grated lime zest and the cinnamon together in a jar with about the same amount of cold water as almond milk. Wait 5 minutes, stir again so nothing clumps, then cover and chill overnight.
In the morning, toast the pecans in a dry pan over medium heat until they smell nutty, about 3 minutes. Toss with the chili powder.
Stir the pudding. It should be thick and spoonable, like a loose rice pudding, so add a splash more almond milk if it has set firm. Top with the spicy pecans.
tip: Make two jars on Sunday night for Monday and Wednesday. On Friday night, make Saturday's chocolate jar and one more plain jar for Sunday. They keep 3 days in the fridge.
ingredients: juice, plus a little grated zest

name: Peruvian sea bass ceviche in lettuce cups with avocado and pepita crunch
inspiredBy: Peruvian ceviche clásico, with pepitas in place of the toasted corn, lettuce in place of sweet potato
about: Very fresh sea bass cut in cubes and cured in lime juice with red onion, ají amarillo and plenty of cilantro, the way a Lima cevichería does it, spooned into crisp romaine cups. Avocado makes it rich, toasted pepitas stand in for the crunchy cancha corn, and it brings **vitamin C, vitamin A and lean protein** with almost no carbs.
steps: Rinse the sliced red onion in cold water for a minute, then drain. This takes the harsh edge off.
Toast the pepitas in a dry pan over medium heat until they pop and smell nutty, about 2 minutes. Cool them on a plate.
Stir the lime juice, ají amarillo paste, jalapeño and the salt together in a bowl. This is the leche de tigre, so taste it: it should be sharp, a little hot and well seasoned.
Add the fish and stir to coat. Let it sit for 8 to 10 minutes, just until the outside turns opaque and the middle is still tender.
Fold in the onion, cilantro and cucumber. Set the romaine leaves on a plate, spoon the ceviche into them, and top with the avocado and pepitas. Drink the leftover leche de tigre from the bowl.
tip: Ask for corvina or sea bass, or any very fresh firm white fish, previously frozen if you are unsure. Eat it the same day.
ingredients: very fresh, skinless, cut in 2 cm cubes

name: Carne asada with grilled nopales, cebollitas, garlicky collards and guacamole
inspiredBy: Northern Mexican carne asada with grilled nopales
about: Lean beef marinated in lime, garlic and ancho and seared hot, then sliced thin, with charred nopales and scallions, a roasted salsa roja, collard greens sautéed with garlic and a scoop of guacamole. Nopales and collards are the quiet stars here, with **fibre, calcium and vitamin C** for almost no carbs. This makes two portions, so tomorrow's lunch is done.
steps: Cover the ancho with hot water and let it soften for 15 minutes. Drain, then blend it with the vinegar, half the lime juice, most of the garlic, the cumin, oregano and half the salt into a paste.
Pound the steak to an even thickness with a mallet or a heavy pan, then rub the paste over it. Marinate 30 minutes to 4 hours, no longer, or the acid turns lean beef chalky.
Char the tomato and jalapeño in a hot dry skillet until blackened in spots, about 8 minutes. Chop them with half the cilantro for a chunky salsa roja.
Mash the avocado with the remaining lime juice, the remaining cilantro and a pinch of salt for a quick guacamole.

Heat a cast iron pan or grill until very hot. Brush the nopales and scallions with most of the olive oil and cook 4 to 5 minutes a side, until browned and tender. The nopales go from bright to olive green and lose their slime.
Sear the steak 1½ to 2 minutes a side, so it stays pink in the middle, then rest it 5 minutes and slice it thin against the grain. Lean beef gets tough past medium.
In the hot pan, warm the last of the olive oil with the last of the garlic, sliced, and toss in the collard ribbons with a splash of water for 3 to 4 minutes, until bright green and tender.
Plate the steak with the nopales, scallions, collard, salsa and guacamole. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch and keep the guacamole separate so it stays green.
tip: Rinsed jarred nopalitos work if you cannot find fresh paddles, or use thick zucchini planks. Eat tomorrow's beef cold or warm it in a hot pan for 30 seconds, because lean beef toughens when it is reheated.
ingredients: juice, divided between marinade and guacamole
stems out, cut in thin ribbons

name: Trout in ají amarillo and pecan sauce with salsa criolla and green cauliflower rice
inspiredBy: Peruvian trucha with ají amarillo and arroz verde, with the pecans many Peruvian cooks use in ají de gallina, and cauliflower for the rice
about: Trout fillet seared skin side down until crisp, on a pool of creamy ají amarillo and pecan sauce, a nod to ají de gallina, with a sharp Peruvian salsa criolla of red onion and lime. The cauliflower rice is cooked with spinach and cilantro like an arroz verde, and the trout brings **omega-3, vitamin D and B12**.
steps: Toast the pecans in a dry pan until they smell nutty, about 3 minutes. Blend them with the ají amarillo paste, the garlic, a spoonful of the olive oil, a tablespoon of water and a pinch of salt, adding more water a little at a time until it blends smooth, then simmer in a small pan for 2 minutes until it thickens like thin cream.
Make the salsa criolla: toss the red onion and tomato with the lime juice and a pinch of salt. Let it sit and soften. Season the trout with a pinch of salt.
Heat half of the remaining olive oil in a nonstick pan over medium-high. Cook the trout skin side down for 4 minutes without moving it, until the skin is crisp, then flip for 1 to 2 minutes.
Wipe the pan, add the remaining oil, and warm it for 30 seconds. Add the cauliflower rice and stir for 3 minutes.
Stir in the spinach and most of the cilantro and cook until the spinach wilts and the rice is tender but not mushy, 2 to 3 minutes. Add a pinch of salt.
Spoon the ají and pecan sauce around the trout, not over the crisp skin. Serve it with the green rice and the salsa criolla, with the last of the cilantro on top.
ingredients: juice, all for the salsa criolla

name: Chicken fajita bowls with cauliflower rice, peppers, spinach and guacamole
inspiredBy: Tex-Mex fajitas, served over cauliflower rice and greens instead of tortillas
about: Chicken breast sliced thin and seared with chili, cumin and smoked paprika, piled over cauliflower rice and a bed of baby spinach with sizzling peppers, poblano and onion, then topped with guacamole. The peppers and spinach bring **vitamin C, vitamin A and iron**, and the leftovers taste just as good cold or reheated for tomorrow's lunch.
steps: Toss the chicken with the chili powder, cumin, smoked paprika, garlic, half the lime juice and half the salt. Leave it 15 minutes.

Heat half the olive oil in a big skillet over high heat. Cook the chicken in a single layer, in batches if the pan is crowded, 3 to 4 minutes, turning once, until browned and just cooked through. Move it to a plate. Breast dries out fast, so do not go past that.
In the same pan, cook the peppers, poblano and onion for 6 to 7 minutes, until charred at the edges and still a bit crisp.
Heat the remaining oil in a second pan and cook the cauliflower rice with a pinch of salt for 4 to 5 minutes, until tender.
Mash the avocado with the remaining lime juice, the cilantro and a pinch of salt.

Build the bowls on the baby spinach, which wilts a little under the hot food: cauliflower rice, chicken, peppers, then guacamole. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch, with the guacamole in a separate container.
tip: Reheat the chicken in a pan with a splash of water, and keep the spinach cold.

name: Camarones a la diabla with garlicky zucchini and spinach
inspiredBy: Mexican camarones a la diabla, with zucchini instead of rice
about: Shrimp in a smoky, brick-red sauce of guajillo, chipotle and tomato, the devilled shrimp of Mexican seaside restaurants, with garlicky zucchini, wilted spinach and avocado to cool it down. The sauce and spinach bring **vitamin A, vitamin C and potassium**, and the shrimp bring lean protein and iodine.
steps: Cover the guajillo with hot water and soften 10 minutes. Drain, keeping the soaking water, then blend the chile with the tomato, chipotle, half the garlic, half the onion and about 3 tablespoons of the soaking water, enough for a smooth, pourable sauce.

Heat half the olive oil in a skillet and cook the zucchini with the remaining onion and garlic for 8 to 10 minutes, until tender and lightly golden. Stir in the spinach for the last minute, until wilted. Move to a plate.
Wipe out the pan and toast the pepitas in it, dry, until they pop, about 2 minutes. Tip them out.

Add the remaining oil to the pan, pour in the sauce and let it fry and bubble 3 to 4 minutes, stirring, until it darkens. Add a splash of the soaking water if it gets thicker than ketchup. The chipotle is salty, so taste before adding any salt.
Slide in the shrimp and cook 2 to 3 minutes, until pink and curled. Squeeze in the lime and take the pan off the heat so they do not turn rubbery.
Serve the shrimp over or beside the zucchini and spinach with the avocado, pepitas and cilantro.

name: Achiote pork tenderloin with pickled red onion and lime slaw
inspiredBy: Yucatecan cochinita pibil, with lean tenderloin roasted instead of slow-cooked shoulder
about: Pork tenderloin marinated in achiote, lime and oregano, the flavours of Yucatán cochinita pibil, then roasted and sliced over a crunchy cabbage and romaine slaw with quick pickled red onion. Pork tenderloin is a good source of **thiamin**, one of the vitamins keto eating tends to miss. This makes two portions, so tomorrow's lunch is done.
steps: Whisk the achiote paste with half the lime juice, half the vinegar, the garlic, oregano and cumin. Coat the pork in it and marinate at least 30 minutes, or overnight.
Make the pickle: cover the red onion with the remaining lime juice and vinegar and a pinch of salt. Squeeze it with your fingers and leave it until it turns bright pink.
Heat the oven to 200°C (400°F). Sear the pork in a hot oven-safe pan with most of the olive oil, 2 minutes per side, until deeply red-brown.
Roast the pork 12 to 15 minutes, until it reaches 63°C (145°F) in the thickest part. Rest 5 minutes.
Toast the pepitas in a dry pan until they pop. Toss the cabbage and romaine with the cilantro, a spoonful of the pickling liquid, a little olive oil, the pepitas and a pinch of salt.
Slice the pork. Serve it on the slaw with the pickled onion and avocado. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: Dress the slaw only when you eat it, so the lunch portion stays crisp.

name: Argentine grilled steak with chimichurri, grilled vegetables and green salad
inspiredBy: Argentine bife a la parrilla with chimichurri, made with lean peceto (eye of round), pounded so it grills fast
about: Lean steak grilled hot and rested, sliced thin and spooned with a garlicky parsley and red wine vinegar chimichurri, with a tray of grilled peppers, zucchini and red onion and a peppery arugula and lettuce salad. It eats like a weekend parrilla plate, and the parsley, greens and peppers bring **vitamin K, vitamin C and vitamin A**. This makes two portions, so tomorrow's lunch is done.
steps: Make the chimichurri first so it can sit: chop the parsley and garlic very fine and stir them with most of the olive oil, the vinegar, oregano, cayenne, smoked paprika and half the salt. Leave it 20 minutes at least.
Heat a grill or a large cast iron pan to high. Toss the zucchini, pepper and onion with the rest of the olive oil and a pinch of salt.
Grill the vegetables 4 to 5 minutes a side, until charred and tender but not collapsing. Move them to a platter.

Pound the steak to about 1.5 cm and season it with the rest of the salt. Grill it hot, 2 minutes a side, until deeply browned outside and still pink in the middle. Rest it 5 minutes, then slice thin against the grain.
Toss half the arugula, romaine and tomato with a spoonful of the chimichurri oil and a pinch of salt. Keep the other half undressed for tomorrow.
Spoon the chimichurri over the steak and vegetables and serve with the salad. Pack the second portion, with its sauce and the undressed greens, for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: Eat the second portion cold, sliced over the salad, not reheated. The chimichurri is better after a night in the fridge. Make it on Friday if you want to start the weekend ahead.
ingredients: or a pinch of chili flakes, ají molido

name: Brazilian fish moqueca with garlicky couve and pecan farofa
inspiredBy: Moqueca capixaba, the coconut-free Espírito Santo style, with a little light coconut milk borrowed from Bahia and pecans in place of the cassava farofa
about: A bright, gently spiced fish stew in the Espírito Santo style, of sea bass, tomato, pepper and onion simmered in light coconut milk with colorau and plenty of cilantro and lime, with garlicky collard greens and a crunchy toasted pecan farofa on top. The light coconut milk keeps saturated fat low, and the stew and couve bring **vitamin A, vitamin C, folate and calcium**.
steps: Make the farofa: toast the pecans in a teaspoon of the olive oil in a small pan until they smell nutty, about 3 minutes. Tip them out, then toss with a pinch of salt and a pinch of the colorau. Chopped fine, they stand in for the toasted cassava flour.

Toss the fish with half the lime juice, a little of the garlic and a pinch of the salt, and leave it while you make the sauce. Heat half the olive oil in a wide pan over medium heat. Soften the onion and pepper for 5 minutes, then add half the garlic and the colorau and stir for 30 seconds.

Add the tomato and cook 3 to 4 minutes, until it collapses into a sauce. Pour in the coconut milk and enough water to make a loose sauce that will half cover the fish, about 120 ml, season with half the salt, and simmer 5 minutes until it tastes like a proper broth.
Nestle the fish into the sauce, cover, and cook on low for 6 to 8 minutes, until it just flakes. Do not stir hard.
Meanwhile, heat the remaining oil in a second pan. Add the remaining garlic and the collard and toss for 2 to 3 minutes, until bright green and just tender, with a pinch of salt.
Finish the stew with the rest of the lime juice and most of the cilantro. Serve with the collard alongside, and scatter the farofa and the last of the cilantro over everything.
tip: Cod, halibut or snapper work as well as sea bass.
ingredients: stems out, rolled up and sliced into very thin ribbons

name: Palta rellena with tuna, egg and lime on romaine
inspiredBy: Peruvian palta rellena
about: A ripe avocado piled with tuna, chopped boiled egg, cucumber, red pepper and red onion in a lime and olive oil dressing, the Peruvian palta rellena found in every lunch spot in Lima, on a bed of crisp romaine. It is cool, creamy and crunchy, and brings **potassium, choline and B vitamins**.
steps: Boil the egg (or eggs) for 9 minutes, cool under cold water, then peel and chop.
Whisk the olive oil, lime juice, salt and pepper into a loose dressing.
Flake the tuna into a bowl and fold in the egg, cucumber, red pepper, red onion, cilantro and dressing.
Toss the shredded romaine with a spoonful of the dressing and spread it on a plate. Set the avocado halves on top.
Mound the tuna salad into the avocado halves and over the top. Eat it with a spoon, scooping avocado with each bite.
tip: Boil a few eggs on Sunday and keep them in the shell in the fridge, so this takes 10 minutes.

name: Sardine and avocado romaine boats with jalapeño salsa
inspiredBy: Mexican tostadas de sardina, with lettuce instead of the fried tortilla
about: Canned sardines with their soft bones, lime, tomato and onion piled into crisp romaine boats that stand in for the tostada, the way Mexican seaside tostadas de sardina are topped. It takes 10 minutes with no cooking, and the sardines, soft bones and all, bring **calcium, omega-3 and vitamin D**.
steps: Wash the romaine and pat the leaves dry. Lay the biggest, crispest ones on a plate, like boats.
Mix the tomato, red onion, jalapeño, half the lime juice, the cilantro and a pinch of salt for a quick salsa.
Lay a few slices of avocado in each boat, then mash the sardines roughly with the olive oil and the remaining lime juice and spoon them on top.
Finish each boat with a spoonful of the salsa and eat them right away while the lettuce is still crisp.

name: Guacamole with cucumber sticks
about: Chunky guacamole with lime, onion, jalapeño and cilantro, scooped up with cool, crunchy cucumber sticks instead of chips. Avocado gives you **potassium and healthy fat**, and the vegetable sticks give the crunch.
steps: Mash the avocado roughly with a fork, leaving it chunky.
Stir in the lime juice, onion, jalapeño, cilantro and salt. Taste and add more lime if it needs it.
Serve with the cucumber sticks for scooping.

name: Chile and lime pepitas
about: Pumpkin seeds toasted in a dry pan until they puff and pop, then tossed with lime juice, chili and salt. They are crunchy, a little sour and a little hot, and a good handful gives you **magnesium, zinc and iron**.
steps: Toast the pepitas in a dry pan over medium heat, shaking often, until they puff and pop, about 3 minutes.
Take them off the heat, add the lime juice, chili powder and salt, and toss. They will sizzle and dry in a few seconds.
tip: Toast a bigger batch and keep it in a jar for a week.

name: Nopales salad with tomato, cilantro and toasted pepitas
inspiredBy: Mexican ensalada de nopales
about: Tender cooked nopales tossed with tomato, onion, cilantro and lime, the ensalada de nopales you find at every Mexican market, with toasted pepitas for crunch. Nopales are low in carbs and give you **fibre, calcium and vitamin C**.
steps: Boil the diced nopales in salted water for 6 to 8 minutes, until tender and a darker olive green. Drain and rinse well under cold water to wash off the slime.
Toast the pepitas in a dry pan until they pop, about 2 minutes.
Toss the nopales with the tomato, onion, cilantro, lime juice, olive oil and a pinch of salt.
Spoon into a bowl and top with the pepitas.
tip: Rinsed jarred nopalitos work too, or cook a double batch of fresh ones and keep half in the fridge for 3 days.

name: Avocado with lime, chile and salt
about: A whole ripe avocado, halved, with a squeeze of lime, a dusting of chili and a pinch of salt, eaten with a spoon, the way you would at a Mexican market stall. Simple, creamy and filling, with **potassium and folate**.
steps: Halve the avocado and remove the pit.
Squeeze the lime into each half and sprinkle with the chili powder and salt.
Eat it straight from the skin with a spoon.

name: Shrimp ceviche cups with cucumber and avocado
inspiredBy: Mexican coctel and ceviche de camarón, with the shrimp poached first
