steps: Warm the oil in a non-stick pan over medium-high heat. Add the mushrooms in a single layer and leave them alone for 3 minutes, then stir and cook for another 3 minutes until browned and their juices have cooked off.
Add the onion and cook for 2 minutes until soft, then add the spinach by the handful and stir until it just wilts.
Beat the eggs with the salt and pepper. Pour them over the vegetables, turn the heat to low and fold gently for 2 to 3 minutes, until softly set and still glossy.
Scatter on the scallion and serve on the hot toast.
tip: Brown a double batch of mushrooms on Wednesday and keep half in the fridge for Friday, and that breakfast takes 8 minutes. A splash of hot sauce at the table is very good here.

name: Cottage cheese with pineapple, lime and toasted almonds
about: Creamy cottage cheese under juicy pineapple chunks, with warm toasted almonds and a squeeze of lime. It brings **a big helping of protein** and plenty of vitamin C, and takes ten minutes, or five with almonds toasted ahead.
steps: Toast the almonds in a dry pan over medium heat for 3 to 4 minutes, shaking often, until they smell nutty. Tip them onto a plate.
Spoon the cottage cheese into a bowl and top with the pineapple.
Squeeze over the lime and scatter on the warm almonds.
tip: Peaches, mango or a handful of berries work in place of pineapple.

name: Salmon, chickpea and tomato salad with lemon and oregano
inspiredBy: Inspired by Tuscan tonno e fagioli, with canned salmon and chickpeas
about: Flaked canned salmon over baby spinach with chickpeas, sweet cherry tomatoes and paper-thin onion, tossed in a bright olive oil and lemon dressing, with a slice of garlic toast. It is a quick cousin of Tuscan tuna and beans, and the salmon and chickpeas give you **omega-3, protein and fibre** on one big plate.
steps: Soak the onion slices in half the lemon juice for 5 minutes while you prep. It softens the bite.
Whisk the rest of the lemon juice with the minced garlic, oregano, Aleppo pepper, olive oil, salt and pepper.
Toss the chickpeas and tomatoes with most of the dressing and the onion with its juices.
Pile the spinach on a plate, spoon over the chickpea salad and flake the salmon on top. Drizzle with the last of the dressing.
Toast the bread, rub it with the garlic you kept back while it is hot, and serve alongside.
tip: Choose canned salmon with the bones in. They mash into the fish and are a good source of calcium.
ingredients: minced, with a little kept back to rub on the toast

name: Sesame-ginger chicken and cabbage crunch salad
inspiredBy: Inspired by the Chinese-American chicken salad
about: Poached chicken shredded over a mountain of crunchy cabbage, spinach, carrot and edamame, in a gingery rice vinegar, soy and lime dressing with a little toasted sesame oil. It is the **big crunchy bowl** of a Californian Chinese chicken salad, with a spoonful of mashed pineapple in place of the usual sugar.
steps: Cover the chicken with cold water in a small pot, add a slice of the ginger and the scallion tops, bring to a gentle simmer and cook for 12 to 15 minutes, until it is white all the way through. Lift it out, let it cool a few minutes, then shred it with two forks.
Whisk the rice vinegar, soy sauce, both oils, ginger, lime juice and the mashed pineapple into a dressing.
Toss the cabbage, spinach, carrot, edamame, scallion and cilantro with most of the dressing.
Pile onto a plate, top with the chicken, spoon over the rest of the dressing and finish with a few more cilantro leaves.
tip: Poach the chicken the night before and the salad takes five minutes at lunch. Keep the dressing separate until you eat.

name: Turkey chili with black beans, mushrooms and avocado
inspiredBy: Inspired by American weeknight chili, with lean turkey and black beans
about: A thick, smoky chili made with very lean ground turkey, black beans and tomatoes, with finely chopped mushrooms stirred in for extra volume and a meaty bite. Topped with avocado and cilantro, with lime stirred through. The **beans, turkey and vegetables together** make a bowl high in protein and fibre, and it makes tomorrow's lunch.
steps: Warm the oil in a large pot over medium heat. Cook the onion and mushrooms for 8 to 9 minutes, until soft and the mushroom juices have cooked off.
Add the turkey and break it up with a spoon. Cook for 5 to 6 minutes, until no pink is left.
Stir in the garlic, chili powder, cumin, smoked paprika, cayenne and oregano and cook for 30 seconds, until it smells toasty.
Add the crushed tomatoes, the beans, the salt and a splash of water. Simmer, partly covered, for 25 minutes, stirring now and then, until thick and the flavours have come together.
Stir in the spinach and let it wilt for a minute, then the lime juice. Divide into two portions. Top one with the avocado and cilantro and eat it now.
Cool the second portion, cover and refrigerate for tomorrow's lunch. Add its toppings fresh when you reheat it.
tip: This freezes well for up to 3 months, so doubling it is an easy way to bank two more lunches.

name: Miso soup with tofu, shrimp, edamame and soba
inspiredBy: Inspired by Japanese miso shiru, with shrimp and soba added to make it a meal
about: A big, comforting bowl of mushroom-ginger miso soup with soft tofu, shrimp, edamame, cabbage, carrot and a little soba, so it eats like a noodle-shop dinner. The tofu and shrimp give you **plenty of lean protein**, and it comes together in about 40 minutes. It makes two portions, so lunch tomorrow is ready.
steps: Warm the oil in a big pot over medium-high heat. Brown the mushrooms for 4 to 5 minutes until golden, then add the ginger, garlic and carrot for a minute.

Pour in about 400 ml of water per portion (800 ml for both), or 300 ml per portion if your list shows less than a tablespoon of miso, so the broth stays full-flavoured. Bring to a simmer and cook for 10 minutes, until the mushrooms have flavoured the broth.
Meanwhile, cook the soba in a separate pot of boiling water for the time on the packet, usually 4 to 5 minutes. Drain and rinse under cold water so the noodles do not turn gummy.
Add the cabbage and edamame to the broth and simmer for 2 minutes, then slide in the tofu and shrimp and cook for 2 to 3 minutes more, until the shrimp are pink and curled. Turn the heat to low.
Ladle a little hot broth into a small bowl, stir the miso into it until smooth, then stir it back into the pot. Do not boil the soup after the miso goes in, or it loses its flavour.

Divide the soba into two bowls and ladle the soup over. Finish with the scallion and sesame seeds, and eat one now. Cool the second portion of soup separately from its noodles, cover and refrigerate for tomorrow.
tip: Keep the soba separate from the soup in the fridge and combine them when you reheat, so the noodles stay springy. Do not boil the soup again, or the miso goes dull.

name: Smoky lime chicken burrito bowl on crisp greens
inspiredBy: Inspired by the Tex-Mex burrito bowl, with greens in place of most of the rice
about: Smoky lime chicken, black beans and a small scoop of brown rice on a big bed of romaine, with crunchy cabbage, fresh pico de gallo and avocado. It has **all the burrito-bowl flavour** with the greens doing most of the filling. Makes two portions, so the second is tomorrow's lunch.
steps: Mix half the lime juice with the garlic, chili powder, smoked paprika, cumin and a pinch of the salt, and coat the chicken in it. Leave for 15 minutes or up to 8 hours in the fridge.
Cook the brown rice in plenty of simmering water for about 30 minutes until tender, then drain. Make enough for both portions.
Stir the tomato, onion and cilantro with the rest of the lime juice, a pinch of cayenne and the rest of the salt to make a quick pico de gallo.

Warm the oil in a skillet over medium-high heat and cook the chicken for 5 to 6 minutes a side, until browned and cooked through. Rest it for 5 minutes, then slice. Warm the beans in the same pan for a minute.
Build the bowls on a bed of romaine and cabbage with the rice, beans, chicken, pico and avocado.
Pack the second portion for tomorrow, keeping the greens and pico in a separate container from the warm parts so nothing goes soggy.
tip: Marinate the chicken in the morning and dinner takes 20 minutes.

name: Shrimp and vegetable stir-fry with ginger, garlic and brown rice
inspiredBy: Inspired by Cantonese-style shrimp and vegetable stir-fry
about: Plump shrimp tossed in a hot pan with broccoli, spinach and mushrooms in a savoury ginger-garlic sauce, over a modest scoop of brown rice. The shrimp bring **lean protein for very few calories**, and the heap of vegetables keeps the plate big. The second portion is tomorrow's lunch.
steps: Cook the brown rice in plenty of simmering water for about 30 minutes until tender, then drain. Make enough for both portions.
Stir the soy sauce and rice vinegar with a tablespoon of cold water in a small bowl. Pat the shrimp dry.

Heat a large wok or skillet over high heat until it is properly hot. Add half the oil and the shrimp, in two batches if your pan is small, and cook for about 90 seconds a side until just pink. Tip them out.

Add the remaining oil and the broccoli and mushrooms. Stir-fry for 3 to 4 minutes, until the broccoli is bright green and still has bite. Add the garlic, ginger, scallion and spinach for the last minute, stirring until the spinach just wilts.

Return the shrimp, pour in the sauce and toss over high heat for 30 seconds, until it bubbles. The spinach adds its juices, so you get a light, savoury pan sauce that soaks into the rice. Finish with the sesame oil and scatter with the sesame seeds.
Serve one portion over the rice. Cool the second portion with its rice, cover and refrigerate for tomorrow.
tip: Reheat the leftovers in a hot pan for 2 minutes rather than the microwave, so the shrimp stay tender. Many frozen shrimp are brined, so look for a bag with no added salt or phosphates.

name: Sicilian-style sardine, chickpea and tomato stew with garlic toast
inspiredBy: Inspired by Sicilian pasta con le sarde and Tuscan chickpea stews
about: Canned sardines folded into a garlicky tomato and chickpea stew with carrot, fennel seed and spinach, finished with lemon and served with garlic toast. Sardines and fennel are the classic Sicilian pair, and because you eat the soft bones it carries **omega-3 and calcium**, with some vitamin D.
steps: Warm the oil in a wide pot over medium heat. Cook the onion and carrot for 7 to 8 minutes, until soft and starting to turn golden. Add most of the garlic, the fennel seed and the Aleppo pepper and cook for 30 seconds, until fragrant.
Add the oregano, crushed tomatoes, chickpeas, salt and a splash of water. Simmer for 15 minutes, until thick and glossy.
Stir in the spinach by the handful until it wilts, then break the sardines into big pieces and fold them in gently. Warm through for 2 minutes and finish with the lemon juice and pepper.
Toast the bread and rub it with the reserved garlic while it is hot. Serve the stew in a wide bowl with the toast.
tip: Choose sardines packed in olive oil, and keep the bones in: they melt in the stew and carry the calcium.
ingredients: sliced, with a little kept back to rub on the toast

name: Pork pozole rojo with cabbage, lime and avocado
inspiredBy: Inspired by Jalisco-style pozole rojo, with lean pork tenderloin in place of shoulder
about: A deep red guajillo chile broth with tender lean pork and white hominy, finished with a big pile of crunchy cabbage, cilantro, lime and a little avocado. It is **lean, filling and high in protein**, and the toppings make it feel like a feast. It is the weekend project, and the second portion is Sunday's lunch.
steps: Put half the onion, half the garlic and a pinch of the cumin in a large pot with about 1 litre of water. Bring to a simmer and cook for 20 minutes to make a quick broth.
Meanwhile, toast the guajillo chiles in a dry pan over medium heat for about 30 seconds a side, until fragrant. Do not let them blacken. Soak them in hot water for 15 minutes.
Blend the soaked chiles with the rest of the onion and garlic, the rest of the cumin, the oregano, half the salt and a cup or so of their soaking water until smooth.
Lift the onion out of the broth. Strain the chile sauce into the pot, add the hominy and simmer for 20 minutes, until the broth is deep red and tastes rich.
Add the pork and the rest of the salt and keep the pot at a bare simmer for 10 to 12 minutes, until the pork is just cooked through and still juicy. Stir in half the lime juice.
Ladle into big bowls and pile on the cabbage, cilantro and avocado, with the rest of the lime. Cool the second portion without its toppings and refrigerate for tomorrow.
tip: Tenderloin stays juicy only if it never boils, so keep the pot barely trembling once the pork goes in, and warm the leftover gently. Make the chile sauce a day ahead and the project is half done.

name: Blackened salmon with garlicky greens, lemon and brown rice
inspiredBy: Inspired by Louisiana blackened fish
about: Sockeye salmon with a smoky, peppery Cajun crust, seared in a hot pan and served with garlicky broccoli and spinach, a squeeze of lemon and a small scoop of brown rice. The salmon gives you **omega-3 and vitamin D**, and the crust makes a lean fillet taste rich.
steps: Start the rice first: simmer the brown rice in plenty of water for about 30 minutes until tender, then drain.
Pat the salmon dry, rub it all over with most of the oil and press the Cajun seasoning firmly onto the flesh side.

Heat a heavy skillet, cast iron if you have one, over medium-high heat for about 3 minutes until very hot, and turn the fan on, because blackening smokes a little. Lay the salmon in flesh side down and cook for about 3 minutes, until a dark crust forms. Flip it and cook the skin side for 2 to 4 minutes more, until the centre is just opaque. A little translucent in the middle is fine. Move the salmon to a plate.

Turn the heat to medium. Add the rest of the oil and the garlic to the same skillet for 20 seconds, then the broccoli and a splash of water, cover and steam for 3 minutes. Add the spinach by the handful and stir until just wilted, about 2 minutes.
Season the greens with half the lemon juice and the pepper. Serve the salmon over the rice with the greens alongside and the rest of the lemon squeezed over the fish.
tip: Oiling the fish rather than the pan is the classic blackening trick: the crust sets without sticking. If the blend is very salty, use a little less.

name: Warm edamame with lemon and Aleppo pepper
inspiredBy: Inspired by Japanese izakaya edamame
about: A bowl of warm shelled edamame with a little salt, a good squeeze of lemon and a pinch of Aleppo pepper. It is **plant protein and fibre** in a snack that takes five minutes.
steps: Simmer the edamame in a small pot of water with a pinch of the salt for 3 to 4 minutes, until bright green and tender. Drain well.
Toss with the lemon juice, the rest of the salt and the Aleppo pepper and eat warm.

name: Apple slices with almonds
about: Crisp apple slices with some almonds, toasted if you have a minute. The apple brings **fibre and crunch**, and the almonds make it last.
steps: Slice the apple into wedges and fan them on a plate.
Serve with the almonds alongside, warm from a dry pan if you have a minute.

name: Smoky roasted chickpeas
inspiredBy: Inspired by Spanish garbanzos fritos
about: Canned chickpeas roasted until crisp with smoked paprika, cumin and a little salt. They give you **fibre and plant protein** in something that crunches like chips.
steps: Heat the oven to 220 C. Pat the chickpeas very dry with a clean towel, which is the secret to crunch.
Toss with the olive oil, paprika, cumin and salt on a baking tray in one layer.
Roast for 20 to 25 minutes, shaking the tray halfway, until golden and crisp. They crisp up more as they cool.
tip: Keep leftovers in an open container, not a sealed one, so they stay crisp for a day.
ingredients: no salt added, drained and dried well

name: Lemony sesame chickpea hummus with carrot and broccoli sticks
inspiredBy: Inspired by Levantine hummus, with toasted sesame seeds in place of tahini
about: A quick, smooth hummus made from chickpeas, toasted sesame seeds, lemon, garlic and a little cumin, with raw carrot and broccoli sticks for scooping. The vegetables bring **crunch, fibre and vitamin A**, and it takes ten minutes.
steps: Toast the sesame seeds in a dry pan over medium heat for 2 minutes, until golden and fragrant. Crush them in a mortar or whizz them in a spice grinder until sandy. A spoonful of seeds just spins around in a food processor.

Put the ground sesame in a small food processor with the chickpeas, lemon juice, garlic, oil, cumin, salt and a splash of cold water. Blitz until smooth, adding water a spoonful at a time until it is creamy and spoonable, scraping down the sides once or twice.
Serve with the carrot sticks and broccoli florets.
tip: Double the hummus. It keeps for 4 days in the fridge, and a few ice cubes in the blender make it extra creamy.

name: Cottage cheese with cherry tomatoes and cracked pepper
about: Cool, creamy cottage cheese with sweet halved cherry tomatoes, a squeeze of lemon and lots of black pepper. It is a savoury, **very high-protein snack** that takes two minutes.
steps: Spoon the cottage cheese into a bowl.
Pile the tomatoes on top, squeeze over the lemon and finish with a pinch of salt and plenty of cracked pepper.

name: Pineapple with lime and chili
inspiredBy: Inspired by Mexican fruta con limón y chile
about: Juicy pineapple chunks with a squeeze of lime and a dusting of cayenne, the way Mexican street carts serve it. It is **sweet, sharp and big on volume** for very few calories.
steps: Toss the pineapple chunks with the lime juice.
Dust with the cayenne and a tiny pinch of salt, and eat right away.

name: Greek yogurt with pear, walnuts and cinnamon
inspiredBy: Greek yiaourti me karydia, the everyday bowl of thick yogurt and nuts
about: Thick nonfat Greek yogurt with sliced pear, a handful of toasted walnuts and a dusting of cinnamon. It feels like a treat but carries **a big helping of protein**, so it keeps you going well past mid-morning.
steps: Toast the walnuts in a dry pan over medium heat for 3 to 4 minutes, shaking now and then, until they smell nutty. Tip them onto a plate to cool, then chop roughly.
Spoon the yogurt into a bowl and fan the pear slices over it.
Scatter on the warm walnuts and dust with cinnamon.
tip: Toast a jar of walnuts on Sunday and breakfast takes two minutes. Swap the pear for whatever fruit is in season: apple, plums or a few grapes all work.

name: Kagianas-style tomato eggs with feta and warm pita
inspiredBy: Greek kagianas, eggs scrambled into juicy tomatoes, with extra egg whites for protein
about: Ripe tomatoes cooked down until jammy, then softly scrambled with one whole egg, a few extra whites and a little crumbled feta. It is a very Greek breakfast, and the whites give it **a big protein hit** for few calories.
steps: Warm the olive oil in a small pan over medium heat and soften the onion for about 3 minutes.
Add the tomatoes, a pinch of salt and the oregano. Cook for 6 to 8 minutes, mashing with the spoon, until the juices have mostly cooked away and the tomatoes look jammy.
Whisk the egg and egg whites together and pour them into the tomatoes. Stir gently over low heat for 2 to 3 minutes until softly set and still glossy.
Crumble in the feta, scatter with parsley, add a squeeze of lemon and serve with the warm pita.
tip: Keep a carton of liquid egg whites in the fridge, so you are not left with a bowl of yolks. One white is about 2 tablespoons.
ingredients: from a carton or separated eggs
warmed, cut into strips for scooping

name: Spinach, zucchini and feta frittata
inspiredBy: Inspired by Italian frittata and Greek spanakopita filling
about: A thick, herby oven frittata packed with spinach and zucchini, mostly egg whites with two whole eggs for flavour and colour. It makes two portions, so the second one is **a cold breakfast ready** for tomorrow.
steps: Heat the oven to 180 C. Warm the olive oil in an oven-safe 20 cm pan over medium heat and soften the onion for 3 minutes.
Add the grated zucchini and cook for 3 to 4 minutes, until it has given up its water and is soft. Add the spinach by the handful until it wilts, about 2 minutes.
Whisk the eggs and the egg whites with the salt, pepper, dill, parsley and lemon juice. Pour over the vegetables and dot with the feta.
Cook on the stove for 1 minute to set the edges, then bake for 12 to 15 minutes, until just set and still slightly soft in the middle. Do not overbake, or the whites turn rubbery.
Cut it in half. Serve one half warm with the sliced tomato, cucumber and pita. Cool the other half, cover and refrigerate for tomorrow.
tip: Reheat it gently, or eat it cold from the fridge with the tomato and cucumber, which is just as good.
ingredients: 1 large egg per serving, so 2 in the pan
about 3 whites per serving, so 6 or 7 in the pan

name: Tuna, white bean and spinach salad
inspiredBy: Inspired by Tuscan tonno e fagioli
about: The Tuscan classic: tender white beans, good tuna, red onion and lemon, piled on baby spinach with capers for salt and bite. **Beans and tuna together** give you protein and fibre that fill you up on one plate.
steps: Soak the red onion slices in the lemon juice and vinegar for 5 minutes while you prep. It softens the bite.
Toss the beans with the shaved fennel, parsley, capers, olive oil and the onion with its juices. Season with pepper.
Pile the spinach on a big plate, spoon the beans over it and flake the tuna on top.
Serve with the warm pita.
tip: Use a tin of tuna packed in water, drained well, and let the olive oil in the dressing do the richness.

name: Big Greek salad with lemon-oregano chicken
inspiredBy: Greek horiatiki, with grilled chicken, chickpeas and a bed of baby spinach to make it a meal
about: Juicy lemon-oregano chicken over a big bowl of baby spinach, cucumber, tomato, peppers and olives, with feta and chickpeas. The plate is huge but light, and the **chicken, chickpeas and feta** carry the protein. It makes two portions, so tomorrow's lunch is done.
steps: Slice the chicken breasts in half horizontally so they are thin. Rub with half the lemon juice, the garlic, half the oregano and a pinch of salt. Leave for 10 minutes or up to a few hours.
Heat a grill pan or heavy skillet over medium-high heat. Cook the chicken for 3 to 4 minutes a side, until golden and no pink remains. Rest for 5 minutes, then slice.
Whisk the olive oil, the red wine vinegar, the rest of the lemon juice and the rest of the oregano in a jar. Chop the cucumber, tomato, onion and pepper.

Toss half the chopped vegetables, half the chickpeas and half the olives with half the dressing in a big bowl. Fold in half the spinach, top with half the chicken and half the feta, and serve with the warm pita.

Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch: the vegetables, chickpeas, olives, spinach, chicken and feta in one container, and the rest of the dressing in a small jar. Toss it together when you eat so everything stays crisp.
tip: No grill pan? Roast the thin cutlets at 220 C for 10 to 12 minutes instead.
ingredients: half for the chicken, half for the dressing

name: Cod, white bean and fennel stew with saffron
inspiredBy: Inspired by Spanish cod and white bean stews, with fennel and saffron
about: Flaky cod simmered in a saffron and fennel tomato broth with creamy white beans and a handful of spinach. It is light and deeply savoury, and the **cod, beans and greens** make a very filling bowl for the calories. Two portions: dinner now, lunch tomorrow.
steps: Warm the olive oil in a wide pot over medium heat. Cook the fennel and onion for 8 minutes, until soft and just turning golden at the edges. Add the garlic for the last minute.
Crumble in the saffron, then add the passata, the beans, 150 ml of water, the salt and pepper. Simmer for 10 minutes until it tastes like a proper stew.
Stir in the spinach until it wilts. Nestle in the cod, cover, and cook for 5 to 6 minutes, until it flakes easily.
Finish with the lemon juice and parsley. Serve in wide bowls with the warm pita for the broth.
Cool the second portion and keep it in the fridge. Reheat gently tomorrow, so the fish stays tender.
tip: Hake, haddock or any white fish works, and so does a handful of frozen peas at the end.
ingredients: passata or crushed tomatoes, no salt added (not paste)
warmed, cut into strips for dunking in the broth

name: Turkey keftedes in tomato sauce with zucchini and bulgur
inspiredBy: Greek keftedes, made with lean turkey and oats, in a simple tomato sauce
about: Herby baked meatballs scented with mint and oregano, simmered in tomato sauce with zucchini and chard, over fluffy bulgur. Fat-free ground turkey keeps them **high in protein**, and grated onion, zucchini and a few oats keep them tender. They reheat beautifully.
steps: Heat the oven to 200 C and line a tray. Mix the turkey, egg white, oats, grated onion, grated zucchini, the grated garlic, parsley, mint, oregano, most of the salt and the pepper with your hands until it just holds together. Roll into about 16 small balls.
Bake the keftedes for 14 minutes, turning once, until browned and cooked through.

Meanwhile, warm the olive oil in a wide pan and soften the sliced garlic for 30 seconds. Add the passata, diced zucchini, the last pinch of salt and a splash of water. Simmer for 10 minutes, until the zucchini is tender.
Stir in the chard, then slide the keftedes into the sauce and simmer for 5 minutes.
Cook the bulgur in twice its volume of boiling water for about 12 minutes, until tender. Fluff with a fork. At the Light size this is just a few spoonfuls, enough to catch the sauce.
Serve the keftedes and sauce over the bulgur with a squeeze of lemon. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: Roll a double batch of keftedes and freeze half raw on a tray, then bag them.
ingredients: 1 or 2 egg whites for the whole batch, as binder
grated and squeezed, for the meat mix
passata or crushed tomatoes, no salt added (not paste)

name: Spanish lentils with garlic shrimp and chard
inspiredBy: Spanish lentejas, with garlic shrimp (gambas) instead of chorizo
about: A pot of tender green lentils in a smoky pimentón sofrito, finished with sherry vinegar and garlicky shrimp. The **lentils and shrimp together** are a lot of protein for a modest plate, with iron from the lentils and chard, and the sherry vinegar brightens everything. It makes two portions.
steps: Warm half the olive oil in a pot over medium heat. Cook the onion, carrot and pepper for 8 minutes, until soft and sweet. Add half the garlic and the pimentón and stir for 30 seconds.
Add the lentils, passata, bay leaf, salt and enough water to cover by 3 cm. Simmer for 25 to 30 minutes, until the lentils are tender but still hold their shape.
Stir in the chard for the last 5 minutes until tender, then take off the heat and stir in the sherry vinegar.
Heat the rest of the oil in a skillet over high heat. Sear the shrimp with the rest of the garlic in two batches so they brown rather than steam, about 90 seconds each, until pink and curled.

Ladle half the lentils into a bowl, top with half the shrimp and the parsley. Keep the rest of the lentils and shrimp apart in the fridge for tomorrow, and warm the shrimp just through so they stay tender.
tip: Freeze the lentils alone for up to 3 months and cook fresh shrimp whenever you reheat.
ingredients: passata or crushed tomatoes, no salt added (not paste)
peeled and deveined, plain (the bag should list only shrimp)

name: Sicilian-style sardine, fennel and orange salad with chickpeas
inspiredBy: Inspired by Sicilian sardine and fennel pairings, with orange and olives
about: Crisp shaved fennel, juicy orange and peppery arugula with canned sardines, chickpeas and a few olives. The sweet and sharp mix is a classic, and the **sardines bring omega-3 and calcium** from their soft bones.
steps: Shave the fennel as thinly as you can with a knife or mandoline, and keep the feathery fronds.
Whisk the olive oil, lemon juice and vinegar in a big bowl. Add the fennel, chickpeas, onion and olives and toss.
Lay the arugula on a plate, spoon the fennel mix over it and add the orange rounds.
Top with the sardines, broken into big pieces, then the parsley, fennel fronds and a sprinkle of Aleppo pepper. Serve with the warm pita.
tip: Salad too sharp? Add a few more orange slices. Fresh sardines, grilled, are lovely here when you can get them.
ingredients: canned in olive oil, drained, bones in

name: Pork souvlaki with tzatziki, cabbage salad and pita
inspiredBy: Greek souvlaki, with a winter lahano salad instead of fries
about: Lemon, oregano and garlic pork skewers with a thick garlicky tzatziki, a crunchy lemony cabbage and carrot salad and a warm pita. The pork tenderloin is very lean and the **nonfat yogurt sauce** adds protein, not just flavour. It is the weekend project of the week, and it makes two portions.
steps: Cut the pork into 3 cm cubes. Mix with half the lemon juice, half the oil, half the garlic, the oregano, half the salt and the pepper. Leave for at least 1 hour in the fridge, or overnight.
For the tzatziki, stir together the yogurt, grated cucumber, the rest of the garlic, half the dill and a squeeze of lemon. Chill until needed.
Toss the cabbage and carrot with the rest of the lemon juice and oil, the parsley, the remaining dill and a pinch of salt. Leave it for 10 minutes so the cabbage softens a little.
Thread the pork onto skewers, soaked first if they are wooden. Grill or broil for 8 to 10 minutes, turning, until browned and just cooked through. Warm the pita on the grill for the last minute.
Serve half the pork and tzatziki with the cabbage salad and pita. Chill the rest, kept apart, for tomorrow.
tip: Tomorrow, slice the cold pork over the salad and spoon the tzatziki on top.

name: Chicken, chickpea and chard soup with lemon
inspiredBy: Inspired by Greek lemony chicken soups and Spanish chicken and chickpea pots
about: A bright, brothy soup with shredded chicken, chickpeas, carrots and plenty of chard, finished with lots of lemon and dill. It is warming but light, and the **chicken and chickpeas** give you plenty of protein.
steps: Warm the olive oil in a pot over medium heat and cook the onion and carrot for 6 minutes, until soft and golden. Add the garlic for 30 seconds.
Add the chicken whole, the chickpeas, the oregano, bay leaf, salt, pepper and 450 ml of water. Bring to a simmer and cook gently for 12 to 15 minutes, until the chicken is cooked through.
Lift out the chicken and shred it with two forks. Return it to the pot with the chard and cook for 4 minutes, until the chard is tender.
Take off the heat, stir in the lemon juice and dill, and serve with the warm pita.
tip: Saturday is a cooking day, so make the soup on Friday evening while you put the sardine salad together, and add the lemon and dill when you reheat it. For an avgolemono finish, whisk one egg with the lemon juice, stir in a ladle of hot broth, then stir it back in off the heat.

name: Roasted salmon with tomatoes, artichokes and white beans
inspiredBy: Inspired by Cretan baked fish and vegetables
about: A tray of zucchini, peppers, tomatoes, artichoke hearts and olives roasted until sweet and jammy, with a salmon fillet laid on top and white beans warmed in the juices. The **salmon brings omega-3 and vitamin D**, and the tray is mostly vegetables.
steps: Heat the oven to 220 C. Toss the zucchini, pepper, tomatoes and onion with half the olive oil, the oregano, salt and pepper on a big tray. Roast for 20 minutes, until soft and starting to blister.
Stir in the beans, artichoke hearts, olives and capers and make a gap in the middle of the tray.
Rub the salmon with the rest of the oil and lay it in the gap. Roast for 6 to 8 minutes, until it just flakes. Wild salmon is lean, so take it out the moment it does.
Squeeze over the lemon juice, scatter with parsley and add a pinch of Aleppo pepper if you like.
tip: Chop the vegetables a little smaller and they roast faster. Any leftover roasted vegetables are lovely cold in a pita. Coho or farmed salmon work too.
ingredients: wild sockeye, fresh or thawed from frozen, skin on or off
frozen artichoke hearts, thawed and halved

name: Lupini beans with lemon, olives and parsley
inspiredBy: Inspired by Spanish altramuces and Italian lupini
about: Firm, nutty lupini beans from the jar, dressed with lemon, parsley and a few olives. Lupini are **unusually high in protein**, so this little bowl is a satisfying, salty snack.
steps: Rinse the lupini well and drain them, then pat dry.
Toss with the lemon juice, parsley, olives, olive oil and Aleppo pepper.
tip: Pinch the skins off if you like: they slip right off, but they are fine to eat.

name: Orange and walnuts
inspiredBy: Greek fruit and nut snacks
about: Juicy orange segments with a small handful of walnuts, a sweet and crunchy snack. The orange covers **a full day of vitamin C** and the walnuts add omega-3 fat.
steps: Peel the orange and break it into segments.
Serve with the walnuts in a small bowl.

name: Dried figs with walnuts
inspiredBy: Inspired by Greek sika me karydia, figs with walnuts
about: Chewy dried figs with a small handful of walnuts, the classic Greek pairing. The figs bring **fibre and a little calcium** and the walnuts add omega-3 fat.
steps: Halve the figs.
Serve with the walnuts.

name: Roasted chickpeas with smoked paprika
inspiredBy: Inspired by Spanish garbanzos fritos, roasted not fried
about: Crunchy oven-roasted chickpeas with smoked paprika and a little cumin. They are an easy, **fibre-rich** way to scratch the crunchy itch.
steps: Heat the oven to 220 C. Drain the chickpeas and pat them very dry with a clean towel.
Toss with the olive oil, smoked paprika, cumin and salt on a tray.
Roast for 25 to 30 minutes, shaking the tray halfway, until crisp and deep golden.
tip: They are crispiest the day you make them. Roast a double batch on Wednesday alongside the keftedes (give them 30 to 35 minutes at 200 C) and keep the rest in a jar for Friday.

name: Cannellini and garlic dip with crunchy vegetables
inspiredBy: Inspired by Tuscan crema di cannellini
about: A smooth, lemony cannellini dip with garlic and olive oil, scooped up with cucumber and carrot. It is **creamy and filling** without any cream.
steps: Mash or blitz the beans with the lemon juice, garlic, olive oil and a splash of water until smooth.
Spoon into a bowl, drizzle with a few drops of the oil, dust with oregano and serve with the carrot and cucumber sticks.
tip: Make a double batch on Tuesday and keep half covered in the fridge for Wednesday's snack.

name: Tzatziki with pepper and carrot sticks
inspiredBy: Greek tzatziki, thick and garlicky
about: A big scoop of thick nonfat Greek yogurt tzatziki with cucumber, garlic and dill, for dipping crunchy pepper and carrot. It is **a protein-rich snack** that tastes like a meze.
steps: Stir the yogurt with the grated cucumber, garlic, dill, lemon juice, olive oil and salt.
Serve with the carrot and pepper sticks for dipping.

name: Foul medames with boiled eggs, tahini, raw onion and radish
inspiredBy: Jordanian and Palestinian foul, the breakfast of the foul stands in Amman, with a little chickpea in the pot as Lebanese cooks like it
about: Warm, creamy fava beans and chickpeas mashed with garlic, cumin and lemon, with a swirl of tahini, two boiled eggs and a pile of raw onion, radish, tomato and parsley on top. Scoop it all up with warm whole-wheat pita. The beans bring **fibre, folate and iron**, and the eggs add choline.
steps: Lower the eggs gently into a small pot of boiling water and cook for 8 minutes, then cool them under cold water and peel.

Mash the garlic with the salt into a paste. Warm the fava beans and chickpeas in a small pot with the garlic, the cumin and a splash of water, stirring now and then, until they are steaming hot, about 5 minutes.
Mash roughly with a fork. You want a creamy base with some whole beans left in it. Stir in the lemon juice and half the olive oil.
Stir the tahini with a spoonful of water until it is pourable, like thin cream.
Spoon the beans into a shallow bowl, drizzle with the tahini and the rest of the olive oil, and pile the tomato, onion, radish and parsley on top. Add the halved eggs.
Warm the pita in a dry pan or the toaster, tear it up and use it to scoop.
tip: A 400 g tin of foul makes two portions, so two foul mornings need only one tin. A pinch of chili flakes or a few chopped pickles on top is welcome.
ingredients: from a tin, drained and rinsed

name: Za'atar pita with labneh, olives, egg and cucumber
inspiredBy: the za'atar and olive oil breakfast of Jordan and Lebanon, in the style of a man'oushe
about: Warm pita brushed with za'atar and olive oil, a swirl of labneh, a soft-boiled egg, olives, cucumber and fresh mint. It is the everyday breakfast table in one plate. The labneh and egg bring **protein, calcium and choline**.
steps: Lower the egg gently into a small pot of boiling water and cook for 7 minutes for a jammy yolk. Cool it under cold water, then peel. You can boil a few ahead and keep them in the fridge.
Stir the za'atar into most of the olive oil to make a paste. Spread it over the pita and warm it in a dry pan or a hot oven for a couple of minutes, until it smells toasty.
Stir a pinch of salt into the labneh and swirl it onto a plate. Pour the rest of the olive oil into a little well in the middle.
Halve the egg and arrange it with the olives, sliced cucumber and mint around the labneh. Tear the pita and scoop.
tip: No labneh? Spoon thick Greek yogurt into a sieve lined with a clean cloth the night before, stir in a pinch of salt and let it drain in the fridge.

name: Balila, warm chickpeas with tahini, lemon, cumin and a boiled egg
inspiredBy: Lebanese and Palestinian balila, the warm chickpea breakfast
about: Warm, soft chickpeas in a little of their liquid with lemon, garlic and cumin, finished with a spoon of tahini, parsley and a good pour of olive oil, with a boiled egg alongside. It is simple, savoury and very filling. The chickpeas bring **fibre and protein** and the egg adds choline.
steps: Lower the egg gently into a small pot of boiling water and cook for 8 minutes, then cool it under cold water and peel.
Mash the garlic with the salt into a paste. Warm the chickpeas in a small pot with the garlic, the cumin and a splash of water for 5 minutes, until they are very hot and soft.
Mash a few of them against the side of the pot so the liquid turns creamy, and stir in the lemon juice.
Whisk the tahini with a spoonful of water until pourable.
Spoon the chickpeas and some of their liquid into a bowl. Drizzle over the tahini and the olive oil and scatter with the parsley.
Halve the egg and lay it on top. Warm the pita and serve with the radish on the side.
tip: Add a pinch of chili flakes or a few drops of hot sauce, the way balila is often served in Beirut.

name: Ijjeh, a herb and chard omelette with radish and mint salad
inspiredBy: Levantine ijjeh (eggah), with chard folded in and no flour
about: A thick, green, herby omelette packed with parsley, chard, onion and a little grated halloumi, cut into wedges and eaten with warm pita, crunchy radishes, cucumber and mint. It makes two portions, and the cold wedge is just as good tomorrow morning. The eggs bring **protein and choline**, and the parsley and chard bring vitamin K.
steps: Finely chop the parsley, chard and onion. Keep the chard stems, they stay pleasantly crisp.
Beat the eggs in a bowl with the baharat and half the salt, then stir in the grated halloumi, herbs, chard, onion and walnuts. It should look more green than yellow.

Heat the broiler. Warm half the oil in a medium oven-safe non-stick pan over medium-low heat. Pour in the egg mixture, cover, and cook gently until the edges are set and the top is almost firm, about 8 minutes.
Brush the top with the rest of the oil and slide the pan under the broiler for 2 minutes, until puffed and golden. Cut into wedges.
Slice the radishes and cucumber, toss with the mint, lemon juice and the rest of the salt, and serve beside a wedge with warm pita.
Wrap the second portion for tomorrow. Make a fresh salad then, and eat the wedge cold or tucked into pita.
tip: Leave out the walnuts if you like it softer. A pinch of cinnamon is traditional in some Syrian kitchens.

name: Lamb kafta pita with roasted cauliflower, tarator and tomato
inspiredBy: Lebanese and Palestinian kafta sandwiches, made with lean lamb and finished with tahini sauce and roasted cauliflower, as karnabeet is eaten
about: Finger-shaped patties of lean lamb, parsley and onion with baharat, tucked into warm whole-wheat pita with golden roasted cauliflower, tomato, a sumac onion salad and a lemony tahini sauce. It is street food you can make at home. The lamb brings **iron, zinc and vitamin B12**, and the tahini adds calcium.
steps: Heat the oven to 220 C. Toss the cauliflower with half the olive oil and a pinch of salt on a tray and roast until golden at the edges, about 20 minutes.
Pulse the lamb cubes in a food processor, in short bursts with a splash of ice water, until finely ground and sticky. Or ask the butcher to grind lean leg of lamb twice.

Squeeze the grated onion in your hands to get rid of the extra juice. Mix it with the lamb, most of the parsley, the baharat, black pepper and half the salt, kneading for a minute or two. Shape into 3 or 4 fingers about 8 cm long.
Warm the rest of the oil in a non-stick pan over medium-high heat and cook the kafta, turning now and then, until browned all over and cooked through, about 8 minutes.

Make the tarator. Stir the tahini with the lemon juice, the garlic (mashed to a paste), the rest of the salt and 2 to 3 tablespoons of cold water, until pale and pourable. Toss the sliced onion with the rest of the parsley and the sumac.
Warm the pita, fill it with the kafta, cauliflower, sliced tomato and sumac onions, and drizzle with the tarator.
tip: Roast the cauliflower and shape the kafta on Wednesday night while the oven is hot for the salmon. At lunch, fry the kafta and assemble. You can also freeze the shaped raw fingers.
ingredients: most for the kafta, a little for the salad

name: Fattoush with chickpeas and grilled halloumi
inspiredBy: Lebanese fattoush, with chickpeas and halloumi to make it a meal
about: A big, crunchy salad of romaine, radish, cucumber, tomato and mint under shards of toasted pita, with a sumac and pomegranate molasses dressing, spiced chickpeas and slices of golden halloumi. It is sharp, juicy and salty at once. The chickpeas and halloumi bring **protein and calcium**.
steps: Split the pita, tear it into pieces, toss with a little of the oil and toast in a dry pan or a hot oven until golden and crisp, about 5 minutes.
Make the dressing. Mash the garlic with a pinch of salt and whisk it with the lemon juice, pomegranate molasses and the rest of the olive oil.
Toss the chickpeas in a bowl with half the sumac, a pinch of salt and a spoonful of the dressing so they take on some flavour.
Slice the halloumi and cook it in a dry non-stick pan over medium-high heat for about 1 minute per side, until golden.
Chop the romaine, radish, cucumber and tomato into bite-size pieces, tear in the mint and toss with most of the dressing.
Pile on a plate, top with the chickpeas and halloumi, sprinkle with the rest of the sumac and add the pita pieces just before eating.
tip: Grilled chicken or a handful of toasted almonds are good on top too. Use a squeeze of extra lemon if you have no pomegranate molasses.

name: Musakhan-style sumac chicken and onions on pita
inspiredBy: Palestinian musakhan, roasted sumac chicken on bread soaked in onions, made with boneless thighs and a lighter hand with the oil
about: Chicken thighs rubbed with sumac and baharat and roasted until golden, piled on whole-wheat pita with a heap of slowly cooked sumac onions and toasted pine nuts. It is Palestine's best-loved dish, scaled down for a Saturday lunch. The chicken brings **protein and zinc**, and the onions bring plenty of flavour for very little fat.
steps: Heat the oven to 220 C. Rub the chicken with half the sumac, the baharat, the black pepper, a third of the oil and half the salt. Spread it on a small tray.
Roast until golden and cooked through, 25 to 30 minutes.

Meanwhile, cook the onions in the rest of the oil with the rest of the salt in a wide pan over medium-low heat, stirring now and then, until completely soft and golden, about 20 minutes, with a splash of water if they start to stick. Stir in the rest of the sumac and the lemon juice for the last minute.
Toast the pine nuts in a dry pan for 2 minutes, until golden, and watch them closely.
Warm the pita in the oven for the last 5 minutes. Spread the onions over it, lay the chicken on top and scatter with the pine nuts and parsley. Cut it into wedges and eat with your hands.
tip: Serve it with a spoonful of labneh or yogurt on the side if you like. Traditional musakhan is made with much more olive oil, and it is delicious.

name: Adas bi hamod, lemony lentil and chard soup
about: A sunny, sharp Lebanese lentil soup with plenty of chard, finished with crushed garlic and cilantro fried in olive oil and a good squeeze of lemon. It is cosy, hearty and better the next day, so it makes two portions. The lentils and chard bring **iron, folate and fibre**, and the lemon helps your body use that iron.
steps: Soften the onion in half the olive oil in a big pot over medium heat until golden, about 8 minutes.
Add the rinsed lentils and cover with plenty of water, about 4 times their volume. Bring to a boil, then simmer gently until the lentils are nearly tender, about 20 minutes.
Slice the chard stems and add them with a little salt. Cook for 5 minutes, then stir in the leaves and cook until they wilt and soften, about 5 minutes more.

Crush the garlic with a pinch of salt and the cilantro. Warm the rest of the olive oil in a small pan and fry this paste for a minute, until it smells wonderful. Stir it into the soup with the lemon juice.
Taste and add more lemon or salt until it is properly sharp and savoury. Tear the pita into pieces, toast them in a dry pan until crisp and scatter over each bowl.
Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch. The soup thickens as it sits, so loosen it with a splash of water when you reheat it.
tip: For a creamier soup, blitz a ladleful and stir it back in.

name: Shish tawook with parsley tabbouleh and toum-style garlic sauce
inspiredBy: Lebanese shish tawook, with a lighter whipped garlic sauce in place of full toum and a tabbouleh that is mostly parsley
about: Chunks of chicken marinated in yogurt, lemon and garlic and grilled until charred at the edges, with a bright tabbouleh that is mostly parsley and a sharp, punchy garlic sauce. It makes two portions, so tomorrow's lunch is covered. The chicken brings **protein and niacin**, and all that parsley brings vitamins K and C.
steps: Stir the yogurt with a third of the garlic (mashed to a paste), a third of the lemon juice, the baharat, the black pepper and half the salt. Add the chicken and turn to coat. Marinate for at least 30 minutes and up to 6 hours in the fridge.
Cover the bulgur with hot water and leave it for 15 minutes, until tender, then drain well and squeeze out the water.
Mix the bulgur with the parsley, mint, onion, half the remaining lemon juice, half the olive oil and a pinch of salt. Keep the tomato aside and add it at serving, so the tabbouleh stays fresh.
Thread the chicken onto skewers, or spread it on a tray, and grill or broil on high, turning once or twice, until charred at the edges and cooked through, 10 to 12 minutes.

Make the garlic sauce. Pound the rest of the garlic with a pinch of salt, then slowly whisk in the rest of the olive oil and the last squeeze of lemon, a few drops at a time, until it turns thick and creamy. It is a quick toum.
Serve the chicken with the tabbouleh, the tomato, the sauce and the romaine leaves to scoop. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch, with the tomato and sauce in separate containers.
tip: Chicken breast works too, but thighs stay juicier. If the garlic sauce splits, whisk in a teaspoon of cold water.
ingredients: boneless, skinless thighs, cut in 3 cm chunks

name: Samke harra, Lebanese spicy cilantro and walnut baked salmon with tomato bulgur
inspiredBy: Lebanese samke harra from Tripoli, with salmon in place of white fish, baked with a hot cilantro paste and topped with toasted walnuts
about: Salmon fillet rubbed with a fiery paste of cilantro, garlic, chili, cumin and lemon and baked until it flakes, with a tomato bulgur pilaf (burghul bi banadoura) and a handful of toasted walnuts on top. It is the Lebanese coast on a plate. The salmon brings **omega-3 fats and vitamin D**, and the walnuts add crunch.
steps: Heat the oven to 220 C. Soften half the onion, diced, in a third of the olive oil in a small pot, about 5 minutes, without browning it. Add half the chopped tomato and cook for 3 minutes, then stir in the bulgur, add double its volume of water and a pinch of salt, cover and simmer on low for 12 minutes. Leave it covered.
Meanwhile, pound or blitz the cilantro, garlic, chili, all the cumin, half the lemon juice, half the remaining oil and a pinch of salt into a rough, spoonable paste.
Rub the paste all over the fish, pressing it in well. Set the fish on a lined tray and bake until it flakes easily with a fork, 12 to 15 minutes.
Toast the walnuts in a dry pan for 2 minutes, until they smell nutty, and chop them roughly.
Toss the rest of the tomato and the sliced onion with the rest of the lemon juice, the last of the oil and a pinch of salt.
Serve the fish on the bulgur, scattered with the walnuts, with the tomato salad on the side.
tip: Sea bass, grouper, cod or halibut make the traditional version, and trout is lovely too. Use a smaller chili or leave out the seeds if you want less heat.
ingredients: seeded if you like less heat
chopped, half for the pilaf and half for the salad
half diced for the pilaf, half sliced for the salad

name: Mujadara hamra, lentils and bulgur with caramelised onions and malfouf salad
inspiredBy: Lebanese and Palestinian mujadara hamra, the version made with bulgur
about: Brown lentils and bulgur cooked with cumin and baharat and topped with deeply browned onions, with a crunchy mint, lemon and olive oil cabbage and carrot salad on the side. It is humble, filling and very much a Levantine home dinner. The lentils and bulgur bring **iron and fibre**, the carrot brings vitamin A, and it makes two portions for tomorrow's lunch.
steps: Simmer the lentils with the cumin in plenty of water for about 15 minutes, until they are almost tender but still have some bite. Drain, keeping the cooking water.

While they cook, cook the sliced onions in two-thirds of the olive oil with a pinch of salt in a wide pan over medium-low heat, stirring often, until they are deep golden brown and sweet, 30 to 35 minutes. Most of this time is hands-off. Lift out about a third for the top.

Add the lentils, bulgur, baharat and the rest of the salt to the pan with the remaining onions. Pour in enough of the lentil water to cover by about 1 cm, bring to a simmer, cover and cook on the lowest heat for 15 minutes.
Turn off the heat and leave it covered for 10 minutes so the bulgur finishes steaming, then fluff with a fork.
Make the cabbage salad, salata malfouf. Mash the garlic with a pinch of salt and toss it with the cabbage, carrot, lemon juice, mint and the rest of the olive oil.
Top the mujadara with the caramelised onions and serve with the salad. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch, with the salad dressed fresh. It reheats well, or eat it at room temperature.
tip: Slow, patient onions are the secret. If they start to catch, add a splash of water and keep going.

name: Spicy tomato sardines on toasted pita with parsley and onion salad
inspiredBy: the chili, garlic and tomato fish dishes of the Lebanese and Palestinian coast, made with canned sardines
about: Canned sardines warmed through in a garlicky, chili-spiked tomato sauce and spooned over toasted pita, with a sharp parsley, onion and sumac salad. It is on the table in about 35 minutes. Sardines are one of the best sources of **omega-3, calcium and vitamin D**, because you eat the soft bones.
steps: Warm the olive oil in a wide pan over medium heat. Cook the diced onion until soft, about 5 minutes, then add the garlic, chili and cumin and stir for a minute, until fragrant.
Add the tomatoes and half the salt. Simmer, pressing them down with the back of a spoon, until they collapse into a thick, jammy sauce, 12 to 15 minutes.
Nestle the sardines into the sauce, spoon some over the top and warm them gently for 3 to 4 minutes without stirring, so they stay in nice pieces.
Toss the sliced onion with the parsley, sumac, half the lemon juice and a pinch of salt. Toast the pita until crisp at the edges.
Squeeze the rest of the lemon over the sardines and serve with the pita and the parsley salad.
tip: Fresh sardines or small mackerel, seared and slipped into the sauce, are the classic version if you can find them at a fishmonger or Middle Eastern market. Use about 200 g of cleaned, butterflied fish.

name: Baked kibbeh with spiced lamb and walnut filling and tomato sumac salad
inspiredBy: Lebanese and Syrian kibbeh bil sanieh, made with lean lamb and plenty of bulgur
about: A tender layer of spiced lamb and bulgur dough over a savoury filling of onion, spiced lamb and walnuts, baked until the top is crisp and golden, with a tomato, onion and sumac salad. It is the weekend project dish. Lamb and bulgur bring **iron, zinc and B vitamins**, and it makes two portions.
steps: Rinse the bulgur, cover it with cold water and leave it for 20 minutes, then squeeze it very dry. Heat the oven to 200 C and brush a 20 cm square baking dish with a little of the oil.
Pulse the lamb cubes in a food processor, in short bursts, until finely ground. Or ask the butcher to grind lean leg of lamb twice. Set a third aside for the filling.

Make the filling. Soften half the kibbeh onion, finely chopped, in a spoonful of the oil. Add the reserved lamb and cook, breaking it up, until browned, about 5 minutes. Stir in the walnuts, a third of the baharat and a pinch of salt. Set aside to cool slightly.

Make the dough. Grate or blitz the other half of the kibbeh onion. Put the rest of the lamb, the squeezed bulgur, the grated onion, the rest of the baharat, the black pepper and the salt in the food processor and pulse in short bursts, adding a spoonful of ice water, until it is a smooth, sticky paste. Chill it for 15 minutes if it feels too soft.
With wet hands, press half the dough into the dish in a flat, even layer. Spread the filling over it, then pat the rest of the dough over the top, smoothing it to seal in the filling.
Score the top in diamonds with a wet knife, drizzle with the rest of the oil and bake until deep golden brown and crisp at the edges, 35 to 40 minutes. Rest for 10 minutes before cutting.
Meanwhile, slice the tomato and the salad onion very thinly, and toss with the parsley, sumac, lemon juice and a pinch of salt. Serve a portion with the salad.
Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch. Reheat the kibbeh in a hot oven and make a fresh salad.
tip: Keep the dough and the knife wet, it is what makes the top smooth. Kibbeh freezes very well, baked or unbaked.
ingredients: most for the kibbeh, a little for the salad

name: Baked mackerel on collapsed eggplant with tarator
inspiredBy: the Levantine pairing of fish with tarator, the tahini and lemon sauce, served over silky roasted eggplant
about: Mackerel fillets roasted over eggplant that has collapsed into a soft, silky bed with lemon, garlic and parsley, drizzled with a creamy tahini tarator. It is bold, rich and ready in about an hour, mostly in the oven. Mackerel is one of the richest sources of **omega-3 and vitamin D**, and the tahini adds calcium.
steps: Heat the oven to 230 C. Score the cut side of the eggplant halves in a diamond pattern, brush with half the olive oil and sprinkle with half the salt and the cumin. Roast cut side down on a tray until completely soft and collapsing, about 30 minutes.
Mash half the garlic with a pinch of salt. Mix it with a third of the lemon juice and a little of the olive oil, and chop most of the parsley into it.

Turn the eggplant cut side up and scoop and mash the flesh roughly with a fork on the tray. Spoon over the dressing, tuck the tomato halves around it and lay the mackerel on top, skin side up. Brush the fish with the rest of the olive oil.
Roast for 10 to 12 minutes more, until the fish flakes easily and the skin is crisp.
Make the tarator. Stir the tahini with the rest of the garlic, the rest of the lemon juice, a pinch of salt and 3 to 4 tablespoons of cold water until pale and pourable.
Serve the fish on the eggplant, drizzled with the tarator and the rest of the parsley, with warm pita.
tip: Any oily fish works here. The roasted eggplant keeps well, so roast extra for a baba ghanoush-style spread.

name: Silky hummus with radish and cucumber sticks
about: A proper creamy hummus made from a tin of chickpeas, with plenty of tahini and lemon, served with crunchy radishes and cucumber. Make the batch once and it covers both hummus snacks, with some left for the table. The chickpeas and tahini bring **fibre, protein and calcium**.
steps: Make a batch of 4 portions: blitz 1 tin of chickpeas (about 240 g drained) with 4 tablespoons of tahini, the juice of 1 lemon, 2 cloves of garlic, a pinch of cumin, a good pinch of salt and 4 to 6 tablespoons of ice-cold water for 3 to 4 minutes, until pale and silky. Keep it in the fridge for up to 4 days.
Spoon one portion (about a quarter of the batch) into a bowl, make a well in the middle and drizzle with the olive oil. Serve with the radish and cucumber sticks.
tip: Ice-cold water and a long blitz are the secret to a smooth, pale hummus. Rubbing the skins off the chickpeas makes it even silkier.

name: Dried figs and almonds
about: Chewy dried figs and a small handful of almonds, a pairing found on every Levantine market stall. It is sweet, crunchy and easy to carry. The figs bring **calcium and fibre** and the almonds bring vitamin E.
steps: Put the figs and almonds in a small bowl or a bag and eat together.
tip: In fig season, two or three fresh figs or a bunch of grapes are lovely in place of the dried figs.

name: Pomegranate seeds with toasted almonds
about: Juicy pomegranate seeds with a small handful of toasted almonds, sweet-sour with a crunch. It is bright, cool and a little festive. The almonds bring **vitamin E and protein** and the pomegranate brings fibre and vitamin C.
steps: Tip the pomegranate seeds into a small bowl.
Scatter with the toasted almonds and eat with a spoon.
tip: Pomegranates are in season in the fall. The rest of the year, buy a tub of seeds, or use fresh figs or grapes in season.

name: Grilled halloumi, cucumber and mint in pita
about: A few slices of golden grilled halloumi tucked into warm whole-wheat pita with cool cucumber and fresh mint, the way it is eaten in Lebanon and Jordan. It is salty, chewy and fresh. The halloumi brings **calcium and protein**.
steps: Slice the halloumi and cook it in a dry non-stick pan over medium-high heat for about 1 minute per side, until golden.
Warm the pita, tuck in the halloumi, sliced cucumber and mint, and add a squeeze of lemon.

name: Pomegranate seeds with walnuts
inspiredBy: the pomegranate and walnut pairing of Levantine muhammara
about: Juicy pomegranate seeds with a handful of walnuts, sweet and sour with a crunch, like the flavours of a muhammara dip. The walnuts bring **omega-3 fats** and the pomegranate brings vitamin C and fibre.
steps: Tip the pomegranate seeds into a small bowl.
Scatter with the walnuts and eat with a spoon.

name: Pita with tahini and dried figs
inspiredBy: tahini with date or grape molasses, a Levantine breakfast sweet, made with figs
about: Warm whole-wheat pita spread with tahini and topped with chopped dried figs, nutty and sweet. It is a good, filling snack. The tahini and figs bring **calcium and copper**.
steps: Warm the pita in a dry pan or the toaster.
Spread with the tahini, scatter over the chopped figs and fold.

name: Pomegranate bowl with mint and lemon
about: Juicy pomegranate seeds with torn mint and a squeeze of lemon, sweet, sour and very refreshing. It is a light bowl after a rich meal. The pomegranate brings **vitamin C and fibre**.
steps: Tip the pomegranate seeds into a bowl.
Tear over the mint and squeeze over the lemon juice.
tip: Pomegranates are in season in the fall. The rest of the year, buy a tub of seeds.

name: Za'atar pita with olives
inspiredBy: the zeit w za'atar plate of Jordan and Lebanon
about: Warm whole-wheat pita brushed with olive oil and za'atar, with a few olives on the side. It is a simple snack from a Levantine breakfast table. The whole-wheat pita brings **fibre and B vitamins**.
steps: Stir the za'atar into the olive oil and brush it over the pita.
Warm the pita in a dry pan or a hot oven for 2 minutes and serve with the olives.

name: Dried figs stuffed with walnuts
inspiredBy: the figs and walnuts of Levantine sweet trays
about: Soft dried figs with a walnut half tucked into each one, chewy and nutty. They taste like a sweet from a Levantine tray but are made of just two ingredients. The walnuts bring **omega-3 fats** and the figs bring calcium and fibre.
steps: Snip the stems off the figs and slit each one open.
Tuck a walnut half into each fig and eat the rest of the walnuts alongside.
tip: In fig season, use fresh figs or a bunch of grapes with the walnuts.

name: Yogurt with chopped figs and toasted almonds
about: Thick, cool yogurt with chopped dried figs for sweetness and crunchy toasted almonds on top. It is creamy, a little sweet and very quick. The yogurt brings **calcium and protein**, and the figs add more calcium.
steps: Stir most of the chopped figs into the yogurt.
Spoon into a bowl and top with the rest of the figs and the almonds.

name: Pita with olives, cucumber and mint
about: Warm whole-wheat pita with crunchy cucumber, a few olives and torn mint, the kind of plate you might pick at on a Levantine afternoon. It is fresh and filling. The cucumber and mint bring **vitamin K and potassium**.
steps: Slice the cucumber and toss it with the olives, mint, olive oil and salt.
Warm the pita and eat it with the salad, tucked inside or on the side.

name: Labneh, olive and mint pita roll
inspiredBy: the labneh sandwiches of Lebanese bakeries
about: Warm whole-wheat pita spread with labneh, olive oil and chopped olives, rolled up with fresh mint. It is a quick, filling snack. The labneh brings **protein and calcium**.
steps: Warm the pita in a dry pan or the toaster.
Spread it with the labneh, drizzle with the olive oil, scatter over the olives and mint, and roll it up.

name: Huevos rancheros on one tortilla with pinto beans
inspiredBy: Mexican huevos rancheros, with one tortilla and the beans doing more of the work
about: Fried eggs on a single warm corn tortilla, with a quick tomato and serrano salsa, creamy pinto beans, a little queso fresco and a few slices of avocado. The tortilla is counted, and the **beans and eggs slow the starch down** so the plate keeps you full until lunch.
steps: Make the salsa first. Warm half the oil in a small pan, then cook the tomato, onion, serrano and garlic for about 8 minutes, until the tomato has broken down and smells sweet. Mash it a little with the back of a spoon, stir in the lime juice and the salt, and keep it warm.
Tip the beans into a second small pot with a splash of water and a spoon of the salsa, mash about half of them, and warm them for 3 to 4 minutes until creamy.
Warm the tortilla in a dry skillet for about 30 seconds a side, until it is soft and has a few toasty freckles.
Fry the eggs in the rest of the oil over medium heat until the whites are set and the yolks are still runny, about 3 minutes.
Put the tortilla on a plate, set the eggs on top, spoon the beans beside them and cover everything with the warm salsa. Finish with the queso fresco, avocado and cilantro.
tip: Make the salsa the night before and the plate comes together in about 10 minutes. Leave out the serrano seeds for a milder version.

name: Arepa with pinto beans, queso fresco and avocado
inspiredBy: Colombian breakfast arepas, with a bowl of frijoles alongside as in a calentado
about: A crisp-edged arepa filled with crumbly queso fresco and avocado, next to a bowl of warm mashed pinto beans with a fresh tomato topping. Beans beside the arepa is a very Colombian way to start the day, and the **beans and cheese give the corn staying power**.
steps: Mix the masarepa with a pinch of the salt and just enough warm water to make a soft, damp dough, about 1 minute of kneading. Let it rest for 5 minutes, then shape it into a round about 1 cm thick. It is palm-sized at the Standard size and a small arepita at the Light size.
Heat the oil in a skillet over medium heat and cook the arepa for 5 to 6 minutes a side, until the outside is golden and crisp and it sounds hollow when you tap it.
While it cooks, warm the beans with the cumin and a splash of water for 4 minutes, then mash them roughly with a fork.
Toss the tomato, onion and cilantro with the lime juice and the rest of the salt.
Split the arepa and fill it with half the queso fresco and the avocado. Spoon the beans into a bowl, top them with the rest of the cheese and the tomato mixture, and eat them with the arepa.
tip: Cook a few arepas at once and freeze them. They reheat from frozen in a toaster or a dry pan in about 8 minutes. Choose no-salt-added beans and rinse them well; if yours are salted, skip the pinch of salt.

name: Papaya with Greek yogurt, lime, almonds and pepitas
inspiredBy: Mexican papaya with lime and chile, turned into a breakfast with yogurt, almonds and pepitas
about: Cold, thick yogurt with ripe papaya, a squeeze of lime and a handful of toasted almonds and pepitas, finished with a pinch of chile. It is a Mexican fruit-and-lime breakfast with **more protein from the yogurt and nuts**, so the fruit never arrives alone.
steps: Toast the almonds and pepitas in a dry skillet over medium heat for 3 to 4 minutes, shaking often, until the pepitas puff and pop and the almonds smell nutty. Tip them onto a plate to cool, then roughly chop the almonds.
Spoon the yogurt into a bowl and pile the papaya on top.
Squeeze over the lime, scatter on the nuts and seeds, and finish with a pinch of chile and a tiny pinch of salt.
tip: Toast a jar of almonds and pepitas on Sunday. Not a papaya fan? Cubed mango or a small orange does the same job.

name: Quinoa and chickpea salad with queso fresco and ají amarillo
inspiredBy: Peruvian quinoa salads and solterito, with chickpeas and hominy in place of fava beans and choclo
about: Fluffy quinoa tossed with chickpeas, tomato, hominy, onion and queso fresco in a lime and ají amarillo dressing. It borrows from the quinoa and queso fresco salads of Peru, and the **chickpeas and quinoa bring fibre and protein** for a modest spoonful of grain.
steps: Rinse the quinoa, then simmer it with twice its volume of water and a pinch of salt for about 14 minutes, until the little tails pop out. Fluff it, spread it on a plate and let it cool for 10 minutes.
Whisk the ají amarillo paste with the lime juice, oil and the rest of the salt.
Put the cooled quinoa, chickpeas, tomato, hominy and onion in a bowl, pour over the dressing and toss.
Fold in the cilantro and queso fresco just before serving.
tip: Cook the quinoa on Sunday and this lunch takes 5 minutes. Rinse it really well so it is not bitter. Freeze the rest of the hominy tin for Saturday's pozole.

name: Black bean soup with a poached egg, tortilla strips and radish
inspiredBy: Cuban sopa de frijoles negros, finished with Mexican-style toppings: tortilla strips, queso fresco and crema
about: A smoky, garlicky black bean soup built on a Cuban-style sofrito, with a poached egg, crisp baked tortilla strips, radish, a little queso fresco and a spoon of yogurt crema. The beans are the star, so it is **mostly fibre and protein** with just one tortilla for crunch.
steps: Heat the oven to 200°C (400°F). Toss the tortilla strips with a few drops of the oil and bake on a tray for 6 to 8 minutes, until crisp and golden.

Warm the rest of the oil in a pot and cook the onion and red pepper over medium heat for about 6 minutes, until soft. Add the garlic, cumin and oregano and stir for 30 seconds, until you can smell them.
Add the beans, the bay leaf and enough water to just cover, then simmer for 12 minutes. Mash about a third of the beans against the side of the pot to thicken the soup.
Take out the bay leaf and stir in the vinegar, lime juice and salt. Taste it, because it should be bright.
Crack the egg into the simmering soup, put the lid on, and poach it for about 3 minutes, until the white is set and the yolk is still soft.
Ladle into a bowl with the egg on top, then add the tortilla strips, radish, queso fresco, cilantro and a spoon of yogurt mixed with a squeeze of lime, as crema.
tip: Double the soup and freeze a portion without the toppings. It thaws well and the beans stay creamy. Choose no-salt-added beans and rinse them well; if yours are salted, use half the salt.

name: Shrimp ceviche with avocado on a baked tostada
inspiredBy: Mexican ceviche de camarón, with the shrimp briefly cooked first, one tostada and crunchy jícama
about: Shrimp quickly poached, then cured in lime juice with onion, tomato, cucumber, serrano and cilantro, and spooned over one crisp baked tostada with avocado. It is bright, cold and filling, and the **shrimp carry almost all the protein** with hardly any starch.
steps: Bring a pot of salted water to a boil and drop in the shrimp for 1 to 2 minutes, just until pink and curled. Drain, cool in cold water, then chop into bite-sized pieces.
Toss the shrimp with the lime juice and the onion and chill for 15 minutes. The lime will turn the onion pink and take the edge off it.
Meanwhile, heat the oven to 200°C (400°F) and bake the tortilla on a rack for 8 to 10 minutes, until crisp like a tostada.
Stir the tomato, cucumber, serrano, cilantro and salt into the shrimp, then fold in the avocado gently at the last minute.
Spoon the ceviche over the tostada and serve with the jícama and carrot sticks.
tip: You can use cooked, peeled shrimp from the fish counter and skip step one. Fresh tomatoes and lime make all the difference, so don't rush those.

name: Chicken tinga lettuce tacos with one tortilla and black beans
inspiredBy: Mexican tinga de pollo, usually served on tostadas, here in lettuce cups with one tortilla
about: Shredded chicken simmered in a smoky chipotle and tomato sauce, piled into crisp lettuce cups, with one warm corn tortilla and a bowl of black beans on the side. The **lettuce and beans stretch the meal**, so you get tacos without a stack of tortillas.
steps: Put the chicken in a pot with water to cover, the chunk of onion, the bay leaf and a pinch of the salt. Bring to a simmer and cook gently for 15 to 18 minutes, until the chicken is cooked through and pulls apart.
Lift the chicken out, keep a cup of the broth, and shred the meat with two forks.

Warm the oil in a wide pan and cook the sliced onion for 5 minutes, until soft. Add the garlic, oregano and cumin, then the tomato and chipotle, and cook for about 8 minutes, until the sauce thickens and darkens.
Stir in the shredded chicken with a splash of the broth and simmer for 5 minutes. Add the lime juice and the rest of the salt.
Warm the black beans with a little of the broth, and warm the tortilla in a dry skillet.
Fill the lettuce cups with the tinga and scatter the cilantro on top. Serve the beans and the tortilla on the side. This makes two portions, so pack the second one for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: Chipotles in adobo vary in heat. Start with half and add more at the end. The tinga freezes well for a month. Choose no-salt-added beans and rinse them well; if yours are salted, skip the pinch of salt.
ingredients: a small chunk for the pot, the rest thinly sliced

name: Mackerel escabeche with ají amarillo, camote and chickpeas
inspiredBy: Peruvian pescado en escabeche, with mackerel, chickpeas and the usual camote kept small
about: Seared mackerel under a warm, tangy pile of onion and ají amarillo cooked with vinegar, served with a few slices of roasted sweet potato and warm chickpeas. The **mackerel is a rich source of omega-3**, and the vinegar keeps the whole plate bright.
steps: Heat the oven to 220°C (425°F). Toss the sweet potato with a little of the oil and half the salt and roast on a tray for 20 to 25 minutes, turning once, until soft and browned at the edges.

Warm half the remaining oil in a skillet and cook the onion with the bay leaf for about 6 minutes, until soft. Add the garlic, ají amarillo paste and cumin, stir for 1 minute, then pour in the vinegar and a splash of water and simmer for 3 minutes. Take out the bay leaf.
Pat the mackerel dry and season with the rest of the salt. Sear it skin side down in a hot pan with the last of the oil for about 4 minutes, until the skin is crisp, then flip for 1 minute.
Warm the chickpeas with a spoonful of the onion sauce and the lime juice.
Lay the tomato slices on a plate, set the chickpeas and sweet potato beside them, put the mackerel on top and spoon the warm onion sauce over. Finish with the cilantro.
tip: Escabeche is just as good cold. Double the onion sauce and keep it for 3 days in the fridge. No Atlantic mackerel? Salmon or trout fillet works in the same sauce.

name: Arroz con pollo with brown rice and a big salad
inspiredBy: Caribbean and Colombian arroz con pollo, with brown rice and a lot more vegetables
about: Chicken thighs and brown rice simmered together with sofrito, achiote and carrot, served next to a big, lime-dressed cabbage, lettuce and tomato salad. The rice is a **modest portion that stays tender in the pot**, and the salad does the filling.
steps: Season the chicken with half the salt and the cumin. Warm the oil in a wide, heavy pot and brown the chicken for about 5 minutes, then move it to a plate.
In the same pot, cook the onion and red pepper for 5 minutes. Add the garlic, achiote paste, tomato paste and oregano and stir for 1 minute, until the pastes melt and the pot turns a deep orange.
Stir in the rice, return the chicken, and add water to cover the rice by about a finger. Bring to a boil, cover, and cook on the lowest heat for 35 minutes.
Scatter the carrot over the top, cover again, and cook for 10 more minutes, until the rice is tender and the liquid is gone. Rest it, covered, for 5 minutes, then fold in half the cilantro.
Toss the cabbage, lettuce and tomato with the lime juice, the rest of the cilantro and the rest of the salt.
Serve the rice and chicken with a big pile of salad. This makes two portions, so pack the second one for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: Use a 3 litre lidded pot. The rice is mostly hands-off, so make the salad while it cooks. Add a splash of water when you reheat the leftovers.

name: Ropa vieja with black beans and baked plantain
inspiredBy: Cuban ropa vieja, with more beans and vegetables and a small portion of ripe plantain
about: Cuban shredded flank steak simmered with peppers, tomato and a splash of vinegar, served with black beans, a few slices of baked ripe plantain and a crunchy slaw. It is rich, and the **beans and slaw come alongside the plantain** so the sweetness is not alone.
steps: Season the beef with the cumin and half the salt. Warm half the oil in a heavy pot and brown the pieces for about 3 minutes a side. Add water just to cover and the bay leaf, bring to a simmer, cover, and cook for about 90 minutes, until a fork pulls it apart.
Meanwhile, heat the oven to 200°C (400°F) and bake the plantain slices on a tray for 20 minutes, turning once, until soft and caramelized at the edges.
Lift the beef out and shred it along the grain with two forks. Pour off most of the broth, keeping about half a cup.

Warm the rest of the oil in the pot and cook the onion and red pepper for 6 minutes. Add the garlic, oregano and tomato paste, stir for a minute, then add the tomato and the reserved broth and simmer for 8 minutes.
Return the beef to the sauce and simmer for 8 to 10 minutes. Stir in the vinegar and most of the rest of the salt. Warm the beans with a splash of water and the last pinch of salt.
Toss the cabbage with the lime juice and cilantro. Serve the ropa vieja with the beans, plantain and slaw. This makes two portions, so pack the second one for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: A pressure cooker does the beef in about 50 minutes. Braise it on Sunday and Thursday's dinner takes 30 minutes. Choose no-salt-added beans and rinse them well; if yours are salted, skip the pinch of salt.

name: Salmon with salsa verde, curtido and pinto beans
inspiredBy: Mexican salsa verde and Salvadoran curtido, here with salmon
about: Pan-seared salmon on a bright tomatillo and serrano salsa, with a crunchy Salvadoran-style curtido and warm pinto beans. The **salmon brings omega-3 and vitamin D**, and the tangy curtido and beans keep the plate balanced.
steps: Make the curtido first. Toss the cabbage, carrot and onion with the vinegar, oregano and a pinch of the salt, and squeeze it with your hands for a minute until it starts to soften. Leave it for at least 15 minutes.
Broil or pan-roast the tomatillos, serrano and garlic for about 8 minutes, until blistered and soft. Blend them with the cilantro, lime juice and a pinch of salt into a loose salsa.
Warm the beans in a small pot with a splash of water and mash them lightly. Warm the tortilla in a dry skillet.
Pat the salmon dry and season it with the remaining salt. Sear it skin side down in the oil over medium-high heat for 4 to 5 minutes, until the skin is crisp, then flip for 1 to 2 minutes.
Spoon some salsa onto a plate, set the salmon on top, and serve with the curtido, the beans topped with queso fresco, and the tortilla.
tip: Make the curtido on Sunday. It keeps 5 days and is great on anything with beans. Drained canned tomatillos work out of season.

name: Pozole rojo with lots of cabbage and radish
inspiredBy: Mexican pozole rojo, with a lot more cabbage and radish and a smaller scoop of hominy
about: The big weekend pot: pork simmered with hominy in a rich guajillo broth, then piled with shredded cabbage, radish, onion and lime. It is warming and festive, and the **mountain of cabbage and radish** keeps the hominy portion modest.
steps: Put the pork in a big pot with half the onion, half the garlic, the bay leaf and enough water to cover by a few finger-widths. Bring to a boil, skim off the foam, then simmer gently for about 75 minutes, until the pork is tender.
Toast the guajillo in a dry pan for about 30 seconds a side until fragrant, then cover with hot water and soak for 15 minutes.

Blend the soaked chiles with about a cup of fresh water (the soaking water can taste bitter), the rest of the garlic and half the oregano until completely smooth. It is a lot of chile, and that is what makes the broth deep and brick red. Fry the paste in the oil for 3 to 4 minutes in a small pan, until it darkens and smells rich, then scrape it into the pot.
