Make the bhindi: warm the canola in a wide pan over medium-high heat, add the okra in two batches so it browns instead of steaming, and cook, stirring only now and then, until it is browned and no longer sticky, about 8 minutes in all. Add the crushed coriander, the last pinch of turmeric, a pinch of the cumin and a pinch of salt.

Knead the atta with a little water into a soft dough and rest it for 15 minutes. Roll a thin round for each portion (a small, palm-sized one on the lighter sizes) and cook on a hot dry pan until it puffs and has brown spots.

Warm the ghee in a small pan. Add the cumin and mustard seeds and let them pop, then the garlic, hing, curry leaves and the rest of the green chili. Take the pan off the heat, stir in the Kashmiri chili and pour the tadka over the dal. Stir in the cilantro.
Serve the dal with the bhindi and a roti each. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch, and warm the roti in a dry pan or wrapped in foil.
tip: An Instant Pot or pressure cooker gets the dal done in about 12 minutes. Soak the dal for 30 minutes and it takes about 25 in an open pot. Kokum is the traditional souring agent if you have it. Knead dough for four rotis at once and keep it in the fridge for 2 days, or use a frozen whole-wheat roti from the South Asian grocer.
ingredients: washed, dried well and cut in rounds

name: Tandoori chicken tray with roasted chickpeas, kachumber and mint raita
inspiredBy: Punjabi tandoori chicken, baked on a tray at home
about: Chicken thighs marinated in yogurt and Kashmiri chili, roasted on one tray with cauliflower, carrot, onion and chickpeas until the edges char, with a cooling mint raita and a tomato and onion kachumber. The chickpeas and vegetables give **protein, fibre and crunch** next to the chicken, with one roti for the starch.
steps: Make the marinade: stir the marinating yogurt with the grated ginger and garlic, half the lemon juice, the Kashmiri chili, garam masala, cumin, coriander, turmeric, kasuri methi (crushed between your fingers), about half a teaspoon of the oil and the salt. Coat the chicken and leave it for at least 30 minutes, or overnight in the fridge.

Heat the oven to 230°C (450°F) and line a big tray. Toss the chickpeas with a little of the oil and a pinch of salt and roast them alone for 10 minutes while the oven finishes heating and the chicken sits.

Toss the cauliflower, carrot and onion wedges with the rest of the oil and a pinch of salt, add them to the tray with the chickpeas and nestle the chicken on top. Roast for 25 to 30 minutes, turning the chicken once, until it is charred at the edges and cooked through, and the chickpeas are crisp.

Make the raita: stir the chopped mint and a pinch of salt into the remaining yogurt. Toss the tomato and the rest of the onion, finely chopped, with the remaining lemon juice and the chaat masala for the kachumber.

Knead the atta with a little water into a soft dough, rest it 15 minutes and roll it into one thin round. On the lighter sizes it is a small roti, about the size of your palm, and that is plenty next to everything else on the plate. Cook it on a hot dry pan until it puffs and has brown spots.

Toast the almonds in a dry pan and scatter them over the tray. Serve the chicken tray with the kachumber first, then the raita and the roti. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch, with the raita and kachumber in separate containers.
tip: Marinate it in the morning if you can; even 15 minutes helps. Reheat the leftover tray for 8 minutes at 200°C so the edges crisp again. Knead dough for four rotis at once and keep it in the fridge for 2 days, or use a frozen whole-wheat roti from the South Asian grocer.
ingredients: skinless thighs, cut in big chunks
about 3 tablespoons for the marinade, the rest for the raita
55 g in wedges for the tray, the rest for the kachumber
toasted and chopped, for the top

name: Pepper and tamarind salmon with parippu and spinach mallung
inspiredBy: Sri Lankan ambul thiyal (sour fish curry, usually tuna), with parippu and a mallung
about: Salmon rubbed with black pepper and tamarind and cooked until sticky, with a creamy red lentil parippu, a spinach mallung and a spoonful or two of brown basmati. It is a Sri Lankan rice-and-curry plate where the lentils and greens take up most of the room, and the salmon brings **omega-3 and vitamin D**.
steps: Use the brown basmati you froze on Sunday, thawed overnight in the fridge, and warm your portion with a splash of water. Cooking this on its own? Boil about 100 g raw in plenty of water for 25 minutes, drain, and keep the rest up to 4 days

Make the parippu: put the lentils in a pot with half the turmeric, the cinnamon, the cardamom, half the garlic, half the onion and plenty of water. Simmer until the lentils collapse into a creamy dal, about 18 minutes. Stir in half the coconut and half the salt. Finish the parippu with a quick tempering: pop a few of the mustard seeds and a few curry leaves in about half a teaspoon of the oil and stir it in.
Mix the black pepper, half the turmeric, the tamarind, the ginger, the lemon juice and a pinch of salt into a paste and rub it over the salmon.
Warm half of the remaining oil in a non-stick pan over medium heat. Cook the salmon for 3 to 4 minutes per side, spooning over any paste left in the bowl, until it is sticky and just cooked through.

Make the mallung: in a second pan, warm the last of the oil, pop the rest of the mustard seeds, then add the rest of the curry leaves, the Kashmiri chili, the rest of the garlic and onion and the green chili. Add the spinach and a splash of water, cook for 2 to 3 minutes until wilted, then stir in the rest of the coconut and a pinch of salt.
Serve the salmon with the parippu, the mallung and the rice, starting with the greens. Eat this one fresh rather than saving it for tomorrow.
tip: Ambul thiyal cooks dry in a clay pot with tuna and goraka (a sour fruit), so this is a quicker pan version with tamarind. Mackerel works as well as salmon.
ingredients: skinless fillet, in two or three pieces
half for the parippu, half for the mallung; fresh grated, or unsweetened desiccated
30 g for the parippu, 30 g for the mallung

name: Barley haleem with goat and dals
inspiredBy: Pakistani and Hyderabadi haleem, with barley doing most of the wheat's job
about: The slow, rich Pakistani stew of tender goat, barley and lentils beaten smooth and finished with fried onions, ginger, lemon and fresh herbs, with a crisp cucumber and onion salad. Barley digests slowly, and together with the dals it makes a pot **full of fibre and protein**.
steps: Soak the barley and the dals in plenty of water for at least 4 hours or overnight, then drain.

Warm the canola in a heavy pot over medium heat. Fry the thinly sliced onion, stirring often, until it is deep golden brown and crisp at the edges, about 12 minutes. Lift out about two thirds and keep it for the top.

Add the chopped onion to the pot with the bay leaf, cumin, clove and cinnamon and cook for 4 minutes. Add the grated ginger, the garlic and the goat, and brown the meat for about 5 minutes. Stir in the turmeric, Kashmiri chili, coriander, black pepper and salt.
Add plenty of water to cover and simmer the goat, partly covered, until it is very tender, about 1 hour 15 minutes, or 30 minutes in a pressure cooker.
Add the drained barley and dals and more hot water, and cook gently, stirring now and then, until everything is falling apart, about 45 minutes, or 25 minutes in a pressure cooker.

Pick out any bones and the bay leaf. Beat the haleem hard with a wooden spoon, or give it a few pulses with a hand blender, until the meat shreds and it turns thick and stretchy. Stir in the garam masala and the ghee.

Toss the cucumber with the onion you kept for the salad, thinly sliced, a squeeze of the lemon and a pinch of salt. Toast the almonds in a dry pan until golden. Serve the haleem topped with the fried onions, the almonds, the ginger strips, the rest of the lemon juice, the green chili and the cilantro, with the salad to eat first.
Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch. Haleem keeps for 4 days in the fridge and freezes well.
tip: Make a double batch in a pressure cooker, which cuts the cooking to about an hour, and freeze two portions. Boneless lamb or beef works in place of goat.
ingredients: bone-in or boneless goat stewing meat, cut in chunks
35 g sliced thinly for frying, 20 g for the salad, the rest chopped
half grated, half cut in thin strips to serve

name: Palak paneer with a roti and cucumber-onion salad
inspiredBy: Punjabi palak paneer
about: Soft cubes of paneer in a smooth, garlicky spinach gravy with ginger and garam masala, with one fresh whole-wheat roti and a cucumber and onion salad. The spinach brings **folate and vitamin A**, and the paneer and yogurt are the protein.
steps: Boil a pot of water, drop in the spinach and push it under for 1 minute, then drain and rinse under cold water so it stays bright green. Squeeze it lightly and blend with the green chili to a smooth purée.
Warm the oil in a pan over medium heat. Add the cumin seeds, then the onion for the gravy and cook until golden, about 7 minutes. Add the ginger and garlic and stir for 1 minute.
Stir in the turmeric, the crushed coriander and the Kashmiri chili, then the chopped tomato, and cook until it breaks down into a thick paste, about 5 minutes.

Pour in the spinach purée with a splash of water and simmer for 5 minutes. Add the paneer, the salt and the garam masala, crush the kasuri methi in over the top and simmer for 3 minutes more. Take the pan off the heat and stir in the yogurt.

Knead the atta with a little water into a soft dough, rest it 15 minutes and roll it into one thin round. On the lighter sizes it is a small roti, about the size of your palm, and that is plenty next to everything else on the plate. Cook it on a hot dry pan until it puffs and has brown spots on both sides.
Toss the cucumber and the sliced onion with the lemon juice and a pinch of salt, and serve with the palak paneer and the roti, eating the salad first.
tip: Firm tofu cubes are a good swap for the paneer, and they take on the gravy just as well. Knead dough for four rotis at once and keep it in the fridge for 2 days, or use a frozen whole-wheat roti from the South Asian grocer.
ingredients: 55 g for the gravy, the rest sliced for the salad

name: Guava chaat with almonds
inspiredBy: Pakistani and Punjabi roadside fruit chaat
about: Ripe guava chunks tossed with lemon and chaat masala, with a small handful of almonds for crunch. Guava is one of the **highest-fibre fruits**, and the almonds bring protein and healthy fat, so the fruit never comes on its own.
steps: Toss the guava with the lemon juice, chaat masala and black salt, and eat it with the almonds.
ingredients: cut in chunks, seeds and all

name: Oven-roasted masala chickpeas
inspiredBy: Indian roasted chana, made from canned chickpeas
about: Crunchy chickpeas roasted with chaat masala, amchur and a little Kashmiri chili. A **protein and fibre snack** you can keep in a jar for a day or two.
steps: Heat the oven to 220°C (425°F). Pat the chickpeas completely dry with a towel, since dry chickpeas get crunchy.
Toss them with the oil, chaat masala, amchur, Kashmiri chili and salt, spread them on a tray and roast for 25 to 30 minutes, shaking the tray halfway, until crisp.
Squeeze over the lemon juice and eat warm.
tip: Roast a double batch and keep half in a jar for another day. Once cooled, they stay crunchy for a day or two.

name: Chickpea sundal
inspiredBy: Tamil sundal
about: Tamil temple-style chickpeas with mustard seeds, curry leaves and a bit of raw onion. Warm, savoury and full of **plant protein and fibre**.
steps: Warm the oil in a pan. Pop the mustard seeds, then add the Kashmiri chili, curry leaves, hing and chopped green chili for 20 seconds.
Add the chickpeas and the salt and toss for 3 minutes until hot. Stir in the onion and finish with the lemon juice.

name: Cucumber and mint raita
inspiredBy: North Indian and Pakistani raita
about: Cold yogurt with grated cucumber, mint and roasted cumin, with a pinch of black salt. **High in protein and calcium**, it is a snack you eat with a spoon.
steps: Loosen the yogurt with a splash of water, then stir in the grated cucumber, mint, crushed cumin and black salt.
ingredients: thinned with a splash of water

name: Sprouted moong kosambari
inspiredBy: Karnataka kosambari
about: A Karnataka salad of sprouted moong with carrot, tomato, a little coconut and lemon, tempered with mustard seeds. Crunchy, light and a good **hit of protein and fibre** for very few calories.
steps: Toss the sprouts, carrot, tomato, coconut, cilantro and green chili in a bowl.
Warm the oil in a small pan, pop the mustard seeds, and pour it over the salad with the lemon juice and the salt. Toss and eat right away.

name: Masala peanuts
inspiredBy: Indian and Pakistani masala peanuts
about: Warm roasted peanuts tossed with chopped onion, tomato, green chili, lemon and chaat masala, as sold at every Pakistani and Indian street corner. A small bowl gives you **protein and healthy fats** with some freshness on top.
steps: Toss the peanuts with the onion, tomato, cilantro and green chili, then add the lemon juice, chaat masala and salt. Eat it right away so the peanuts stay crunchy.

name: Masala boiled egg with carrot sticks
inspiredBy: Indian masala egg
about: A hard-boiled egg with chaat masala, black pepper and lemon, with crunchy carrot sticks on the side. Small, quick and **a good source of choline**.
steps: Lower the egg into boiling water and cook for 9 minutes. Cool it in cold water, peel and halve.
Sprinkle the egg with the chaat masala, pepper, salt and lemon juice and eat it with the carrot sticks.
tip: Boil a few eggs on Sunday and keep them in their shells in the fridge for the week.

name: Egg chaat
inspiredBy: Pakistani and Delhi anda chaat
about: A boiled egg chopped with raw onion, tomato, cilantro and green chili, with lemon and chaat masala, the way it is sold from street carts in Pakistan and Delhi. Small, sharp and a good source of **choline and protein**.
steps: Lower the egg into boiling water and cook for 9 minutes. Cool it in cold water, peel and chop it roughly.
Toss the egg with the onion, tomato, cilantro and green chili, then add the lemon juice, chaat masala, pepper and salt and eat it right away.
tip: Use one of the Sunday eggs and it is ready in 5 minutes, or boil one while you chop.

name: Toor dal rasam in a mug
inspiredBy: Tamil milagu rasam
about: A thin, peppery South Indian rasam with a spoon of toor dal, tomato, garlic and curry leaves, sipped warm. It gives you **a little protein and fibre** and a lot of flavour.
steps: Simmer the dal with plenty of water until very soft, about 30 minutes (12 in a pressure cooker), and whisk it smooth.
Add the tomato, garlic, tamarind, rasam powder, pepper, salt and a cup of water and simmer for 10 minutes.
Warm the oil in a small pan, pop the mustard seeds and curry leaves, pour it in and finish with cilantro. Sip it hot.
tip: Make a double batch on Sunday and keep it in the fridge for 3 days; reheat a mug at a time.

name: Haldi doodh with cardamom and almonds
inspiredBy: Indian haldi doodh (turmeric milk)
about: Warm milk simmered with turmeric, black pepper and cardamom, with finely crushed almonds on top and no sugar. A glass gives you **calcium, protein and B12**, and it is a lovely way to end a day.
steps: Stir the turmeric into a splash of the cold milk until no lumps are left, then pour it into a small pot with the rest of the milk, the pepper and the cardamom. Warm, stirring, until it just starts to steam, about 5 minutes. Do not let it boil over.
Crush the almonds very fine, pour the milk into a mug and stir them in.
tip: No sugar is needed, but a pinch of cinnamon makes it taste sweeter.

name: Moong dal shorba in a mug
inspiredBy: Pakistani and Punjabi dal shorba
about: A light, lemony moong dal soup with ginger, garlic and cumin, sipped warm. Moong cooks to a soft, silky soup and gives you **plant protein and fibre** in a mug.
steps: Rinse the dal and simmer it with the tomato, half the ginger, the turmeric and plenty of water until completely soft, about 20 minutes. Whisk it smooth.
Warm the oil in a small pan and cook the cumin, the rest of the ginger and the garlic until fragrant, about 1 minute. Stir it into the soup with the pepper and the salt.
Finish with the lemon juice and cilantro and sip it hot.
tip: It keeps for 3 days in the fridge. Add a splash of water when you reheat it.

name: Paneer tikka bites with mint
inspiredBy: Punjabi paneer tikka
about: Cubes of paneer rubbed with Kashmiri chili, ajwain and lemon and roasted until the edges are golden, with fresh mint. A small, **high-protein** snack that holds its shape.
steps: Heat the oven to 220°C (425°F). Toss the paneer cubes with the oil, Kashmiri chili, ajwain, half the lemon juice and the salt.
Roast on a tray for 10 to 12 minutes, turning once, until golden at the edges.
Toss with the mint, the chopped green chili, the chaat masala and the rest of the lemon juice, and eat them warm.

name: Chakchouka with green pepper, harissa and two eggs
inspiredBy: Chakchouka, the Algerian and Tunisian cousin of shakshuka
about: Eggs poached in a thick, spicy sauce of tomato, green pepper, harissa and caraway, with warm khobz for scooping. It is the everyday breakfast across Algeria and Tunisia. The eggs add **protein and choline**, and the tomato and pepper bring vitamin C.
steps: Warm the olive oil in a wide pan over medium heat. Cook the onion and green pepper until soft and just turning golden, about 8 minutes.
Stir in the garlic, harissa, cumin, paprika and caraway for a minute, until it smells toasty. Add the crushed tomato and the salt.
Simmer for 8 minutes, stirring now and then, until the sauce is thick and jammy.
Make two wells with the back of a spoon and crack an egg into each. Cover and cook for 4 to 5 minutes, until the whites are set and the yolks are still soft.
Scatter with the cilantro. Warm the pita in a dry pan and tear it up for scooping.
tip: Make the sauce the night before. In the morning, reheat it and crack in the eggs, which takes about 8 minutes.

name: Bissara with olive oil, cumin and olives
inspiredBy: Moroccan bissara, made in a pot of two so the second breakfast is already waiting
about: A thick, silky Moroccan fava bean soup, served warm with a pool of olive oil, cumin and paprika and a few olives, with khobz for dunking. It is the street breakfast of Marrakech and Fes. The fava beans bring **fibre, folate and iron**.
steps: The evening before, while another pot is simmering, rinse the dried fava beans and put them in a pot with the garlic and plenty of water, about 4 times their volume for the two portions. Use split, peeled fava, which cook in about 40 minutes. Whole ones need an overnight soak, peeling and about 1½ hours.
Simmer gently for about 40 minutes, until the beans fall apart when pressed, adding hot water if they get dry.
Blitz with a stick blender or mash well until thick and silky. Stir in half the cumin and the salt, and thin with hot water to a soupy hummus.
Ladle one portion into a bowl, make a pool in the middle for the olive oil, then dust with the paprika and the rest of the cumin and add the olives.
Warm the pita and use it to dunk. Chill the second portion, and reheat it with a splash of water when you want it.
tip: A tin of fava beans in a hurry works too. Blitz about 400 g of beans and their liquid with the garlic and cumin, and heat it through for 8 minutes.
ingredients: dried, split and peeled if you can find them

name: Cinnamon oat porridge with dates, orange, almonds and walnuts
inspiredBy: Inspired by the warm, milky cereals of the Maghreb, made here with oats
about: Creamy oats cooked in milk with cinnamon and a whisper of orange blossom water, sweetened by soft dates and topped with orange segments and a toasted almond and walnut crunch. The milk and nuts bring **calcium, vitamin E and plant omega-3**.
steps: Toast the almonds and walnuts in a dry pan over medium heat until golden and fragrant, about 3 minutes. Tip them out so they do not burn.
Put the oats, milk, cinnamon and salt in a small pot over medium heat. Stir often for 6 to 7 minutes, until thick and creamy.
Stir in the dates and the orange blossom water and let the dates soften for a minute.
Spoon into a bowl and top with the orange and the toasted nuts.
tip: A spoonful of honey is lovely on top if your dates are not very sweet. Toast a handful of almonds and walnuts the Sunday before so they are ready all week.

name: Whole-wheat msemen-style flatbread with fried eggs, olives and tomato
inspiredBy: Moroccan msemen, made with whole-wheat flour and a quicker fold
about: A flaky, pan-cooked flatbread folded around a little olive oil, served with two fried eggs, olives and juicy tomato. It is the slow weekend breakfast of Moroccan homes, in a whole-wheat version. The eggs and whole grain bring **protein, choline and fibre**.
steps: Mix the flour and half the salt with about 60 ml warm water and a teaspoon of the olive oil. Knead for 8 minutes, until smooth and soft, then cover and rest for 30 minutes.

Divide the dough into 2 balls. Oil your counter and your hands, then stretch each ball into a thin sheet about the size of a saucer. It may tear in places, so just patch the holes with a pinch of dough.
Brush each sheet with olive oil and fold it into a small square, like an envelope. Press it flat with your palm.
Cook each square in a dry non-stick pan over medium heat for 2 to 3 minutes a side, until golden with flaky layers.
Wipe the pan, add a little oil and fry the eggs with the cumin and a pinch of salt until the whites are set.
Serve the msemen with the eggs, olives, tomato and cilantro. Tear and scoop.
tip: Real msemen is made with white flour, semolina and butter. This version keeps the folded, flaky idea with whole-wheat flour. Skip the eggs and drizzle honey for a sweet version.
ingredients: part in the dough, part for folding and the pan

name: Moroccan carrot and orange salad with tinned mackerel on khobz
inspiredBy: Moroccan carrot and orange salad, with the tinned mackerel that North African cooks love on bread
about: Sweet grated carrot and juicy orange dressed with lemon, cinnamon and a touch of orange blossom water, with a lemony mash of tinned mackerel spread on warm khobz. Sunny, crunchy and quick. The carrot and orange bring **vitamin A and vitamin C**, and the mackerel brings **omega-3 and vitamin D**.
steps: Whisk half the lemon juice with the olive oil, cinnamon, orange blossom water and the salt in a large bowl.
Add the grated carrot, orange pieces, olives and half the parsley and toss well.
In a small bowl, mash the mackerel with the rest of the lemon juice, the cumin, the grated onion and the rest of the parsley.
Warm the pita, spread it with the mackerel, and serve it with the salad.
tip: The salad keeps well for a day, so pack it for the office and keep the mackerel and pita separate.

name: Slata mechouia with tuna, egg and olives
inspiredBy: Tunisian slata mechouia. Tuna and egg are the traditional toppings
about: Peppers and tomatoes charred until sweet and smoky, chopped with garlic, caraway, harissa and lemon, then topped with tuna, a boiled egg and olives. It is the Tunisian salad you find on every table, served with bread. The peppers and tomato bring **vitamin C**, and the tuna and egg bring protein.
steps: Heat your oven grill (broiler) to high. Lay the peppers and tomatoes on a tray and char them, turning now and then, until the skins blacken and blister, about 15 to 20 minutes.
Meanwhile, lower the egg into boiling water and cook for 9 minutes, then cool under cold water and peel.
Pop the peppers in a bowl, cover, and leave for 10 minutes so the skins loosen. Peel off the skins and the tomato skins, and pull out the pepper seeds.
Chop the peppers and tomatoes roughly with a knife until it is a chunky, juicy mash.
Mash the garlic with the salt and stir it in with the harissa, caraway, lemon juice and olive oil.
Spoon onto a plate, then top with the tuna, the halved egg, olives and parsley. Warm the pita and scoop.
tip: Char the peppers and tomatoes the night before while the oven is already hot from dinner. Keep them in the fridge and dress them at lunch.

name: Sardine kefta in khobz with warm zaalouk
inspiredBy: Moroccan sardine balls (boulettes de sardines) simmered with zaalouk, shaped as patties for a quicker lunch
about: Little patties of tinned sardines, parsley, cilantro and cumin, seared briefly and finished in a silky, garlicky zaalouk of eggplant and tomato, then tucked into warm khobz. Sardines with their soft bones bring **calcium, omega-3 and vitamin D**, and the eggplant brings fibre and potassium.
steps: Put the eggplant, crushed tomato, garlic, half the olive oil, half the cumin, half the paprika and half the salt in a pan with a splash of water. Cover and simmer for 20 to 25 minutes, until the eggplant is completely soft.
Mash the zaalouk with a fork until chunky. Stir in half the lemon juice and half the cilantro.
Mash the sardines in a bowl with the onion, parsley, the rest of the cilantro, cumin, paprika, lemon juice and salt, and the flour. Chill for 15 minutes, then shape into 4 small patties.
Sear the patties in the rest of the olive oil over medium heat for 2 minutes a side, until golden. Turn them gently, since they are soft.
Slide the patties into the warm zaalouk and simmer for 3 minutes so they take on the sauce.
Warm the pita and open it. Fill it with the sardine kefta and the zaalouk.
tip: Make the zaalouk on Friday night while the mackerel roasts. On Saturday, mix, sear and warm the kefta through the zaalouk in about 20 minutes.

name: Moroccan chicken tagine with apricots, almonds and chickpeas
inspiredBy: Moroccan chicken tagine with apricots, with chickpeas and pumpkin added for more fibre and vitamin A
about: Tender chicken thigh simmered with onion, saffron, ginger, cinnamon and ras el hanout, with sweet dried apricots, chickpeas and golden pumpkin, and crunchy toasted almonds on top. A lemon squeeze at the end keeps it bright. The chicken and chickpeas bring **protein and iron**, and the pumpkin and apricots bring **vitamin A**.
steps: Rub the chicken with the ras el hanout, ginger, pepper, half the cinnamon and the salt. Brown it in the olive oil in a wide, heavy pot over medium-high heat, about 5 minutes. Lift it out.
Crush the saffron into 2 tablespoons of warm water. Soften the onion in the same pot until golden, about 8 minutes.
Return the chicken with the chickpeas, apricots, the saffron water, the rest of the cinnamon and about 250 ml of water. Cover and simmer gently for 15 minutes.
Add the pumpkin and simmer, partly covered, for another 20 minutes, until the pumpkin is tender and the sauce is thick and glossy.
Toast the almonds in a dry pan until golden, about 3 minutes.
Stir the lemon juice and half the cilantro into the tagine. Scatter with the almonds and the rest of the cilantro and serve with warm khobz. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: No tagine pot needed. A heavy pot with a tight lid does the same job.
ingredients: in big chunks, butternut or kabocha squash works

name: Harira with lentils, chickpeas and tomato
inspiredBy: Moroccan harira, vegetarian, with mashed lentils instead of the flour thickener
about: The thick, fragrant Moroccan soup, with lentils, chickpeas, tomato and celery, scented with cinnamon and pepper and thickened with beaten egg, then finished with lots of cilantro and parsley and a squeeze of lemon. It is hearty enough for dinner. The lentils and chickpeas bring **iron, folate and fibre**, and the lemon helps your body absorb the iron.
steps: Warm the olive oil in a large pot over medium heat. Cook the onion and celery until soft, about 8 minutes.
Stir in the turmeric, ginger, cinnamon and pepper, then add the crushed tomato, the lentils, the salt and 1 litre of water for the two portions.
Bring to a boil, then simmer gently for 25 minutes, until the lentils are soft.
Add the chickpeas and simmer for 15 more minutes. Mash a ladleful against the side of the pot to thicken the soup.
Turn the heat to low. Pour in the 2 beaten eggs in a thin stream, stirring, so they set in silky threads. Stir in the cilantro, the parsley and the lemon juice, and add salt if it needs it.
Serve with warm khobz. Cool the second portion and keep it in the fridge for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: Many Moroccan cooks add a few cubes of lamb too. Harira is traditionally the soup that breaks the fast in Ramadan, eaten with dates.
ingredients: 2 eggs for the pot of two, beaten

name: Chermoula sardines roasted over potatoes and carrots
inspiredBy: Moroccan sardines mchermla, roasted rather than fried, with chermoula carrots alongside
about: Fresh sardines rubbed with chermoula, the garlicky cilantro, cumin and preserved lemon paste of Morocco, then roasted on a tray over potato, carrot and tomato. A sizzling tray, ready in about 45 minutes, mostly in the oven. Sardines bring **omega-3 and vitamin D**, and the carrot brings vitamin A.
steps: Heat the oven to 220°C (425°F). Toss the potato slices and carrot sticks with half the olive oil and half the salt on a large baking tray. Roast for 15 minutes.

Meanwhile, make the chermoula. Mash the garlic with the rest of the salt, then chop or blitz it with the cilantro, parsley, cumin, paprika, preserved lemon rind, lemon juice and the rest of the olive oil.
Rub most of the chermoula over the sardines, inside and out, keeping a spoonful for the vegetables.
Toss the spoonful of chermoula through the vegetables, add the tomato slices, nestle the sardines on top, and roast for 10 to 12 minutes, until the skin is blistered and the flesh flakes easily.
Scatter with the olives and serve from the tray.
tip: Ask the fishmonger for sardines scaled and gutted, with the heads on. Frozen ones work well once thawed. Open a window, since sardines are fragrant. Mackerel works too.

name: Algerian-style couscous with beef, chickpeas and vegetables
inspiredBy: Inspired by Algerian couscous with meat and vegetables, with whole-wheat couscous and more vegetables
about: Fluffy whole-wheat couscous under a fragrant stew of tender beef, carrot, zucchini and chickpeas, with a dab of harissa on the side. It is the Friday-table dish of Algeria, built with extra vegetables. The chickpeas and vegetables bring **fibre and vitamin A**, and the beef brings iron and zinc.
steps: Heat most of the olive oil in a large pot and brown the beef in batches, about 5 minutes. Lift it out.
Soften the onion in the same pot for 6 minutes. Stir in the cinnamon, pepper and ras el hanout until fragrant.
Return the beef with the crushed tomato, the salt and 600 ml of water for the two portions. Bring to a boil, then cover and simmer gently for 45 minutes.
Add the carrots and chickpeas and simmer for 15 minutes, then add the zucchini and simmer for 10 more minutes, until the beef is tender and everything is soft.

While it simmers, put the dry whole-wheat couscous for both portions in a bowl and pour over about 1¼ times its weight of boiling water, just enough to wet the grain. Cover and rest for 10 minutes, then rub in the rest of the olive oil and fluff with a fork.
Pile the couscous on plates, ladle the beef and vegetables over it, scatter with cilantro and serve with the harissa on the side.
Whisk the yogurt with a little cold water and a pinch of salt into a thin, cool drink, the lben-style glass that often goes with couscous.
Pack the second portion for tomorrow, with the couscous and the drink in separate containers.
tip: On a weeknight, use a pressure cooker: the beef is tender in 25 minutes. Keep the stew and the couscous apart in the fridge so it does not go soggy. Buttermilk (lben) is the classic drink if you can find it.

name: Tunisian harissa mackerel with barley and chickpea salad and a chopped salad
inspiredBy: Tunisian mackerel with harissa, a pairing that suits oily fish well
about: Mackerel fillets rubbed with harissa, garlic, caraway and lemon and roasted until the skin crackles, with a warm barley and chickpea salad with preserved lemon, olives and lots of parsley, and a crunchy diced tomato and cucumber salad. Mackerel carries **omega-3, vitamin D and B12**, and the barley brings fibre.
steps: Cover the barley with plenty of boiling water and simmer for 25 to 30 minutes, until tender but still a little chewy. Drain well.
Heat the oven to 220°C (425°F). Mix the harissa, garlic, caraway, half the lemon juice and a pinch of salt and rub it all over the mackerel.
Lay the fillets skin side up on a lined tray and roast for 10 to 12 minutes, until the skin is crisp and the flesh flakes.
Toss the warm barley with the chickpeas, preserved lemon, olives, most of the parsley and half the olive oil.
Toss the tomato and cucumber with the rest of the parsley, the rest of the lemon, the rest of the olive oil and a pinch of salt.
Serve the mackerel over the barley with the salad on the side.
tip: Cook the barley earlier in the week if you like, since it keeps 4 to 5 days in the fridge. Then Friday is just the fish and the salads.

name: Lamb and prune tagine with toasted almonds and a cucumber and carrot salad
inspiredBy: Moroccan lamb tagine with prunes and almonds, the kind served at celebrations
about: Lamb shoulder slowly braised with onion, cinnamon, ginger and pepper until it falls apart, then finished with sweet prunes, honey and toasted almonds. A lemony cucumber and carrot salad cuts the richness. The lamb brings **iron, zinc and B12**, and the prunes bring potassium.
steps: Brown the lamb in the olive oil in a heavy pot over medium-high heat, about 6 minutes. Add the onion, cinnamon, ginger, pepper and the salt.
Add 300 ml of water. Cover and simmer very gently for 1 hour 15 minutes, until the lamb is tender.
Add the prunes and honey and simmer uncovered for 15 minutes, until the sauce is thick and syrupy.
Toast the almonds in a dry pan until golden, about 3 minutes.
Toss the cucumber, grated carrot and parsley with the lemon juice, the cumin and a pinch of salt.
Spoon the tagine over the plates, scatter with the almonds and serve with the salad and warm pita. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: In a pressure cooker the lamb takes 30 minutes. Finish the prunes uncovered on the stove.

name: Algerian chicken tajine zitoune with potatoes and chard
inspiredBy: Algerian tajine zitoune, the chicken and green olive tagine
about: Chicken thighs braised in a golden, gentle sauce of onion, ginger and saffron with green olives, preserved lemon, potato and wilted chard. A pot of comfort that is tangy and savoury. The chard brings **vitamins K and A**, and the chicken brings protein.
steps: Brown the chicken in the olive oil in a heavy pot over medium-high heat, about 5 minutes. Add the onion and garlic and cook for 5 minutes.
Crush the saffron into 2 tablespoons of warm water and add it with the ginger, pepper and the salt.
Add the potatoes and 250 ml of water. Cover and simmer gently for 25 minutes, until the potatoes and chicken are tender.
Stir in the olives, preserved lemon and chard stems. Simmer for 5 minutes.
Add the chard leaves until just wilted, about 2 minutes. Stir in the lemon juice and the parsley.
Serve in a shallow bowl with the sauce spooned over.
tip: Rinse the olives if they are very salty. Add a handful of sliced mushrooms with the potatoes if you like.

name: Yogurt with dried apricots, honey and cinnamon
inspiredBy: Inspired by the yogurt and dried fruit snacks of Algeria and Morocco
about: Thick yogurt with chopped dried apricots, a drizzle of honey and a pinch of cinnamon. Creamy and sweet. The yogurt brings **calcium and protein**.
steps: Stir the apricots into the yogurt, drizzle with the honey and dust with the cinnamon.

name: Yogurt with chopped dates and cinnamon
inspiredBy: Inspired by the yogurt and dried fruit snacks of Algeria and Morocco
about: Thick yogurt with chopped soft dates and a pinch of cinnamon, sweet enough without any honey. Creamy and a little chewy. The yogurt brings **calcium and protein**, and the dates bring potassium.
steps: Stir the dates into the yogurt and dust with the cinnamon.

name: Plain yogurt with a spoon of honey
about: Thick, cold yogurt with a spoon of honey, the simplest end to an afternoon. The yogurt brings **calcium and protein**.
steps: Spoon the honey over the yogurt and eat it straight away.

name: Sardines on khobz with tomato, onion and harissa
inspiredBy: Moroccan tinned sardine sandwich
about: Tinned sardines on warm khobz with sliced tomato, raw onion and a smear of harissa, the street-stall sandwich of Moroccan ports. The sardines bring **omega-3, calcium and vitamin D**.
steps: Warm the pita in a dry pan and open it. Smear the inside with the harissa.
Fill with the sardines, tomato and onion, squeeze over the lemon juice and press closed.

name: Dates stuffed with almonds
inspiredBy: Inspired by the stuffed dates served with tea in Morocco and Algeria
about: Soft medjool dates with a toasted almond tucked into each. A tiny sweet that goes with mint tea across the Maghreb. The almonds bring **vitamin E and magnesium**.
steps: Toast the almonds in a dry pan until golden, about 3 minutes. Split the date, remove the pit, tuck two almonds inside and eat the rest alongside.

name: Dried apricots with toasted almonds
about: Chewy dried apricots with a handful of toasted almonds, as served with tea across Morocco. The almonds bring **vitamin E and magnesium**, and the apricots bring potassium.
steps: Toast the almonds in a dry pan until golden, about 3 minutes. Eat with the apricots.

name: Khobz with olives and olive oil
about: Warm whole-wheat khobz with salty green olives and a little olive oil for dipping and a pinch of cumin. Simple and satisfying. The whole grain brings **fibre**.
steps: Warm the pita in a dry pan. Tear it up, stir the cumin into the olive oil and dip. Eat with the olives.

name: Dates and walnuts with warm milk and cinnamon
about: Soft dates and a few walnuts with a mug of warm milk and cinnamon. Algerian and Tunisian hosts serve dates and walnuts together, and milk is the old companion. The milk brings **calcium**, and the walnuts bring plant omega-3.
steps: Warm the milk in a small pot or the microwave with the cinnamon. Drink it with the dates and walnuts on the side.

name: Boiled egg with cumin and salt
inspiredBy: Moroccan and Tunisian street-cart boiled egg with cumin
about: A warm boiled egg with a little cumin and flaky salt for dipping, the street-cart snack of Morocco and Tunisia. The egg brings **protein and choline**.
steps: Lower the egg into boiling water and cook for 9 minutes, then cool it under cold water and peel.
Mix the cumin and the salt and dip the egg into it as you eat.

name: Roasted chickpeas with cumin and paprika
inspiredBy: Inspired by the cumin chickpeas sold in paper cones by Moroccan street vendors
about: Crunchy oven-roasted chickpeas with cumin, paprika and a squeeze of lemon. A savoury snack in the style of Moroccan street-cart chickpeas. The chickpeas bring **protein and fibre**.
steps: Heat the oven to 220°C (425°F). Pat the chickpeas very dry.
Toss with the oil, cumin, paprika and salt on a tray.
Roast for 25 minutes, shaking the tray halfway, until crisp. Squeeze over the lemon juice and let them crisp more as they cool.
tip: They stay crunchy for about 3 days in a jar. Roast a fresh batch the day before you want them.

name: Orange slices with cinnamon and orange blossom
inspiredBy: Moroccan orange with cinnamon
about: Juicy orange slices with cinnamon and a few drops of orange blossom water, a Moroccan classic that works as a snack or dessert. The orange brings **vitamin C**.
steps: Arrange the orange on a plate, sprinkle with the orange blossom water and dust with the cinnamon.

name: Overnight oats with Greek yogurt, figs and almonds
inspiredBy: Greek yogurt with honey, figs and nuts, turned into make-ahead oats
about:
Rolled oats soaked overnight in thick Greek yogurt with chopped dried figs and a little chia, then topped with chopped almonds and a drizzle of honey. It is **ready when you wake up**, creamy, a little sweet and nicely crunchy on top.

The oats and chia add fibre, the figs add a little calcium and the almonds bring vitamin E.
steps: The night before, stir the oats, yogurt, chia and chopped figs together in a jar or bowl with about 100 ml (⅓ cup) of milk or water. It should look a little too runny, since the oats and chia will drink it up.
Cover and chill overnight. The figs soften and sweeten the oats as they sit.
In the morning, give it a stir. It should be thick and spoonable, and a splash more milk or water loosens it if it has gone stiff.
Roughly chop the almonds and scatter them on top with a drizzle of honey.
tip: Swap the figs for berries or a chopped orange, whatever you have. Make a few jars at once on Sunday, Tuesday and Thursday evenings.

name: Strapatsada, Greek tomato and feta scrambled eggs with spinach
inspiredBy: Greek strapatsada, with a handful of spinach folded in
about: Soft eggs scrambled into juicy cherry tomatoes with crumbled feta, oregano and a little spinach, with an orange on the side. It is a proper hot breakfast in **about ten minutes**. Eggs bring protein and choline, and the tomatoes and orange bring vitamin C.
steps: Warm the olive oil in a non-stick pan over medium heat. Add the tomatoes with the oregano and cook, pressing them with the back of a spoon, until they collapse into a thick, jammy sauce, about 4 minutes.
Stir in the spinach until it wilts.
Beat the eggs with the salt and pour them in. Stir gently until they are softly set and still glossy, about 2 minutes.
Crumble the feta over the top and eat right away, with the orange alongside.
tip: In the winter, canned tomatoes with no salt added work well here when fresh tomatoes are pale.

name: Spanish potato and kale tortilla with tomato salad
inspiredBy: Spanish tortilla española, with kale folded in and less oil
about:
A thick, soft omelette of slow-cooked potatoes, sweet onion, kale and eggs, served in wedges with a juicy tomato and cucumber salad. It is a slow weekend breakfast that makes two portions, and the cold slice is **just as good tomorrow morning**.

The eggs bring protein and choline and the potato brings potassium.
steps: Warm the olive oil in a non-stick frying pan over medium-low heat. Add the potatoes and onion with a pinch of the salt, cover and cook, stirring now and then, until the potatoes are completely tender but not browned, about 15 minutes. Add a little more oil if it starts to catch.
Stir in the kale and cook until it is tender and bright green, about 3 minutes, then tip everything into a bowl and let it cool for a few minutes.
Beat the eggs with a pinch of salt and fold in the potato mixture. Let it sit for 5 minutes so the egg soaks in.
Pour it back into the pan over low heat and cook until the edges are set and the middle is just a little wobbly, about 6 minutes.
Put a plate over the pan, flip the pan over so the tortilla drops onto the plate, then slide it back into the pan and cook 3 minutes more, until golden on both sides.

Toss the tomatoes and cucumber with the parsley, lemon juice and a few drops of olive oil, and serve a wedge with the salad. Wrap the second portion for tomorrow's breakfast and make a fresh batch of the salad then.
tip: Skip the flip and finish the top under a hot grill if turning it feels scary.

name: Greek meze plate with quick hummus, tzatziki and a boiled egg
inspiredBy: Greek and Cypriot meze tables, built as a quick lunch
about:
A lunch plate to graze from: lemony hummus, a quick garlicky yogurt dip, feta, a boiled egg, olives and crunchy fennel, cucumber and cherry tomatoes. Only the egg gets cooked, and **the hummus comes from your Sunday night batch**.

Chickpeas, yogurt, egg and feta make it a solid protein lunch, and the raw vegetables bring vitamin C.
steps: Make the hummus on Sunday night for the week. The batch uses a whole can of no-salt-added chickpeas, 1 tbsp of tahini, a little garlic, most of a lemon's juice and a pinch of salt, blitzed with a few spoonfuls of ice-cold water for 2 to 3 minutes until pale and silky. It keeps 4 days in the fridge, and today's plate uses a portion of it (the ingredient list shows that portion).
Lower the egg gently into a small pot of boiling water, cook for 8 minutes, then cool it under cold water and peel.
Grate a third of the cucumber, squeeze out the water and stir it into the yogurt with the rest of the garlic, finely grated, and a pinch of salt.

Cut the rest of the cucumber and the fennel into sticks and halve the tomatoes. Spoon the hummus and the yogurt dip onto a plate, squeeze over the remaining lemon juice, and arrange the vegetables, feta, olives and the halved egg around them. Finish with chopped parsley.
tip: Boil a few eggs on Sunday as well, and this lunch takes five minutes. A fresh tub of hummus works too.

name: Village-style salad with chickpeas and feta
inspiredBy: Greek horiatiki, with chickpeas to turn it into a lunch
about:
Chunky tomatoes, cucumber, pepper and red onion with olives, a slab of feta, a spoon of cool yogurt and a pile of chickpeas, all dressed with olive oil, red wine vinegar and oregano. The tomatoes make their own dressing as it sits, so it is **better after five minutes**.

Chickpeas, feta and yogurt make it a real lunch, and the pepper and tomato bring vitamin C.
steps: Halve the tomatoes, cut the cucumber and pepper into thick pieces and slice the red onion thinly.
Toss them in a big bowl with the olives and chickpeas.
Whisk the olive oil, vinegar, oregano and salt together and pour over, then toss well.
Lay the feta on top in one slab, spoon alongside the yogurt, stirred with the finely grated garlic and a pinch of salt, scatter with parsley and let it sit for 5 minutes before eating.
tip: In summer, use big ripe tomatoes cut into wedges. Pack the dressing separately if you take it to work.

name: Sicilian-style fava bean, orange and fennel salad with egg
inspiredBy: Sicilian orange and fennel salad, with fava beans for a lunch, and feta standing in for ricotta salata
about:
Juicy orange segments, shaved fennel, olives and red onion with creamy fava beans, toasted almonds and parsley, in a lemony olive oil dressing with a pinch of chili. It is **bright, crunchy and a little sweet**.

The fava beans, egg and feta carry the protein, and the orange and lemon give you plenty of vitamin C.
steps: Lower the egg gently into boiling water for 8 minutes, then cool and peel it. Toast the almonds in a dry pan until golden, about 3 minutes, then chop roughly.
Slice the fennel very thinly and the red onion into fine rings. Peel the orange, removing the white pith, and cut it into rounds or segments over the bowl so the juice falls in.
Add the fava beans, olives, parsley, the feta, crumbled, and the egg, quartered, to the bowl.
Whisk the olive oil, lemon juice, salt and chili together, pour over and toss gently. Top with the toasted almonds.
tip: Leave out the chili for a milder salad.
ingredients: canned or frozen, cooked and drained

name: Greek lemon chicken with oregano potatoes and red peppers
inspiredBy: Greek kotopoulo lemonato, with roasted kale and a garlicky yogurt on the side
about:
Chicken thighs roasted with lemony oregano potatoes and red peppers until the edges are golden, with kale roasted on a second tray until crisp and a cool garlic yogurt to spoon over. It makes two portions, so **tomorrow's lunch is already done**.

The chicken brings protein, niacin and zinc, and the kale brings calcium and vitamin K.
steps: Heat the oven to 220 C. Toss the potato wedges and pepper strips on a big tray with half the olive oil, the oregano, half the lemon juice and most of the salt. Spread them out in a single layer so they roast instead of steaming.
Roast for 20 minutes, until the potatoes are starting to colour.
Rub the chicken with half the garlic, the rest of the oil and a little of the lemon juice, tuck it in among the potatoes and roast until the chicken is cooked through and golden, 25 to 30 minutes.
Put the kale on a second tray with a few drops of oil and a pinch of salt and roast for the last 8 to 10 minutes, until the leaves are crisp at the edges.
Stir the rest of the garlic, finely grated, and the chopped parsley into the yogurt with a pinch of salt.
Serve one portion now with the kale, the yogurt and a squeeze of lemon. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch.
tip: Leave the skin on if you like, and the chicken stays even juicier. Reheat the second portion in the oven or air fryer for 10 minutes, or eat it at room temperature. A microwave makes roast potatoes sad.

name: Sardines on garlicky white beans with kale and almonds
inspiredBy: Spanish sardines with beans and Italian white bean and sardine toasts, without the bread
about:
Creamy white beans simmered with garlic, onion and smoky paprika, with kale wilted in and canned sardines warmed on top. Toasted almonds, a squeeze of lemon and an optional pinch of chili finish it.

Sardines eaten with their soft bones are **one of the best food sources of calcium**, and they bring omega-3 and vitamin D too.
steps: Toast the almonds in a dry pan over medium heat until golden and fragrant, about 3 minutes, then tip them out and chop roughly.
In the same pan, warm the olive oil over low heat and soften the onion and garlic with the chopped anchovies until sweet and golden and the anchovies have melted away, about 6 minutes.
Stir in the smoked paprika and the chili, if using, then add the beans, a splash of water and the salt and simmer for 6 minutes, mashing a few beans against the pan to thicken the sauce.
Stir in the kale and cook until it is bright green and just tender, 3 to 4 minutes.
Lay the sardines on top for a minute to warm through, then finish with the lemon juice, parsley and toasted almonds.
tip: Mackerel fillets in olive oil work just as well as sardines. Leave out the chili for a mild version.
ingredients: canned in olive oil, with bones

name: Fakes, Greek lentil soup with spinach and feta
inspiredBy: Greek fakes, with spinach stirred in and a splash of vinegar at the end
about:
A thick, comforting Greek lentil soup with tomato, barley and oregano, finished with a splash of red wine vinegar, a raw drizzle of olive oil and crumbled feta. **The vinegar is the secret**, since it wakes everything up.

It makes two bowls and tastes even better tomorrow, and the lentils are a great source of iron, folate and fibre.
steps: Warm half the olive oil in a large pot and soften the onion over medium heat until it is translucent, about 8 minutes.
Stir in the garlic and oregano for a minute until fragrant.

Add the lentils, barley, passata and about four times as much water as lentils. Bring to a boil, then simmer gently, partly covered, until the lentils and barley are completely soft and the soup is thick, 35 to 40 minutes. Add the salt near the end.
Stir in the spinach until it wilts, then take the pot off the heat.
Stir in the vinegar and parsley, taste for salt, and finish each bowl with crumbled feta, a dollop of yogurt and a drizzle of the rest of the olive oil.
Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch. It thickens overnight, so add a splash of water and a fresh splash of vinegar when you reheat it.
tip: In a hurry? Use canned lentils, drained, and simmer for 20 minutes.
ingredients: passata or crushed tomatoes, no salt added (not paste)

name: Salmon with tomatoes, olives and anchovy on lemony barley
inspiredBy: Southern Italian puttanesca flavours, with barley in place of pasta
about:
Salmon roasted over blistered cherry tomatoes, black olives and a few melted anchovies, served on chewy lemony barley with tender kale stirred through. The tomatoes burst into a sauce all on their own.

Salmon is **one of the best food sources of omega-3** and a good source of vitamin D, and the kale adds calcium while the barley adds fibre.
steps: Rinse the barley and simmer it in plenty of salted water until tender but still chewy, about 25 minutes. Add the kale for the last 3 minutes, then drain well.

Meanwhile, heat the oven to 200 C. Chop the anchovies and toss them with the tomatoes, thin onion wedges, garlic and olives on a small tray with half the olive oil and the oregano. Roast for 10 minutes, until the tomatoes begin to burst and the anchovies have melted into the juices.
Nestle the salmon among the tomatoes, brush it with a little of the remaining oil and roast until it just flakes, 10 to 12 minutes.
Toss the drained barley and kale with the lemon juice and the rest of the oil.
Serve the salmon and the tomato juices over the barley and scatter with parsley.
tip: The anchovies melt away and just add savoury depth, so even anchovy skeptics usually enjoy it. Add a pinch of chili flakes if you like heat.

name: Espinacas con garbanzos, Andalusian chickpea and spinach stew
inspiredBy: the Seville tapas classic, with almonds ground into the base instead of fried bread
about:
A smoky, garlicky chickpea and spinach stew thickened with ground toasted almonds, with cumin, paprika and a splash of vinegar to finish. A halved boiled egg, a spoon of cool yogurt and a scatter of crunchy almonds go on top.

It makes two portions, and the **chickpeas, egg and yogurt bring protein** while the almonds bring vitamin E and the chickpeas bring iron and fibre.
steps: Boil the eggs for 8 minutes, cool them under cold water and peel them. Toast the almonds in a dry pan until golden. Set a few aside to chop for the top, and blitz or pound the rest with a third of the garlic, a pinch of salt and a splash of the vinegar into a rough paste.
Warm the olive oil in a wide pot and soften the onion with the rest of the garlic, sliced, over medium heat, about 6 minutes.
Stir in the cumin, smoked paprika and the chili, if using, for 30 seconds, until fragrant.
Add the passata, chickpeas and a mug of water and simmer until the sauce has thickened, about 12 minutes.
Stir in the almond paste, then the spinach in handfuls until it all wilts, about 3 minutes.

Finish with the rest of the vinegar, taste for salt, and top each bowl with a halved egg, a spoonful of yogurt and the chopped almonds. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch and boil a fresh egg to go on top of it.
tip: Leave out the chili for a milder stew.
ingredients: passata or crushed tomatoes, no salt added (not paste)

name: Shrimp saganaki with feta and lemony potatoes
inspiredBy: Greek garides saganaki, with potatoes on the side instead of bread
about:
Plump shrimp in a bright tomato sauce with oregano, topped with feta that melts into creamy pockets, served with warm lemony potatoes to mop it all up. It is **on the table in 30 minutes**.

Shrimp are a lean protein with plenty of selenium, and the feta adds calcium.
steps: Halve the potatoes if they are large and boil them in salted water until tender, about 15 minutes. Drain, then toss with half the lemon juice and a little of the parsley.

Meanwhile, warm the olive oil in a skillet and soften the onion and red pepper over medium heat, about 5 minutes. Stir in the garlic, oregano and the chopped anchovies for a minute, until the anchovies dissolve.
Add the passata with a splash of water and simmer until thick and saucy, about 8 minutes.
Slide in the shrimp and cook until they are pink and curled, 3 to 4 minutes.
Crumble the feta over the top, cover for a couple of minutes until it softens, then finish with the rest of the lemon juice and parsley.
Serve with the potatoes alongside.
tip: Mussels are a classic swap for the shrimp. Add them to the sauce, cover until they open, about 5 minutes, and discard any that stay shut. Pre-cooked shrimp only need the last minute.
ingredients: raw, peeled, plain (the bag should list only shrimp)
passata or crushed tomatoes, no salt added (not paste)

name: Saffron barley with chicken, peas and red pepper
inspiredBy: Spanish paella, made with pearled barley in place of rice
about:
A golden, creamy pot of chicken, red pepper, peas and chewy pearled barley, cooked in a smoky tomato sofrito and perfumed with saffron, then topped with toasted walnuts for crunch. It is a **slow weekend dish that makes two portions**.

Barley is full of fibre, and the chicken and peas make this a complete one-pot dinner.
steps: Steep the saffron in a mug of hot water. Rinse the barley. Toast the walnuts in a dry pan until fragrant and chop them roughly.
Warm half the olive oil in a wide, deep pan and brown the chicken on all sides over medium-high heat, then set it aside.

Add the rest of the oil and soften the onion and red pepper over medium heat for 8 minutes. Stir in the garlic and smoked paprika, then the passata, and cook until the sofrito turns dark and jammy, about 5 minutes.
Stir in the barley to coat it in the sofrito, then pour in the saffron water and enough hot water to come to about 2½ to 3 times the barley's volume. Add the salt and the chicken.
Simmer gently, stirring now and then and topping up with hot water if it gets dry, until the barley is tender and the pot is creamy rather than soupy, about 30 minutes.
Scatter the peas over the top for the last 5 minutes, then take the pan off the heat and let it rest, covered, for 5 minutes.
Finish with the lemon juice, parsley and toasted walnuts. Pack the second portion for tomorrow's lunch. It reheats well with a splash of water.
tip: Use boneless thighs for an even juicier pot, or add a handful of mussels or shrimp for the last 5 minutes for a seafood version. Barley will not form a crisp base like rice does, so the walnuts bring the crunch.
ingredients: passata or crushed tomatoes, no salt added (not paste)

name: Greek yogurt with honey, walnuts and figs
about: Thick yogurt with chopped dried figs, crunchy walnuts and a drizzle of honey. It is the classic Greek sweet snack, with protein and calcium from the yogurt and **plant omega-3 from the walnuts**.
steps: Spoon the yogurt into a bowl, top with the chopped figs and walnuts, and drizzle with the honey.

name: Greek yogurt with honey, figs and toasted almonds
about: Thick yogurt with chopped dried figs, warm toasted almonds and a drizzle of honey. It is a classic Greek sweet snack, with protein and calcium from the yogurt and **vitamin E from the almonds**.
steps: Toast the almonds in a dry pan until golden, about 3 minutes. Spoon the yogurt into a bowl, top with the chopped figs and warm almonds, and drizzle with the honey.

name: Fig and almond bites
inspiredBy: Spanish pan de higo and Greek fig and nut sweets
about: Sticky dried figs chopped with almonds and rolled into little balls. They are **chewy, sweet and crunchy at once**, with vitamin E and a little calcium.
steps: Chop the figs and almonds very finely and mash them together with a few drops of lemon juice until they stick.
Roll the mixture into small balls.
tip: Make a batch and keep the balls in a container in the fridge for the week.

name: Orange and toasted almonds
about: A juicy orange with a handful of warm toasted almonds. The **vitamin C and the crunch of the nuts** make a snack that keeps you going, and the almonds bring vitamin E.
steps: Toast the almonds in a dry pan until golden, about 3 minutes. Peel the orange and eat it with the warm almonds.

name: Quick lemony hummus with fennel and cucumber sticks
about: Creamy lemon and garlic hummus with crunchy fennel and cucumber sticks for dipping. The chickpeas and tahini add **iron and fibre**, and tahini adds calcium.
steps: Use a portion of Sunday night's hummus (the batch is a whole can of no-salt-added chickpeas with 1 tbsp of tahini, garlic, lemon and salt). The ingredient list shows this snack's portion. If you are starting fresh, blitz that amount with a few spoonfuls of ice-cold water until pale and silky.
Cut the fennel and cucumber into sticks and dip away.
tip: Thursday is the last day the Sunday batch is at its best.

name: Dried figs and almonds
about: A few soft dried figs with a handful of warm toasted almonds. It is a sweet, chewy and crunchy snack, with **fibre, calcium and vitamin E**.
steps: Toast the almonds in a dry pan until golden, about 3 minutes, and eat them with the figs.

name: Garlic mushrooms with lemon and parsley
inspiredBy: Spanish champiñones al ajillo
about: Mushrooms sizzled in a hot pan with garlic until golden, then finished with lemon and a handful of parsley. They work as a **small savoury snack or a starter**, they are meaty and savoury, and they are a good source of niacin and B vitamins.
steps: Warm the olive oil in a pan over medium-high heat and cook the mushrooms until golden and their water has cooked off, about 6 minutes.
Add the garlic and stir for 30 seconds, then finish with the lemon juice, salt and parsley.

name: Garlic mushrooms with soft eggs and parsley
inspiredBy: Spanish champiñones al ajillo, with eggs on top
about: Mushrooms sizzled with garlic, lemon and parsley, with two soft-boiled eggs to break over the top. It works as a **small savoury snack or a starter**, and it gives you protein, choline and niacin.
steps: Lower the eggs gently into boiling water for 6 to 7 minutes for a soft yolk, then cool and peel them.
Warm the olive oil in a pan over medium-high heat and cook the mushrooms until golden and their water has cooked off, about 5 minutes. Add the garlic and stir for 30 seconds.
Finish with the lemon juice, salt and parsley and serve with the halved eggs on top.

name: Orange and toasted walnuts
about: A juicy orange with a handful of warm toasted walnuts. The vitamin C and the crunch of the nuts make a snack that keeps you going, and the walnuts bring **plant omega-3**.
steps: Toast the walnuts in a dry pan until fragrant, about 3 minutes, and eat them with the peeled orange.

name: Greek yogurt with orange and honey
about: Thick Greek yogurt with juicy orange pieces and a drizzle of honey. It is a bright, simple snack with protein, calcium and **plenty of vitamin C**.
steps: Peel the orange, cut it into pieces over the bowl so the juice falls in, spoon over the yogurt and drizzle with the honey.

name: Sardine tapa with lemon, cucumber and olives
inspiredBy: Spanish and Portuguese tinned fish tapas
about:
A few canned sardines on cool cucumber rounds with a squeeze of lemon, a few olives and a pinch of smoked paprika. It is the kind of thing you would be served with a drink in a Spanish bar, and a hungry-day extra on the larger plans.

Sardines bring omega-3, vitamin D and **calcium from their soft bones**.
steps: Slice the cucumber into thick rounds, top each with a piece of sardine, and finish with the lemon juice, olives, a dusting of smoked paprika and chopped parsley.
ingredients: canned in olive oil, with bones

name: Tzatziki with cucumber and fennel dippers
about: A quick garlicky yogurt and cucumber dip with a drizzle of olive oil, with cucumber rounds and fennel strips for scooping. It is **cool and fresh**, with plenty of protein.
steps: Grate a third of the cucumber, squeeze out the water, and stir it into the yogurt with the finely grated garlic, lemon juice, chopped parsley, salt and the olive oil.
Slice the rest of the cucumber into rounds, cut the fennel into strips and dip away.
tip: Chopped mint or dill is lovely in the dip if you have some.

name: Natto and tamagoyaki rice bowl with tofu miso soup
inspiredBy: Japanese asa-gohan, the classic breakfast tray
about: Warm rice topped with sticky natto, a soft rolled omelette and a small bowl of tofu miso soup. It is a proper Japanese breakfast that takes under 20 minutes. The **natto, egg and tofu** give you a solid hit of protein before you leave the house.
steps: Cook the rice and barley ahead (see the tip) and reheat a portion until steaming hot, 74 °C.
Put the bonito flakes in a small pot with a cup of water. Bring to a simmer for 2 minutes, strain, and return the broth to the pot.
Add the tofu to the broth and warm for 2 minutes. Take the pot off the heat, stir the miso in through a small sieve, and add half the scallion. Do not boil the soup once the miso is in.

Beat the egg with a few drops of the soy sauce and the iodized salt. Pour a thin layer into an oiled small pan over medium-low heat, roll it up as it sets, then pour in the rest and roll again until the omelette is firm all the way through. Slice it.

Spoon the rice into a bowl. Stir the natto briskly with the rest of the soy sauce and a few drops of egoma oil until it is sticky and spoon it on top with the omelette and the remaining scallion. Serve with the soup.
tip: On Sunday, cook about 2 cups (370 g) of brown rice and 1⅓ cups (280 g) of pearled barley together, a little less at Light. That is every rice bowl of the week except the okayu. Simmer them in a big pot of water, like pasta, for 35 to 40 minutes until tender, then drain. Cool within 1 hour in shallow containers, keep 3 days' worth in the fridge and freeze the rest in portions. Reheat from frozen, or thaw in the fridge overnight, until steaming hot, 74 °C, and only once. On warfarin? Skip the natto and add a second egg to the omelette.
ingredients: calcium-set (the label says calcium sulfate), cubed

name: Egg, tofu and shirasu okayu with komatsuna
inspiredBy: Japanese okayu, the gentle rice porridge
about: A soft, savoury rice porridge with silky tofu, a set egg, tiny shirasu fish and bright greens. It is comforting, and quick if you start from cooked rice (see the tip). **Shirasu are eaten whole, bones and all**, and the tofu is calcium-set, so it starts the day with calcium.
steps: Rinse the rice and put it in a pot with about six times its volume of water and the ginger. Bring to a boil, then cover and simmer on low for about 1 hour, stirring now and then, until the grains are very soft and the porridge is thick. Rinse and chop the komatsuna while it cooks.
Add the shirasu and the tofu and simmer for 3 minutes so the fish are cooked through and hot.
Stir in the komatsuna, then pour in the beaten egg in a thin stream and stir gently. Cook for 1 to 2 minutes, until the egg is completely set.
Ladle into a bowl, season with the salt, drizzle with the soy sauce and top with the scallion and sesame.
tip: Use 120 g of cooked rice with 300 ml of water and it is ready in 15 minutes. If you use dried chirimen jako instead of shirasu, pour boiling water over it and drain first: it is salty. Opened tofu keeps in fresh water in the fridge for up to 2 days.
ingredients: calcium-set (the label says calcium sulfate), cubed

name: Kinako soy milk oatmeal with mikan
inspiredBy: Japanese kinako (roasted soybean flour) sweets
about: Creamy oats cooked in soy milk with nutty kinako, walnuts and juicy mikan. It tastes a little like a Japanese sweet. The **soy milk and kinako** carry the protein, and the walnuts add plant omega-3.
steps: Put the oats and soy milk in a pot over medium heat. Stir often for about 5 minutes, until thick and creamy.
Whisk the kinako into the porridge off the heat so it does not clump.
Spoon into a bowl, top with the mikan segments and walnuts and drizzle with the honey.

name: Canned salmon, edamame and sesame rice bowl
inspiredBy: Japanese sake-flake rice bowls
about: Flaked canned salmon with its soft bones, sweet edamame and crisp cucumber over barley rice, dressed with ginger, rice vinegar and sesame. It is cold-friendly and comes together in 15 minutes if the rice is ready. The **soft salmon bones add calcium**, and the salmon brings vitamin D.
steps: Boil the frozen edamame in unsalted water for 3 minutes, drain, cool and shell them. Warm the cooked rice and barley until steaming hot, 74 °C, then let it cool a little.
Rinse the cucumber and scrub the carrot. Whisk the rice vinegar, soy sauce and ginger together in a small bowl. Toss the cucumber and carrot with half of it and leave for 5 minutes.
Mash the salmon with a fork, bones included, and stir in the rest of the dressing.
Pile the rice into a bowl. Top with the salmon, edamame, cucumber and carrot, and scatter over the scallion and sesame.
tip: Taking it to work? Skip the reheating, use rice straight from the fridge, and pack it with an ice pack until lunch.

name: Hiyashi soba with chilled tofu and edamame
inspiredBy: Japanese hiyashi soba and zaru soba
about: Cold buckwheat noodles with creamy tofu, edamame and cucumber with a light bonito sauce poured over. It is refreshing and filling. The **tofu, egg and edamame give the protein**, and the noodles are boiled in unsalted water to keep the sodium down.
steps: Simmer the bonito flakes in half a cup of water for 2 minutes, strain, and stir in the soy sauce, rice vinegar and honey. Set the pan in a bowl of cold water to cool the sauce while you do the rest.

Boil the frozen edamame in unsalted water for 3 minutes, drain, cool and shell. Boil the soba in plenty of unsalted water as the packet says, then rinse well under cold water, rubbing gently, and drain. Choose a soba with little or no added salt.
Rinse the spinach and cucumber. Plunge the spinach into boiling unsalted water for 1 minute, cool in cold water, squeeze dry and cut into short lengths.
Beat the egg and cook it in a thin layer in a lightly oiled non-stick pan until completely set, then slice into ribbons.
Put the noodles in a bowl and arrange the tofu, edamame, spinach, egg ribbons and cucumber on top.
Pour over the cold sauce, drizzle with the egoma oil and finish with the ginger, scallion and sesame.
tip: Egoma (perilla) oil is sold at Korean grocers as deulgireum; flaxseed oil is used the same way. Keep either in the fridge and never heat it. At smaller sizes the noodles shrink to a small nest, and the tofu and edamame carry the bowl.
ingredients: dried, check the label for salt
calcium-set (the label says calcium sulfate), cubed

name: Shrimp and egg donburi with komatsuna
inspiredBy: Japanese tamago-toji donburi (the oyakodon style)
about: Plump shrimp and softly set egg simmered in a light bonito and soy broth over barley rice, with a handful of greens. It is quick and warming. The **shrimp and egg** carry the protein.
steps: Rinse the komatsuna before cutting it. Reheat the cooked rice and barley until steaming hot, 74 °C, and spoon into a bowl.
Simmer the bonito in half a cup of water for 2 minutes, strain, and return it to the pan with the soy sauce, honey and onion. Cook for 3 minutes until the onion is soft.
Add the shrimp and cook for 3 to 4 minutes, until they are pink and opaque all the way through. Add the komatsuna for the last minute.
Pour the egg over in a thin stream. Cover and cook for 1 to 2 minutes, until the egg is completely set.
Slide everything over the rice with the broth.
ingredients: peeled and deveined; if frozen, thaw in the fridge overnight and cook within 2 days

name: Tofu and chicken hambagu with grated daikon and komatsuna
inspiredBy: Japanese tofu hambagu (washoku-style hamburg steak)
about: Tender patties of minced chicken thigh and calcium-set tofu, served with refreshing grated daikon, a vinegar-soy sauce and sesame komatsuna. The tofu keeps them light and moist. The **tofu and komatsuna bring calcium** and the patties carry plenty of protein.
steps: Cook the rice and barley (see the breakfast tip) and keep warm. This recipe makes two portions. Scrub and rinse the daikon and komatsuna, then grate the daikon.

Squeeze the tofu in a clean cloth until it is firm and crumbly, then mash it in a bowl. Add the chicken, onion, egg, ginger, the iodized salt and a third of the soy sauce and mix with your hand until sticky. Shape into two oval patties, pressing the centre thin. Wash your hands and board after handling the raw chicken.

Heat the oil in a frying pan over medium heat. Cook the patties for 4 minutes on each side, then cover and cook for another 5 minutes, until a thermometer in the centre reads 74 °C, with no pink and clear juices.
Boil the komatsuna in unsalted water for 1 minute, cool in cold water, squeeze dry and toss with half the sesame and a little soy sauce.

Squeeze the grated daikon lightly. Mix the rice vinegar with the remaining soy sauce. Serve the patties with daikon on top, the sauce spooned over, the greens and the rice. Cool the second portion and refrigerate within 2 hours for tomorrow's lunch, then reheat until steaming hot throughout, 74 °C.
tip: No komatsuna? Baby bok choy works the same way.
ingredients: calcium-set (the label says calcium sulfate), squeezed in a cloth

name: Grilled salmon with spinach goma-ae and daikon miso soup
inspiredBy: Japanese shioyaki salmon teishoku
about: A simple grilled salmon fillet with sesame-dressed spinach, a small bowl of daikon miso soup and mugi-gohan. It is the classic Japanese dinner in one tray. The **salmon brings omega-3 and vitamin D**.
steps: Cook the rice and barley ahead if you have not (see the breakfast tip) and reheat a portion until steaming hot, 74 °C.

Pat the salmon dry and rub it with the salt, then wash your hands and board after handling the raw fish. Grill or broil it, skin side up, for about 5 minutes, turn and cook for another 4 to 5 minutes, until the fish reaches 70 °C and flakes easily.
Rinse the spinach well. Plunge the spinach into boiling unsalted water for 1 minute, cool in cold water and squeeze dry. Toss with the ground sesame, soy sauce, rice vinegar and honey.

Simmer the bonito in a cup of water for 2 minutes and strain. Add the daikon and simmer for 5 minutes, until it turns translucent. Off the heat, stir the miso in through a small sieve and add the scallion.
Serve the salmon with the spinach, the soup and the rice.
ingredients: scrubbed and cut into thin matchsticks

name: Chikuzen-ni, simmered chicken with root vegetables
inspiredBy: Kyushu chikuzen-ni (iridori)
about: Chicken thigh simmered with lotus root, kabocha, carrot, shiitake and edamame in a light soy and ginger broth, glossy and not too sweet. It is even better the next day. It is a **fibre-rich simmered dish** with plenty of protein.
steps: Cook the rice and barley (see the breakfast tip) and keep warm. This recipe makes two portions.

Soak the dried shiitake in 250 ml of warm water for 30 minutes and keep the soaking water. Scrub and rinse the lotus root, kabocha and carrot. Soak the lotus root slices in cold water for 5 minutes, then drain.

Heat the oil in a wide pot over medium heat and brown the chicken for 4 minutes. Wash your hands and board after cutting the raw chicken. Add the lotus root, carrot, shiitake and ginger and stir for 2 minutes.

Add about 200 ml of the shiitake soaking water, the soy sauce, the salt and the honey. Bring to a simmer, cover and cook for 10 minutes, then lay the kabocha on top, cover again and cook for another 10 minutes, until the vegetables are tender and the chicken reaches 74 °C with no pink.
Add the edamame, then uncover and simmer for 5 minutes, spooning the broth over, until it has reduced to a glaze.
Serve over the rice. Cool the second portion and refrigerate within 2 hours for tomorrow's lunch, and reheat until steaming hot throughout, 74 °C.
ingredients: kabocha or buttercup squash, seeded, cut into chunks
soaked until soft, stems removed, quartered

name: Mackerel simmered in miso and ginger with spinach
inspiredBy: Japanese saba no miso-ni
about: Mackerel fillets simmered gently with ginger and a spoonful of miso, with cubes of tofu in the same pot and a bright spinach ohitashi. The miso sauce is thin and savoury, not heavy. The **mackerel is rich in omega-3**, and the tofu adds calcium.
steps: Cook the rice and barley ahead if you have not (see the breakfast tip) and reheat a portion until steaming hot, 74 °C.
Pour boiling water over the mackerel in a sieve for a few seconds to rinse away any fishy smell, and pat dry. Wash your hands and board after handling the raw fish.

In a small wide pan, bring 100 ml of water, the ginger, honey and half the miso to a simmer. Lay in the mackerel, skin side up, and the tofu. Cover loosely and simmer for 8 minutes, spooning the liquid over.

Stir the remaining miso with a ladle of the hot liquid and stir it back into the pan with the soy sauce. Simmer for 2 more minutes, until the fish reaches 70 °C and flakes easily and the sauce thickens slightly.
Meanwhile rinse the spinach well and boil it in unsalted water for 1 minute, cool in cold water, squeeze dry, cut into short lengths and top with the bonito flakes and sesame.
Serve the mackerel and tofu with the sauce, the spinach, scallion and rice.
ingredients: fillet, cut in two; Atlantic or Pacific, never king mackerel
calcium-set (the label says calcium sulfate), cubed

name: Beef and tofu sukiyaki-style nabe
inspiredBy: Japanese sukiyaki
about: A shallow pot of lean beef, tofu, cabbage, carrot, shiitake and komatsuna in a gently sweet soy and bonito broth. Everything cooks in one pan and the broth soaks into the rice. It is a **calcium-rich, one-pot dinner**, with the tofu and greens doing most of the work.
steps: Cook the rice and barley (see the breakfast tip) and keep warm. This recipe makes two portions.

Soak the dried shiitake in 150 ml of warm water for 30 minutes. Simmer the bonito in 200 ml of water for 2 minutes and strain. Add the shiitake and its soaking water, the soy sauce, honey and salt to make the broth.
Rinse the cabbage, carrot and komatsuna. Put the tofu, cabbage, carrot and scallion in a wide shallow pan with the broth. Bring to a simmer, cover and cook for 8 minutes.
Add the soaked shiitake and cook for 3 minutes. Lay the beef slices on top and simmer for 2 to 3 minutes, until no pink remains and the beef is cooked through. Add the komatsuna in the last minute.
Serve over or beside the rice with some of the broth. Cool the second portion and refrigerate within 2 hours for tomorrow's lunch, and reheat until steaming hot throughout, 74 °C.
ingredients: calcium-set (the label says calcium sulfate), cut into slabs

name: Pork and tofu gyoza with simmered kabocha
inspiredBy: Japanese pan-fried gyoza
about: Juicy gyoza filled with lean pork, tofu and cabbage, pan-fried until crisp underneath and steamed until tender, with a vinegar-soy dip and soft simmered kabocha (or buttercup squash). It is a fun weekend project. The **tofu keeps the filling tender** and adds a little calcium.
steps: Cook the brown rice and barley (see the breakfast tip). This recipe makes two portions.
Scrub and rinse the kabocha. Simmer the chunks in a small covered pot with 100 ml of water and a splash of the soy sauce for 12 minutes, until tender but not falling apart.

Squeeze the tofu in a clean cloth until crumbly. Mix the pork, tofu, cabbage, scallion, ginger, garlic and half the soy sauce by hand until sticky. Fry a small spoonful and taste to check the seasoning.

Put a heaped teaspoon of filling in the middle of each wrapper, wet the edge, and fold and pleat to seal. If filling is left when the wrappers run out, shape it into small flat patties and fry them in the pan with the gyoza. Wash your hands and board when the gyoza are folded.

Heat the canola oil in a non-stick pan with a lid. Arrange the gyoza flat side down and fry for 2 minutes, until golden underneath. Add 80 ml of water, cover and steam over medium heat for 6 minutes, then uncover and cook until the water is gone. Cut one open, and a patty if you made them, to check: the pork must reach 71 °C with no pink.
Mix the vinegar and the rest of the soy sauce for the dip.
